rules.name: rank_based_averaging_for_diverse_calibrations
rules.context: When ensembling models with different architectures and training procedures whose raw probability outputs may be on different calibration scales.
rules.action: Convert each model's predictions to ranks (argsort of argsort) before weighted averaging. Keep the same weights initially to isolate the method change effect. If it matches or beats probability averaging, re-tune weights under the rank-based method. Apply a single rank transform at the end rather than ranking each component independently before blending.
rules.exceptions: Initial rank-based result may only tie probability-based; advantage appears after re-tuning weights (15164527:e4#2). For single-model inference, rank blending can be neutral or harmful (7018718:e2#2).

rules.name: do_not_change_members_and_weights_simultaneously
rules.context: When modifying an ensemble by both changing which models are included and switching the aggregation method (e.g., weighted to mean) at the same time.
rules.action: Change only one thing at a time: either the member set or the weighting scheme, not both. Changing both simultaneously confounds diagnosis of what caused any score change. If you want to simplify to equal weights, first verify all remaining members have similar standalone quality.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: blend_strategy_not_bottleneck_when_scores_close
rules.context: When trying multiple blend strategies (rank, sigmoid, mean) on the same fold ensemble and all yield scores within ~0.001 of each other.
rules.action: Stop iterating on blend strategy and move on to improving individual model quality, adding model diversity, or checkpoint selection. The blend method is not the bottleneck. Never remove fold models to test blend strategies; removing folds degrades the ensemble substantially.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: ensemble_models_before_tta
rules.context: When working with a single strong model and flip TTA shows negligible improvement (e.g., <0.001% gain).
rules.action: Pivot to ensembling multiple independently trained models rather than investing in TTA variants. Multi-model ensembling typically yields 5-50x larger gains than single-model TTA. Reserve TTA effort for after the ensemble baseline is established, where TTA can be applied on top of each ensemble member.
rules.exceptions: TTA may still help when combined with ensembles; the single-model ablation result doesn't fully generalize (15372370:e2#2).

rules.name: prefer_coarse_weights_over_cv_optimized
rules.context: When CV-optimized or fine-grained per-component blend weights produce worse leaderboard scores than simpler uniform or grouped weights, especially when the test set is small or noisy.
rules.action: Prefer coarse, grouped, or near-uniform weights over individually optimized per-fold/per-component weights. Fine-grained CV-optimized weights tend to overfit the validation split. When CV and LB disagree on blend weights, prefer weights closer to uniform or the last LB-validated configuration rather than aggressively trusting CV. Extreme weight skew (nearly zeroing out a model) risks losing diversity.
rules.exceptions: Per-fold blending with OOF optimization can work when the training set is large enough to support reliable per-fold weight estimation (17616127:e23#2).

rules.name: sweep_blend_weight_for_two_model_ensemble
rules.context: When blending exactly two models (e.g., LightGBM + XGBoost, or NN + GBDT) with a single scalar weight parameter.
rules.action: Sweep the dominant model's weight in steps of 0.05-0.10 across [0.5, 0.9]. Use OOF/CV to pre-screen, then confirm on LB. Narrow to 0.01 steps around the best region. Stop when three consecutive points bracket the optimum and further gains are < 0.001. Make the blend weight a configurable parameter with a sensible default.
rules.exceptions: When the public LB is very small (e.g., ~7 rows), weight differences are noisy and membership changes may be more informative than fine-grained weight tuning (18426209:e5#2).

rules.name: weight_strongest_model_highest_in_blend
rules.context: When blending 2-4 models of varying standalone quality (measured by validation or LB scores).
rules.action: Assign the highest blend weight (≥0.5) to the model with the best standalone performance. Give equal smaller weights to remaining models. Start with a simple ratio (e.g., 0.5/0.25/0.25 for three models) rather than equal weighting. Increase the best model's share in ~0.1 steps up to about 0.5-0.6 but do not exceed 0.6 for a single model in a multi-way blend, as diminishing diversity causes regression. When the quality gap is very large (>10% relative), assign weights roughly proportional to model quality (inversely proportional to error), giving weak models small weights (e.g., 0.1) and strong models large weights (e.g., 0.4+). If the weaker model doesn't improve the blend even at low weight, remove it entirely rather than continuing to tune.
rules.exceptions: If models are highly correlated, even 0.5 for the strongest may be too high for the weaker ones to contribute meaningfully. When the quality gap is very large (>30%), even a small weight for the weaker model may add noise; test the stronger model alone first (49524919:e15#1).

rules.name: drop_weak_model_rather_than_tune_weight
rules.context: When a substantially weaker model (by standalone score) is added to an ensemble with a small weight and the blend does not improve, or when sweeping weights across a wide range fails to recover baseline performance.
rules.action: Stop tuning the weak model's weight and either remove it or retrain/replace it with a better checkpoint. Blend weights cannot compensate for a poorly calibrated or fundamentally weak model. Diversity from a much weaker model rarely compensates for its noise.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: prefer_membership_changes_over_weight_tuning_small_lb
rules.context: When the public leaderboard is very small (few evaluation rows) and weight tuning gives noisy signal, or when multiple weight configurations score within noise range of each other.
rules.action: Prefer discrete membership changes (add/remove a model) over fine-grained weight tuning. Use equal weights for remaining members as a default. A single submission suffices to evaluate each membership change. When the blend surface is flat near the optimum, stop tuning coefficients and switch to improving individual component models.
rules.exceptions: When OOF predictions are available for cheap local evaluation, weight tuning can still be productive even with a small LB.

rules.name: allow_negative_blend_weights_for_diverse_models
rules.context: When a weighted ensemble with positive-only normalized weights underperforms a Ridge/linear meta-learner, or when base models are diverse (different algorithms, different target transforms).
rules.action: Expand the weight search range to include negative values (e.g., [-1, 1]) and remove the sum-to-one normalization constraint. This lets the optimizer subtract overconfident or biased base models. Validate on OOF before submitting. If this still underperforms Ridge, the meta-learner's regularization is providing additional value beyond signed weights.
rules.exceptions: Negative weights can cause instability or overfitting to validation folds; even with negative weights allowed, Ridge stacking may still outperform due to regularization (73937748:e16#2).

rules.name: normalize_weights_after_membership_change
rules.context: When ensemble members have been added or removed and hardcoded per-model weights are stale or no longer sum to 1.0.
rules.action: After any change to ensemble membership, add a guard that checks whether weights sum to 1.0; if not, automatically assign equal weights (1/N). This prevents silent score degradation from unnormalized blends. Fix any assertion bugs checking the sum at the same time.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: verify_weaker_modality_helps_before_equal_blend
rules.context: When ensembling models from different input modalities (e.g., raw signal vs. spectrogram, or different feature types) where one modality is substantially stronger by standalone score.
rules.action: Do not default to equal-weight averaging. Either weight by standalone performance or verify on validation that the weaker modality actually improves the blend before submitting. If equal-weight blending degrades the stronger model's score, reduce the weaker modality's weight or remove it.
rules.exceptions: Multimodal blending can still help if the weaker modality provides complementary signal; the next version in 52551258 did improve with a multimodal approach.

rules.name: double_minority_weight_as_first_probe
rules.context: When the current blend weight for a minority component is small (e.g., 0.15-0.20) and you suspect that component has improved or is underweighted.
rules.action: Double the minority component's weight as a first probe (e.g., 0.15→0.30). If this improves the score, continue increasing or do a finer search around the new value. If it regresses, halve the step and try an intermediate value. Keep other ensemble components fixed during this search.
rules.exceptions: The improvement may be within noise; the author in 77450317 reverted to the original weight in a later version, suggesting the gain wasn't robust.

rules.name: equal_weights_for_similar_models
rules.context: When ensembling models of the same architecture or similar individual validation/LB scores (within ~1-2% relative), and you lack strong CV evidence favoring unequal weights.
rules.action: Start with equal-weight averaging. Unequal weights rarely help when models have similar quality. If you try unequal weights and they don't improve over equal weights, revert to equal weighting rather than continuing to search.
rules.exceptions: When models differ substantially in quality (>5-10% relative gap), score-proportional weighting outperforms equal weights (see 50496431:e46#2).

rules.name: test_new_member_solo_before_blending
rules.context: When adding a new model or model family to an existing ensemble and leaderboard submissions are limited.
rules.action: First submit the new model alone (weight=1.0) to establish its standalone LB score. Then blend it with existing members, giving it an initial weight informed by its solo score relative to others. This isolates whether the new member adds value before confounding with weight tuning.
rules.exceptions: 52860091 notes the author didn't always follow isolation-first strictly, sometimes testing blends before solo evaluation.

rules.name: remove_weakest_and_concentrate_weight
rules.context: When you have 3+ blend components and suspect one is dragging down the ensemble, especially when single-model tuning has plateaued.
rules.action: Remove the weakest component and shift its weight primarily to the strongest remaining component (not split evenly among survivors). Submit to verify improvement. If improved, keep the simpler blend. Fewer well-weighted components often outperform a broader but diluted blend.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: partial_revert_on_weight_regression
rules.context: When a weight change of ~0.10-0.20 in an ensemble causes a score regression compared to the previous best configuration.
rules.action: Partially revert the change rather than fully reverting: split the difference between the failed configuration and the previous best. Then probe nearby configurations with smaller steps (~0.05). This narrows the search without discarding the directional hypothesis entirely.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: sweep_blend_weight_one_knob_at_a_time
rules.context: When tuning blend weights between 2-3 models using leaderboard feedback, especially when the LB signal is noisy.
rules.action: Vary only one weight parameter per submission so you can attribute score changes. Sweep in steps of ~0.05 across the plausible range. Once the score drops on both sides of a candidate optimum, bracket it and confirm. Do not combine multiple knob changes in one submission.
rules.exceptions: 55987255:e29#1 notes the author sometimes did full sweeps rather than hill-climbing, and noisy LB (±0.005) made single-point feedback unreliable.

rules.name: retune_weights_after_member_change
rules.context: When any single ensemble member's predictions change substantially (due to bug fix, retraining, architecture swap, or version upgrade).
rules.action: Re-run blend weight optimization on validation data and submit. Previously optimized weights are stale when a member changes. Exception: for minor incremental version upgrades of the same model, try keeping weights fixed first—if the score improves, retuning is unnecessary.
rules.exceptions: 77450317:e11#3 shows that for nearby incremental versions, fixed coefficients may still be adequate.

rules.name: ablate_components_one_at_a_time
rules.context: When an ensemble or pipeline has multiple components (models, feature groups, preprocessing variants) and you want to understand which contribute value.
rules.action: Do not remove or change multiple components simultaneously. Instead, establish a full-pipeline baseline, then ablate one component at a time (single models from ensemble, or one feature group). Rank components by their standalone quality or by the drop when removed. Expect single-component scores to be substantially worse than the ensemble; use ablation for ranking/pruning but return to the full ensemble for final submission.
rules.exceptions: When features are grouped by variant (e.g., all _ppr features), pruning entire groups is acceptable as a single ablation step (55987255:e5#1). Removing too many features at once can confound the signal.

rules.name: retain_handcrafted_features_alongside_transformers
rules.context: When a pipeline combines transformer predictions with handcrafted features (TF-IDF, linguistic metrics) fed into a gradient boosting model, and you suspect the transformer captures most signal.
rules.action: Do not drop handcrafted features without first measuring the transformer-only baseline. If the transformer-only score is substantially lower, the handcrafted features carry unique signal and should be retained. In text/essay tasks, TF-IDF and linguistic features typically complement transformer predictions. Re-add feature groups incrementally to confirm their contribution.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: diversify_ensemble_via_input_variation
rules.context: When an ensemble's members are correlated (same architecture family or similar feature sets) and weighting/pruning existing members does not improve scores.
rules.action: Instead of optimizing weights among existing members, add diversity by running the same model architecture on different input representations (e.g., raw features vs engineered features, different preprocessing variants). Include both variants as separate ensemble members and let a meta-learner (e.g., Ridge) weight them. If uniform weighting and member pruning both fail, the ensemble needs more diversity rather than better weighting.
rules.exceptions: Uniform weighting performed worst when models had meaningfully different quality (18523075:e3#2), so diversity addition is preferred over naive equal weighting.

rules.name: match_backbone_to_checkpoint_weights
rules.context: When swapping a CNN or transformer backbone variant at inference time while loading pretrained/fine-tuned checkpoint weights trained with a different architecture.
rules.action: Never change the backbone architecture without matching checkpoint weights. Use strict=True weight loading to catch key mismatches immediately. If you want to try a different backbone, train new weights for it first. Mismatched architecture+weights cause silent partial loading and catastrophic performance drops (e.g., 0.389→0.572, or base weights with large config).
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: swap_backbone_before_abandoning_simpler_head
rules.context: When simplifying the model head (e.g., multi-head → single-head) causes a performance regression on the same backbone.
rules.action: Try pairing the simplified head with a stronger or different backbone before reverting the head change. The backbone may be the binding constraint rather than the head design. Evaluate backbone swaps (e.g., resnext50→RegNetY032) before abandoning the simpler architecture.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: domain_pretrained_larger_backbone_for_plateau
rules.context: When incremental tuning (augmentation, postprocessing, hyperparameters) of the current backbone has plateaued and a larger backbone with domain-specific or intermediate-task pretraining is available.
rules.action: Replace the backbone with a larger architecture initialized from domain-specific or intermediate-task pretrained weights. Adjust image size or input dimensions to match the new backbone's expected resolution. Re-optimize post-processing (e.g., rounding thresholds) since prediction distributions shift. Expect a step-function improvement rather than incremental gain.
rules.exceptions: Earlier attempts with large backbone without domain/ITPT pretraining (v47-v49 in 55621328) performed worse than base, suggesting large alone isn't sufficient—specialized pretraining is the key differentiator.

rules.name: isolate_backbone_swap_in_ensemble
rules.context: When introducing a new or larger backbone into a mature ensemble or pipeline that is already well-tuned.
rules.action: Change only the backbone/model component in the first submission—do not simultaneously change preprocessing, post-processing, or other model classes. If the new backbone regresses, revert immediately rather than tuning it in-place. Try a different improvement axis (e.g., preprocessing, augmentation) instead of continuing to sweep backbones.
rules.exceptions: 50496431:e47#2 notes that simultaneous changes made it hard to isolate the cause of regression.

rules.name: larger_backbone_needs_batch_size_and_head_adjustment
rules.context: When substituting a significantly larger backbone variant (e.g., B5→B7, base→large) into an existing inference or training pipeline.
rules.action: Update the classifier head's input dimension to match the new backbone's feature size. Halve the batch size to avoid OOM on limited GPU memory. Use strict=True weight loading. Verify locally that loading succeeds and dimensions match before submitting.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: test_model_sizes_with_fixed_postprocessing
rules.context: When trained checkpoints at multiple backbone sizes (small/base/large) are available and you want to identify which size works best.
rules.action: Test each size individually with the same post-processing and ensemble structure to avoid confounding. Keep rounding/post-processing fixed while varying size. If a larger model underperforms, try adding more folds or a newer training run before abandoning it. Limit to 2-3 submissions per size before concluding.
rules.exceptions: 55621328:e17#1 counter-evidence: post-episode v52 showed large eventually beat base with a different checkpoint, so abandoning a size after 2-3 tries may be premature if new training runs become available.

rules.name: diversity_over_scaling_in_ensembles
rules.context: When upgrading all ensemble members from base to large variants of the same architecture regresses or fails to improve the ensemble score.
rules.action: Revert to the best-performing size and instead add architecturally diverse models (different model families, e.g., ALBERT alongside RoBERTa, or EfficientNet alongside ViT) to the blend. Diversity across architectures typically helps more than uniformly scaling a single architecture in an ensemble.
rules.exceptions: 17616127:e7#2 notes the regression could be due to mismatched ridge artifacts rather than backbone size per se.

rules.name: prefer_well_tuned_smaller_backbone_over_early_larger
rules.context: When comparing a well-tuned smaller backbone against a larger or different backbone at an early checkpoint version (v1.0 or first training run).
rules.action: Prefer the well-tuned smaller backbone unless the larger alternative shows competitive performance even at its early stage. A larger backbone at v1.0 that already underperforms a mature smaller model is unlikely to catch up without significant additional tuning. Move on to other improvement levers.
rules.exceptions: 55621328:e17#1 shows that a later training run of the larger model can eventually surpass the smaller one, so this rule applies mainly when no further training budget is available.

rules.name: align_all_dimensions_when_swapping_model_components
rules.context: When switching a model backbone size (e.g., base→large) or loading a custom checkpoint that was trained with a modified architecture (e.g., expanded tokenizer vocab, different hidden dims).
rules.action: Update all dependent components simultaneously: (1) model config parameters (hidden_size, vocab_size), (2) checkpoint/tokenizer paths, (3) all custom head layer dimensions. For expanded tokenizers, call resize_token_embeddings(len(tokenizer)) and pass correct vocab_size in config. For custom checkpoints, set pretrained=False before loading weights. Verify file existence and dimension consistency before running.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: regenerate_derived_artifacts_after_renaming
rules.context: When a feature engineering pipeline dynamically generates column names and a precomputed artifact (e.g., pickled feature-selection list, aggregation aliases) references old names after a rename or refactor.
rules.action: Regenerate the derived artifact (feature-selection list, config) rather than loading a stale version. Assert that all names in the loaded list exist in the current DataFrame. Print lengths and sample names immediately after loading to catch mismatches before training.
rules.exceptions: These two items are from the same kernel; however, they address distinct manifestations (stale pickle vs exhausted file handle) of the same pattern of reusing a consumed/outdated data source.

rules.name: use_unique_variable_names_for_chained_models
rules.context: When an inference pipeline chains multiple ML models (e.g., embedding model, topic model, prediction model) and generic variable names like 'model' are reused, or when mixing Python types (list vs numpy array) in arithmetic expressions.
rules.action: Give each model and each prediction array a unique descriptive variable name. For prediction blending, wrap every component in np.array() before arithmetic. Verify that prediction calls reference the correct feature dataframe by checking variable names match between training and inference. Fix naming and type issues before tuning.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: use_all_fold_checkpoints_in_ensemble
rules.context: When you have K-fold trained checkpoints available for inference and inference time/memory is not a hard constraint.
rules.action: Default to ensembling all available fold checkpoints with equal weights rather than using a single fold. Periodically probe a single-model submission to confirm the ensemble still helps. Only reduce fold count if inference resources are binding. Multi-fold averaging reduces variance and typically outperforms single-fold or reduced-fold submissions.
rules.exceptions: 50376011:e9#1 showed fold-averaged score within one config did not beat ensembling across different configs, suggesting fold averaging within a single config may be less valuable than cross-config diversity.

rules.name: sweep_checkpoint_versions_sequentially
rules.context: When you have multiple sequentially-trained checkpoint versions with similar CV scores and need to find the best one for a fixed inference pipeline.
rules.action: Sweep checkpoint versions in order, submitting each to the leaderboard while holding all other settings fixed. Track LB scores alongside offline validation metrics. Do not revert on a single regression since LB noise can mask true improvements. After covering the range, select the version with the best LB score. If 3+ consecutive versions regress, consider pivoting to a different lever (e.g., ensembling diverse architectures).
rules.exceptions: 49524919:e16#1 showed that persisting past regressions paid off (v64 regressed but later versions recovered), while 49524919:e12#2 suggests stopping after consecutive regressions. The right threshold depends on how noisy the LB is.

rules.name: select_best_validation_checkpoint_per_fold
rules.context: When checkpoint filenames encode per-fold validation metrics and you want to pick the best checkpoint set for inference.
rules.action: For each fold, compare available checkpoint filenames and pick the one with the best validation metric. Submit once to confirm the gain. Expect only marginal improvement (<0.001) when good checkpoints are already in use. If the improvement is negligible, move on to a different lever such as adding a new model family.
rules.exceptions: 49524919:e33#2 showed that checkpoints with better per-fold validation scores yielded a worse LB score (v150), indicating validation metrics don't always transfer to public LB.

rules.name: swap_one_fold_checkpoint_at_a_time
rules.context: When you have multiple training runs per fold producing different checkpoint variants and want to find the best ensemble composition.
rules.action: Track which checkpoint variant is used per fold in a table alongside LB scores. When swapping checkpoints, change only one fold at a time and record the delta. If a swap regresses, revert immediately. Do not combine checkpoint swaps with postprocessing or preprocessing changes in the same submission.
rules.exceptions: 53424936:e10#1 swapped all fold checkpoints simultaneously to isolate training config changes from pipeline changes, which is appropriate when the goal is to test a new training run rather than mix-and-match across runs.

rules.name: match_preprocessing_to_checkpoint
rules.context: When loading a new model checkpoint that was trained with different preprocessing, data transforms, or output heads than the previous checkpoint.
rules.action: Always update the inference preprocessing pipeline to match the training config of the new checkpoint (normalization, cropping, resizing, fill strategy, output activation). Co-vary all transforms with the checkpoint. Never mix a checkpoint with preprocessing from a different training version—this causes silent regression.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: prefer_best_validated_over_last_checkpoint_in_multistage
rules.context: When a multi-stage training pipeline (e.g., pretrain then fine-tune) produces multiple checkpoint types: best-validation, last-epoch, and stage-specific variants.
rules.action: Start with the 'best' checkpoint selected by validation metric across all stages, as it typically generalizes best. 'Last' checkpoints from the final stage tend to overfit to the fine-tuning distribution. If a single later stage consistently beats the multi-stage average, prefer it over averaging stages. Test each variant individually before committing.
rules.exceptions: 49576186:e27#2 showed single stage-3 beat multi-stage averaging, suggesting later-stage checkpoints can be best when the fine-tuning distribution matches the test distribution well.

rules.name: include_diverse_checkpoint_variants_in_ensemble
rules.context: When you have multiple checkpoint variants (e.g., early-stop vs final epoch, different seeds, different training configs) that score comparably but neither dominates.
rules.action: Rather than selecting the single best checkpoint variant, include predictions from all available variants in the ensemble average. This adds diversity at low cost since the architecture is already loaded. Also prefer selecting ensemble members spaced across different training runs or configurations rather than consecutive folds from one run.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: avoid_bundling_checkpoint_swap_with_pipeline_restructure
rules.context: When you want to both swap a pretrained checkpoint and restructure the pipeline (new loss, new ensemble method, code reorganization) in a single submission.
rules.action: Change the checkpoint first, verify its effect in isolation, then layer on pipeline changes incrementally. If you bundle changes and the score regresses, you cannot attribute the cause. If you must bundle, be prepared to decompose and test individually to diagnose the regression.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: single_checkpoint_toggle_for_pipeline_validation
rules.context: When you have a new inference pipeline and need to quickly verify it works correctly before full optimization.
rules.action: Cycle through 2-3 known-good individual checkpoints and a small ensemble. If scores are in the same ballpark as the old pipeline, the new infrastructure is validated. If all checkpoints regress substantially, debug the pipeline rather than the model selection.
rules.exceptions: Scores may fluctuate significantly across checkpoint swaps, making it hard to distinguish pipeline quality from checkpoint variance. Use multiple checkpoints to average out this noise.

rules.name: trust_offline_cv_over_tiny_public_lb
rules.context: When offline cross-validation loss and public leaderboard scores disagree, and the public test set is very small or noisy.
rules.action: Trust offline cross-validation loss for checkpoint selection over a tiny public leaderboard. If you must use the LB, submit each checkpoint once, record scores, then build an ensemble of the top-k rather than picking the single best LB scorer. Do not iterate many single-checkpoint submissions—the noise makes the signal unreliable.
rules.exceptions: 17616127:e1#2 showed the best offline checkpoint did not produce the best single-model LB score, so offline and LB can diverge even directionally on small test sets.

rules.name: match_inference_config_to_checkpoint_training
rules.context: When swapping a model checkpoint that was trained with different hyperparameters (dropout, preprocessing, tokenizer) than the current inference configuration.
rules.action: Update inference-time architecture settings (dropout rate, preprocessing flags, tokenizer) to match the training configuration of the new checkpoint. A mismatch silently degrades predictions. If you don't know the training config, test without preprocessing first, then with it.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: stop_checkpoint_shopping_after_diminishing_returns
rules.context: When swapping checkpoint versions of the same architecture yields inconsistent or diminishing leaderboard improvements after 3+ attempts.
rules.action: Stop iterating on checkpoint selection within the same architecture. Instead, add a new diverse model/architecture to the ensemble or move to ensembling the top 2-3 checkpoints already found. The marginal gain from within-architecture checkpoint selection is small compared to architectural diversity or ensembling.
rules.exceptions: If intermediate/adjacent checkpoint indices remain untested (50376011:e41#2), trying those may still yield gains before giving up.

rules.name: select_best_validation_checkpoint_per_fold_independently
rules.context: When training produces multiple checkpoints per fold with validation metrics available (e.g., encoded in filenames).
rules.action: Select the checkpoint with the best validation metric for each fold independently, even if the selected epochs vary widely across folds. Do not force uniform epoch selection. Use validation scores in filenames to filter; only include checkpoints with competitive fold-level scores. Expect LB improvement to be smaller than CV improvement due to distribution shift.
rules.exceptions: When CV and LB are poorly correlated (49524919:e17#3), fold-level CV selection may not translate to LB gains.

rules.name: sweep_individual_checkpoints_before_ensembling
rules.context: When you have K fold checkpoints or multiple trained model indices and want to build an ensemble.
rules.action: Test each checkpoint individually on the leaderboard first. Run each at least 2-3 times to account for noise. Rank them by score, identify the top 1-2, then build ensembles starting from those. A weak checkpoint can hurt a small ensemble. Do not assume all folds/indices contribute equally.
rules.exceptions: At larger ensemble scales (many diverse models), individual checkpoint quality matters less than diversity (50376011:e26#2 counter_evidence).

rules.name: test_one_variable_at_a_time_when_swapping_checkpoints
rules.context: When switching to a new checkpoint and simultaneously changing other settings (ensemble composition, post-processing, dropout).
rules.action: Change only the checkpoint path while keeping all other settings (ensemble membership, post-processing, architecture config) identical. This isolates the checkpoint's effect. If you must change multiple things, at least write per-model submission files so you can attribute score changes to individual components.
rules.exceptions: During ablation probing (49524919:e34#2), simultaneously swapping checkpoints while probing individual groups can be efficient if the blend is restored afterward.

rules.name: revert_on_large_regression_from_new_checkpoint
rules.context: When a new checkpoint/experiment variant scores much worse (>1% absolute) than the current best on the leaderboard.
rules.action: Treat the large regression as a signal the variant is fundamentally weaker. Revert to the known-best checkpoint set rather than debugging the new variant. If after 2-3 attempts the new architecture/checkpoint still underperforms, abandon it. Reserve the new approach for future investigation but don't block progress.
rules.exceptions: The regression may be due to config mismatch rather than model quality; verify architecture/tokenizer match before fully abandoning (55621328:e38#2 counter_evidence).

rules.name: test_checkpoint_families_homogeneously_then_mix
rules.context: When you have multiple checkpoint families from different training runs/configurations and want to find the best ensemble composition.
rules.action: First test each checkpoint family as a homogeneous ensemble (all folds from one family). If none beats the baseline, try mixing families. Also vary ensemble size (more folds vs. selected subset). If no variant beats the baseline after exhaustive sweep, move to blending or weighting strategies rather than continuing pure checkpoint swapping.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: evaluate_raw_predictions_before_applying_postprocessing
rules.context: When post-processing (binning, rounding, discretization) accounts for a large fraction of total score improvement and you are comparing candidate checkpoints.
rules.action: Evaluate candidate checkpoints without post-processing first to compare raw prediction quality. Pick the checkpoint with the best raw score, then re-tune post-processing on top of it. Do not compare checkpoints using post-processing tuned to a different checkpoint's output distribution.
rules.exceptions: When raw score differences between checkpoints are within noise (~0.01), the selection signal may be unreliable (7018718:e12#2 counter_evidence).

rules.name: try_adjacent_checkpoint_indices
rules.context: When you have exhausted evenly-spaced checkpoint indices (e.g., 0, 4, 8, 12) and the best index is identified.
rules.action: Try adjacent/intermediate indices near the best-performing one (e.g., index 1 next to index 0). These may capture different fold splits or training states and can yield surprising improvements that evenly-spaced sampling misses.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: ensemble_after_single_checkpoint_plateau
rules.context: When individual checkpoint scores have plateaued and the best single-model option has been identified through sweeping.
rules.action: Average predicted probability distributions from the top 2-3 diverse checkpoints (different architectures, hyperparameters, or training variants) and re-normalize. This typically yields a larger gain than further single-checkpoint search. Prefer diversity in architecture over diversity in seeds.
rules.exceptions: Adding too many checkpoints to an embedding-based pipeline can add noise or cause memory issues; add 1-2 at a time (55987255:e16#2).

rules.name: add_transformer_checkpoints_incrementally_to_ensemble
rules.context: When expanding a transformer checkpoint ensemble (for embeddings or predictions) and compute/memory is constrained.
rules.action: Add at most 1-2 new checkpoints at a time and submit. If the score drops, the additional checkpoints likely add noise or cause memory/precision issues. Prune back to the known-good set rather than continuing to add. Prefer checkpoints from the same model family as existing good ones over diverse but untested architectures.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: revalidate_postprocessing_after_ensemble_change
rules.context: You have rank-based or discretization post-processing applied to predictions, and you have just made a significant change to the ensemble (added/removed models, changed blend weights).
rules.action: Re-validate the post-processing contribution by running ablations (with and without) after each major ensemble change. Do not assume prior post-processing gains carry over. For rank-based metrics (e.g., Spearman), expect discretization/scaling post-processing to often still help, but confirm empirically before keeping it.
rules.exceptions: 17616127:e31#2 shows that confidence-based postprocessing from an auxiliary classifier was abandoned without submission, suggesting complex post-processing may not survive ablation even when simpler forms do.

rules.name: metadata_rule_override_for_specific_targets
rules.context: A specific target column has a near-deterministic relationship with observable metadata (e.g., URL domain, category) that the model does not see as input, and the evaluation metric is rank-based.
rules.action: Override or nudge the model's prediction for that column using a heuristic derived from the metadata. Prefer metadata-based indicators (URL, site domain) over content-based ones (keywords, character patterns) because they are more reliable. Use a moderate weight (e.g., 0.5) rather than a full override, and tune via leaderboard feedback.
rules.exceptions: Content-based indicators (e.g., phonetic characters) can hurt the score (v55 in 6803050), reinforcing the preference for metadata-based signals. Limited to cases where the metadata-target relationship is strong and the model genuinely misses the signal.

rules.name: custom_ranking_for_rank_based_metrics
rules.context: The competition metric depends only on prediction ranks (e.g., concordance index, Spearman correlation), and you need post-processing that is either faster or supports custom tie-breaking/group-aware logic not available in generic libraries.
rules.action: Replace generic ranking utilities (e.g., scipy rankdata) with a custom implementation (e.g., numba JIT-compiled ranker) that supports metric-aligned tie-breaking or group-aware ranking. Validate equivalence with the generic method on local CV before submitting to ensure correctness.
rules.exceptions: Gains from custom ranking may be modest (e.g., +0.00058 in 75924487) and may not persist across subsequent versions, suggesting the benefit is sometimes from ensemble selection rather than the ranking mechanism itself.

rules.name: moderate_fold_count_for_tree_ensembles
rules.context: When using tree-based ensembles (LightGBM/XGBoost/CatBoost) on a moderately-sized tabular dataset (~10K-30K samples) and averaging predictions across all fold models, and you need to choose the number of CV folds.
rules.action: Start with a moderate fold count (10-15). If reducing to 5 hurts, the ensemble averaging benefit dominates. If increasing to 20+ also hurts, per-fold validation sets are too small or models overfit. Bracket the optimum with 2-3 trials. For ~17K samples, 15 folds consistently outperformed both 5 and 20 in multiple experiments.
rules.exceptions: Fold count changes were sometimes confounded with other hyperparameter changes, so isolated attribution is uncertain. When iteration speed matters, use fewer folds (e.g., 5) during exploration and restore higher count for final submission (73937748:e3#2).

rules.name: increase_folds_on_small_datasets_for_deep_models
rules.context: When fine-tuning a deep model (BERT, NN) on a small dataset (<10K samples) and hyperparameter tuning gains have plateaued.
rules.action: Increase the number of CV folds (e.g., 10→15 or 5→10) to give each fold model more training data and produce a larger ensemble. On small datasets, the marginal training examples from higher fold counts matter more. Expect meaningful gains when per-fold training set size was previously a bottleneck.
rules.exceptions: For simple models (Ridge/BoW) on small data, fewer folds (3-5) may win because training set size gain outweighs ensemble diversity loss (7676170:e6#3).

rules.name: curate_base_model_subset_for_meta_learner
rules.context: When a stacking meta-learner (Ridge, AutoGluon, SVR) has access to many base-model prediction columns, some of which may be noisy or redundant.
rules.action: Curate a subset of base-model predictions rather than passing all available columns. Examine per-model OOF performance and inter-model correlation. Drop members that are both weak individually and highly correlated with stronger members. Apply the filter before the ensembler trains. Use a feature-selection file specifically computed for each combination when adding new transformer embeddings. Validate by toggling the filter off; if LB drops, keep the filter.
rules.exceptions: The benefit may be marginal (~0.001) and dataset-dependent (75924487). 75924487:e1#1 notes the improvement was barely above noise (+0.00003), suggesting curation benefits may be small when the ensembler already handles redundancy.

rules.name: measure_marginal_contribution_before_removing_ensemble_member
rules.context: When considering removing a sub-model from an ensemble to simplify the pipeline or reduce complexity.
rules.action: Before removing, measure its marginal contribution by comparing ensemble scores with and without it on validation data. Do not bundle the removal with other changes (e.g., changing training setup). Removing a diverse model that contributes even modestly typically hurts, especially in rank-averaged ensembles.
rules.exceptions: If the member's toggle effect is consistently within noise (≤0.0002), it can be safely removed (75145694:e7#2).

rules.name: expand_ensemble_then_optimize_weights
rules.context: When uniform-weight ensemble gains plateau as more models are added, but individual members still contribute positively.
rules.action: First expand the ensemble with uniform weights until gains diminish. Then fix the model set and optimize per-model blend weights offline on validation predictions. Finally, test whether adding back excluded models with new optimized weights helps. If the larger weighted set regresses, keep the smaller optimized set.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: shift_from_adding_models_to_improving_existing_when_saturated
rules.context: When the ensemble already spans multiple model families and multiple target transforms/configurations, and adding new variants of existing families produces no measurable gain.
rules.action: Stop appending marginal model variants. Shift effort to improving individual strong models (architecture, hyperparameters), improving the meta-learner, or optimizing blend weights rather than adding more base models.
rules.exceptions: Adding a genuinely new model family (e.g., NN when only GBDTs exist) can still produce meaningful jumps even at late stages.

rules.name: swap_one_component_at_a_time
rules.context: When you have multiple candidate prediction arrays or model checkpoints for an ensemble and blend weights are already set, and you want to identify which component helps or hurts.
rules.action: Hold the blend structure fixed and swap one component at a time, submitting each swap. If the new component improves the score, keep it; otherwise revert. This isolates each member's marginal contribution on a noisy leaderboard. Avoid changing multiple axes (members + weights) simultaneously.
rules.exceptions: 50496431:e50#2 notes the author sometimes changed both axes simultaneously, which occasionally worked but also failed catastrophically, reinforcing the one-at-a-time rule as safer.

rules.name: revert_weak_ensemble_member_immediately
rules.context: When a newly added model degrades the ensemble score on the leaderboard, especially if it shares the same backbone family as existing members or scores substantially worse standalone.
rules.action: Immediately disable the new member and revert to the previous best configuration. Before re-attempting, compare the candidate's standalone score to existing members. If it is worse than all current members and uses the same architecture family, it likely adds noise rather than diversity. Try a model from a different architecture or with different pooling/features instead.
rules.exceptions: 50376011:e4#2 notes that individual scores alone may not predict ensemble contribution well—a model with a weak solo score can still help if it captures different error patterns (see 49524919:e20#2 where ConvNeXt solo was worse but improved the blend).

rules.name: maximize_architectural_diversity_across_axes
rules.context: When the ensemble is dominated by one model family, one pooling strategy, or one input representation, and you want to reduce ensemble correlation.
rules.action: Add models that differ from existing members on at least two axes: backbone architecture (e.g., CNN vs ViT vs pure convolution), input format (e.g., spectrograms vs raw signals vs different resolutions), and head/pooling strategy (e.g., attention pooling vs mean pooling vs multi-layer concat). Test each new model solo first, then add to the blend. Even individually weaker models can improve the ensemble if they capture complementary patterns.
rules.exceptions: 18837555:e2#1 showed slight regression when adding a multi-layer attention model, suggesting diversity alone doesn't guarantee improvement—the new member must be reasonably strong.

rules.name: prefer_larger_model_in_ensemble_slot
rules.context: When you have trained checkpoints at multiple model sizes (e.g., base vs large) and the task metric is regression or ordinal scoring, and inference memory allows the larger model.
rules.action: Prefer the largest model that fits in inference memory. Add diversity via multiple fold checkpoints or seed runs of the large model rather than switching to a smaller model. If a smaller model is tried and scores lower, immediately revert to the larger model ensemble.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: expand_ensemble_aggressively_then_prune
rules.context: When prior experiments show monotonic improvement from adding ensemble members and you have many available diverse checkpoints (different folds, seeds, or architectures).
rules.action: Expand the ensemble to include all available diverse checkpoints in one step. If that yields a large gain, then try removing individual members one at a time to find the best composition. Stop when single-member removals yield negligible improvement. If runtime is too long, selectively prune weaker members.
rules.exceptions: 50376011:e33#1 notes that earlier in history, reducing from 2 to 1 model actually improved the score, so more members isn't always better—it depends on member quality. 50376011:e5#2 notes diminishing returns after 4 models.

rules.name: add_ensemble_members_in_small_batches
rules.context: When expanding an ensemble pool with many new candidate members and the score regresses after a large batch addition.
rules.action: Add members in small batches (1-3 at a time) and check CV/LB after each batch. If a large batch causes regression, bisect to find harmful members rather than assuming all new members are bad. Ensure artifact paths and preprocessing are consistent before interpreting score changes as signals about member quality.
rules.exceptions: 73671444:e10#1 shows that swapping out weakest contributors (rather than full revert) can recover from regression.

rules.name: revert_auxiliary_features_on_small_datasets
rules.context: When adding handcrafted text-statistic features or auxiliary features to a stacking/ensemble model hurts performance on a small dataset (<5K rows) with strong transformer base models.
rules.action: Revert the feature addition. On small NLP datasets, stacking gains come more from diverse strong base models than from handcrafted features. Focus instead on improving base model quality (head architecture, layer normalization) or adjusting blend weights among existing strong base models.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: use_all_models_for_kl_divergence_metric
rules.context: When the evaluation metric rewards calibrated probability distributions (e.g., KL divergence) and single models score much worse than multi-model ensembles.
rules.action: Use all available diverse checkpoints in the ensemble rather than trying to find a single best one. Averaging predictions from multiple models smooths probability estimates and consistently outperforms individual models for KL-divergence metrics. Do not spend excessive time optimizing which subset to include—start with all of them.
rules.exceptions: 50376011:e5#2 notes that adding a 5th model didn't improve over 4, suggesting diminishing returns exist even for KL metrics.

rules.name: isolate_changes_when_debugging_score_ambiguity
rules.context: Multiple changes (e.g., preprocessing parameters, ensemble composition, modality additions) were bundled in one submission and the resulting score change cannot be attributed to a single cause.
rules.action: Isolate changes by testing them sequentially: either revert exactly one change and resubmit to compare three scores, or stage additions incrementally—first verify a new component in isolation, then blend within its group, then blend across groups. Avoid debugging multiple dimensions simultaneously.
rules.exceptions: When a plateau persists despite incremental changes, a broader simultaneous probe may be warranted (50496431:e54#2), though regressions from such probes require follow-up isolation to diagnose infrastructure vs. modeling issues.

rules.name: pivot_lever_after_stalled_iteration
rules.context: When iterating on a single lever (e.g., checkpoint versions, ensemble membership, head architecture) produces no improvement or slight regression over 2+ attempts, and alternative levers exist (other model families, pipeline changes, or previously successful levers).
rules.action: Stop iterating on the stalled lever and pivot to a qualitatively different lever. If untapped model diversity exists, expand fold/model coverage of a different model family. If ensemble composition is exhausted, invest in improving individual model predictions or the inference pipeline. If exploration has regressed 3+ times, return to the lever that last produced a best score and re-optimize it with the current codebase.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: expand_groupby_aggregations_incrementally
rules.context: When building customer-level features from panel/time-series data for a GBDT model and the current aggregation set is minimal (e.g., only mean or only last), with a large gap (>0.02) to known achievable scores.
rules.action: Expand aggregation functions for numeric features (mean, std, min, max, last) and categorical features (count, last, nunique) either in one large step or incrementally. Validate each addition via CV or LB. Remove near-duplicate aggregations (e.g., var when std is present) if they don't improve validation. Start with core aggregations before adding secondary ones (var, first, count on numerics).
rules.exceptions: When memory is tight, omit std or var initially. var ≈ std² but can still help in some cases (27799930:e6#3 final best used both).

rules.name: lag_diff_features_diminishing_returns_with_rich_aggregations
rules.context: When a GBDT model already has rich aggregation features (mean, std, min, max, last, var) on customer-level time-series data and you want to add lag or difference features (last-minus-second-to-last, last-minus-first, etc.).
rules.action: Test lag/diff features but expect diminishing returns. Prefer vectorized post-hoc computation (compute 'last' and 'second-to-last' separately, then subtract) over custom UDFs in groupby. If validation shows no gain after 2-3 attempts, abandon them—the GBDT can approximate differences from existing features. Custom lag features on variable-length sequences introduce sentinel values that can confuse tree splits.
rules.exceptions: Difference features (last-mean) combined with other changes did help in 27836972:e6#1 and 27799930:e8#1, but isolated contribution was unclear.

rules.name: tail_window_aggregation_for_recency
rules.context: When customer-level aggregation features use the full history but recent behavior may differ from long-term averages (e.g., default prediction with ~13 monthly statements).
rules.action: Compute aggregations over a short recent window (e.g., last 3 rows) for numeric features only. Also try a difference feature (last value minus tail-N mean). Validate via CV. If a longer window (e.g., last 6) doesn't improve over the shorter one, keep the shorter window. Disable categorical tail aggregations if CV drops.
rules.exceptions: Only one LB submission confirmed the tail-3 approach (27836972:e10#1); the diff features in 27799930:e8#1 were bundled with other changes.

rules.name: rounded_numeric_features_for_gbdt
rules.context: When a GBDT model uses high-precision float features (e.g., 'last' aggregation columns) and you want a cheap feature transformation.
rules.action: Round float columns to 2 decimal places and add as new features (or replace originals). This gives tree models cleaner split points. Expect small improvement (~0.001). Consider keeping both rounded and original versions rather than dropping originals.
rules.exceptions: Improvement is marginal; dropping originals loses fine-grained information (27836972:e4#2 counter_evidence).

rules.name: cross_group_interaction_features_keep_small_set
rules.context: When building interaction features (e.g., balance minus payment) for a GBDT model on tabular financial data with domain-meaningful feature groups.
rules.action: Start with a small set of the most interpretable cross-group differences (e.g., balance_last minus payment_last). If those help, try the same differences using different temporal aggregations (tail3m_mean, mean). Do NOT expand to many column pairs at once—if a broad expansion doesn't help, prune back to the original small set. GBDT can learn interactions internally, so explicit ones may not add value.
rules.exceptions: Despite systematic narrowing, no variant of after-pay features beat baseline in 27836972:e9#1, suggesting even small sets may not help when GBDT already captures the interaction.

rules.name: fewer_folds_for_simple_models_small_data
rules.context: When using simple models (Ridge, linear) on small datasets (<10K samples) with an ensemble-averaging pipeline.
rules.action: Try a small number of folds (3-5) to maximize per-fold training set size. Simple models benefit more from additional training data than from ensemble diversity. Compare against higher fold counts (10-20) to confirm.
rules.exceptions: For complex models (BERT, deep NNs) on the same small data, more folds may be better because ensemble diversity matters more (7253130:e5#2).

rules.name: increment_test_time_fold_averaging
rules.context: When you have multiple trained fold checkpoints available and the metric is rank-based or benefits from averaging (Spearman, KL divergence), and you want to find the optimal number of folds for test-time averaging.
rules.action: Include all available fold models in the test-time average. If constrained, increment the number of folds used one at a time (e.g., 4→5→6) and keep increasing as long as each step improves the score. Stop when score plateaus, regresses, or you hit a time/memory budget.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: prefer_model_diversity_over_fold_count
rules.context: When constrained by inference time/memory budget and choosing between more folds of one model versus fewer folds of multiple distinct models.
rules.action: Prefer fewer folds across multiple distinct model checkpoints (different architectures, seeds, or training indices) over many folds of a single checkpoint. Model diversity typically reduces ensemble error more than additional folds of the same model. Test the higher fold count first, then halve folds and add a second model if improvement is insufficient.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: use_domain_meaningful_groups_for_grouped_cv
rules.context: When switching to group-aware cross-validation (GroupKFold, StratifiedGroupKFold) and deciding what column to use as the group variable.
rules.action: Use the domain-meaningful group variable (e.g., prompt/topic ID) rather than synthetic clustering (KMeans). Verify the group variable produces balanced, non-trivial splits before submitting. If grouped CV degrades score substantially (>0.005), check whether the group variable is correct before concluding grouping hurts.
rules.exceptions: When the number of natural groups is very small (<10), GroupKFold yields high-variance OOF predictions; prefer StratifiedKFold with many folds instead (58130512:e25#2).

rules.name: stratified_over_group_kfold_when_few_groups
rules.context: When the dataset has a small number of natural groups (<10) and the test set does not require generalization to completely unseen groups.
rules.action: Prefer StratifiedKFold with many folds (≥10) over GroupKFold. GroupKFold with few groups yields high-variance OOF predictions and unstable downstream optimization. If group-level generalization is not needed for the test set, stratifying by target is more reliable.
rules.exceptions: If the test set truly requires out-of-group generalization, GroupKFold is necessary despite the variance.

rules.name: consistent_fold_scheme_across_ensemble_components
rules.context: When building a multi-model ensemble (e.g., GBDT + NN) where some components use proper K-fold CV and others use ad-hoc training loops.
rules.action: Refactor all components to use the same K-fold scheme: iterate over identical folds, save each fold's model, generate proper out-of-fold predictions, and average fold test predictions. When changing fold count, update all downstream averaging code to match. This ensures OOF predictions are comparable across models for stacking/blending.
rules.exceptions: The improvement from pipeline consistency alone may be small (+0.00027 in one case), suggesting it's necessary but not sufficient.

rules.name: reduce_folds_for_faster_iteration_restore_later
rules.context: When running many feature-engineering or hyperparameter experiments and training time scales linearly with fold count.
rules.action: Reduce folds (e.g., 10→5) during the exploration phase to iterate faster. Submit once to confirm the score impact is negligible. Once iteration is done, restore the higher fold count as a single probe for the final submission. For tree-based ensembles on ~17K samples, going from 5 to 15 folds can yield +0.002-0.004 improvement.
rules.exceptions: The gain from restoring higher folds may be small and fragile if other hyperparameters have shifted during exploration.

rules.name: change_one_cv_element_at_a_time
rules.context: When adjusting CV splits for subpopulation handling or switching CV strategies (e.g., StratifiedKFold to GroupKFold), especially when the dataset has distinct subpopulations.
rules.action: Change only one element at a time (grouping variable, fold count, or index augmentation logic) and submit after each change. Keep feature-selection files and other hyperparameters fixed to isolate the effect. A large regression (>0.005) signals the split change is harmful and should be reverted immediately.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: increase_early_stopping_patience_with_fold_count
rules.context: When increasing CV fold count for tree/neural models and score differences between versions are very small (<0.001).
rules.action: When doubling fold count (e.g., 5→10), also increase early-stopping patience by 2-4× (e.g., 300→700→1300). More folds with undertrained models due to premature early stopping can negate the benefit of additional folds. Accept the increased compute cost for more reliable selection signals.
rules.exceptions: The benefit is inferred from score improvements; no direct CV variance measurements confirm stabilization.

rules.name: let_gbdt_handle_nan_natively
rules.context: When using XGBoost, LightGBM, or CatBoost on numeric features where zero or a sentinel value has real meaning, and the pipeline includes a missing-value imputation step.
rules.action: Do not fill missing numeric features with zero or a shared sentinel before feeding to GBDTs that handle NaN natively. Leave NaN for models that support it. If the ensemble includes models that cannot handle NaN (e.g., sklearn RandomForest), branch the imputation by model type inside the shared feature builder rather than applying a single fill strategy to all models.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: filter_event_positive_outliers_when_plateaued
rules.context: When a survival or binary-event model has plateaued after extensive hyperparameter tuning, and the positive/event class is suspected to contain mislabeled or anomalous samples, and a precomputed outlier list (e.g., from residual analysis) is available.
rules.action: Filter outliers only from the event-positive (minority) training subset using a single anomaly threshold. Evaluate on local CV or a single LB submission. If it improves, keep it and move on rather than sweeping thresholds—the gain is typically small and threshold-insensitive. If no improvement, revert.
rules.exceptions: 77450317's author never confirmed LB improvement; the benefit may be marginal or absent depending on label noise level.

rules.name: prefer_simple_data_selection_over_complex_balancing
rules.context: When training a model on a reasonably-sized dataset with class imbalance and soft/ordinal labels, and considering complex oversampling (SMOTE, class-balanced temporal deduplication) versus simpler filtering or native model handling.
rules.action: Prefer simple deduplication and confidence-based filtering (e.g., keep samples with high vote fraction) over complex synthetic oversampling or elaborate class-balanced sampling. SMOTE and complex balancing schemes often hurt when the target is ordinal/soft-label and the metric is rank- or calibration-sensitive (QWK, KL divergence). Use threshold optimization or sample weighting instead.
rules.exceptions: Class-balanced non-overlapping selection (49576186:e14#3) did help in an earlier stage of the same pipeline, suggesting that moderate balancing can work when data volume is preserved.

rules.name: tighten_sample_filters_cautiously
rules.context: When fine-tuning a model and considering tightening data quality filters (e.g., switching from OR to AND on multiple quality thresholds, or filtering to high-confidence subsets only).
rules.action: When tightening sample selection criteria, expect significant data volume reduction. If the resulting score regresses substantially (e.g., >2× recent improvement magnitude), revert immediately—data volume loss likely outweighs noise reduction. Isolate the filtering change from other changes (e.g., checkpoint switches). For the final fine-tuning stage, the most inclusive (unfiltered) data selection often wins.
rules.exceptions: These are from the same kernel; confidence is limited. Filtering to high-confidence samples of an ambiguous class (49576186:e21#2) did help when combined with label smoothing.

rules.name: checkpoint_loading_strict_mode_strategy
rules.context: Loading a fine-tuned or externally trained checkpoint into a model architecture where the state_dict keys may not perfectly match (e.g., different head, auxiliary components, or pretrained initialization conflict).
rules.action: First attempt load_state_dict with strict=True to surface exactly which keys mismatch. If the checkpoint is a full fine-tune covering all needed layers, set pretrained=False in the model constructor and keep strict=True. If mismatched keys are only auxiliary heads not needed at inference, switch to strict=False and add comments documenting which keys are intentionally missing. Never combine pretrained=True with strict=False, as this silently mixes pretrained and fine-tuned weights.
rules.exceptions: strict=False may hide missing keys that matter; in 55621328:e41#1 the partial load matched but did not improve over a prior result, suggesting auxiliary components weren't fully utilized.

rules.name: precompute_transformer_features_for_gbdt
rules.context: When transformer models (e.g., DeBERTa) have been fine-tuned and their predictions or embeddings are needed as features for a GBDT model (LightGBM/XGBoost), but live transformer inference in the submission kernel is slow, memory-intensive, or error-prone.
rules.action: Precompute transformer predictions or embeddings offline and save as pickles/CSVs. Load them at submission time as additional GBDT features instead of running live inference. Use batched extraction with mean pooling and L2 normalization, and add gc.collect() between folds. This saves GPU time, avoids OOM/timeout, and enables faster iteration on the GBDT layer.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: dense_embeddings_as_tabular_features_for_trees
rules.context: When a tree-based model (e.g., LightGBM) already uses sparse/engineered text features (TF-IDF, topic models) and you want to inject richer semantic signal from transformer or pretrained sentence encoders.
rules.action: Compute dense embeddings (e.g., mean-pooled transformer hidden states, Universal Sentence Encoder vectors) and add them as new columns to the feature table. Simultaneously increase the feature-selection budget so the new dense features survive selection. Submit to check LB lift; if the gain is absent or marginal relative to your best score, remove the heavy features—inference cost and overfitting risk outweigh marginal gains.
rules.exceptions: 58130512:e5#1 notes that hidden vectors didn't beat the overall best, suggesting gains may come from concurrent changes rather than embeddings alone. 55987255:e2#2 saw only marginal improvement from USE embeddings.

rules.name: extract_embeddings_from_failed_predictor
rules.context: When a pretrained model (e.g., generative LLM or fine-tuned transformer) fails at direct prediction (poor calibration, parsing failures, regression in scores) but the model is already loaded and its internal representations may still encode useful information.
rules.action: Instead of using the model's direct output as predictions, extract hidden-state embeddings (e.g., mean-pooled last layer) and feed them as features into a well-calibrated downstream model like LightGBM. This converts an unreliable predictor into a feature extractor. If switching embedding sources regresses scores, revert and investigate whether the original source was actually better calibrated.
rules.exceptions: 18851026:e3#1 shows that switching to checkpoint-based embeddings can regress if precomputed features were from a superior source. 55987255:e8#2 was never submitted so the benefit is unconfirmed.

rules.name: multi_fold_prediction_averaging
rules.context: When multiple K-fold checkpoints are available from cross-validation training and only a single fold's predictions are being used at inference time.
rules.action: Average predictions across all K fold checkpoints before post-processing (rounding, thresholding, etc.). After switching to multi-fold averaging, re-optimize any downstream post-processing thresholds since the prediction distribution changes. Expect modest but consistent variance reduction gains (typically 0.05-0.5% on classification/regression metrics).
rules.exceptions: Architecture quality can outweigh fold-averaging gains: a single checkpoint from a stronger architecture may beat a 5-fold ensemble from a weaker one (15082684:e5#1). Also, fold averaging alone won't help if other pipeline issues dominate.

rules.name: weighted_over_uniform_when_quality_varies
rules.context: When ensemble members have substantially different individual quality scores (e.g., best member is 1.5x+ better than worst on the target metric).
rules.action: Use quality-based weighting (e.g., inverse-score or manually assigned weights favoring stronger models) rather than simple uniform averaging. Down-weight weaker standalone models (e.g., 0.1 weight for models with much worse solo scores) and up-weight stronger ones. Verify against simple mean on leaderboard; if weighted doesn't clearly beat mean, revert.
rules.exceptions: When individual model scores are similar and fold-level quality estimates are noisy (few folds, small data), simple averaging is preferred (7573212:e2#2, 18837555:e4#2).

rules.name: uniform_averaging_when_quality_similar
rules.context: When ensemble members have similar individual quality and you lack a reliable validation set to optimize blend weights (e.g., small dataset, noisy fold estimates).
rules.action: Start with simple uniform average across all model groups. Add one group at a time and verify on leaderboard. Only attempt non-uniform weighting after membership is finalized, and revert if weighted blending does not beat the uniform average. Invest effort in improving individual models or adding diversity rather than tuning weights.
rules.exceptions: If one model is clearly stronger than others, weighted blending helps even without a validation set (50496431:e56#2).

rules.name: tune_new_model_before_blending_at_low_weight
rules.context: When adding an untuned or weakly-tuned new model to a well-optimized ensemble baseline.
rules.action: Tune the new model to comparable standalone quality before blending it in. A very small blend weight (e.g., 5%) for an untuned model is unlikely to improve a well-tuned baseline and may hurt. Either invest in tuning the new model first, or use validation-optimized blend weights rather than arbitrary small ones.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: group_correlated_models_before_blending
rules.context: When some ensemble members are correlated (same architecture, similar training) and others are more independent, and you lack reliable local CV for weight optimization.
rules.action: Group correlated predictors into sub-averages first, then combine sub-group means with roughly equal weight. This prevents correlated models from dominating the blend. Refine within-group weights after establishing the hierarchical structure, but stop if refinement regresses.
rules.exceptions: 18837555:e5#1 notes further refinement within the hierarchical scheme regressed on a noisy 7-row public LB.

rules.name: add_second_model_family_when_single_model_plateaus
rules.context: When single-model hyperparameter tuning has plateaued or regressed on the leaderboard, and you only have one model family.
rules.action: Add a second model from a different family (e.g., XGBoost alongside LightGBM, or a different NN architecture), train both on the same features/folds, and blend predictions with a weighted average. Start with a conservative weight split (e.g., 80/20 favoring the stronger model), verify the ensemble improves, then fine-tune weights.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: prune_weak_ensemble_members
rules.context: When an ensemble member has noticeably worse standalone/OOF scores than other members, or when adding a new member causes a score regression.
rules.action: Remove the weakest or newly-regressing member entirely rather than relying on weight optimization to suppress it. Re-evaluate the ensemble after each removal. Even with optimized blend weights, a weak or redundant member can hurt because the optimizer may overfit to its noise. If removal improves the score, continue pruning the next weakest member.
rules.exceptions: In larger ensembles with many diverse architectures, even weaker members can help through diversity (18757376 notes this). Also, when the number of base models is very small (≤5), removing members may increase variance more than it reduces bias (7573212:e4#2).

rules.name: add_architecturally_diverse_backbone_to_ensemble
rules.context: When an ensemble of models from a single architecture family (e.g., all 2D CNNs, all GBDTs of one type, all RoBERTa) has plateaued and checkpoint/hyperparameter/weight-tuning sweeps yield diminishing returns.
rules.action: Introduce a model from a fundamentally different architecture family (e.g., transformer-based vs CNN-based, DeBERTa when existing are RoBERTa, CatBoost vs LightGBM, CNN on reshaped tabular data vs MLP). Validate the new architecture produces reasonable standalone predictions first, then blend with existing members using a conservative weight for the new member. Submit after each addition to confirm monotonic improvement. If the new backbone doesn't help after 2-3 weight adjustments, remove it before trying others.
rules.exceptions: Not every new backbone improves the score — NextViT-large regressed in 49524919:e26. The new architecture must be genuinely complementary, not just different. Same-family additions (e.g., CatBoost added to LightGBM, Funnel-large when you already have RoBERTa) may provide minimal diversity gain (55431616:e3#2, 18550705). Late-stage additions of same-family variants with different target transforms yield diminishing returns (73937748:e24#2).

rules.name: remove_same_family_redundant_ensemble_member
rules.context: When a newly added ensemble member is from the same model family as existing members (e.g., both tree-based boosting, or near-duplicate training variants) and the combined score regresses or doesn't improve.
rules.action: Remove the redundant member and reallocate effort to improving the remaining model or adding a genuinely different model family. Same-family ensembles often add noise without meaningful diversity. When two models from the same experiment family are both included, test removing one — the marginal gain from a near-duplicate is often negative.
rules.exceptions: If the same-family models differ substantially in training procedure (different objectives, different data augmentation), they may still provide useful diversity.

rules.name: keep_all_folds_in_small_ensemble
rules.context: When the ensemble has ≤5 fold models and you are considering dropping folds to improve quality.
rules.action: Prefer keeping all folds with equal weight. Removing folds from a small ensemble typically increases variance more than it reduces bias. Only pursue fold selection when you have many more base models (≥10) so dropping a few does not materially reduce diversity.
rules.exceptions: If one fold is clearly broken or trained on corrupted data, removing it can still help even in small ensembles.

rules.name: incrementally_add_fold_checkpoints_to_ensemble
rules.context: When multiple fold checkpoints are available and each prior addition has yielded monotonic improvement on the target metric (especially calibration-sensitive metrics like KL divergence).
rules.action: Keep adding fold checkpoints one or a few at a time, submitting after each addition. If each addition improves the score, continue until all available checkpoints are included or scores plateau. Start with a subset (e.g., 2 of 5) to verify the new branch works, then add remaining folds. Reduce per-model batch size proportionally to stay within GPU memory.
rules.exceptions: If models are too correlated (same architecture, same data), adding more may not help. Also, LB noise can make individual checkpoint ranking unreliable (50376011:e25#2).

rules.name: weighted_blend_over_mean_when_quality_varies
rules.context: When ensemble members have substantially different individual scores and you are choosing between simple averaging and weighted blending.
rules.action: Use weighted blending with score-proportional weights, giving ~80-90% weight to the best 2-3 members. Add weaker members with small weights (e.g., 0.1) and submit to check for marginal gain. If adding a member doesn't help, remove it. Gradually shift weight toward the stronger model (e.g., 0.75→0.9→1.0) while monitoring validation to determine if the weaker model contributes at all.
rules.exceptions: When all members have similar quality, simple mean blending may be sufficient and more robust to overfitting blend weights.

rules.name: test_single_model_vs_ensemble_baseline
rules.context: When fold models may be undertrained, inconsistent, or highly correlated, and a single well-trained model or checkpoint is available.
rules.action: Before assuming ensembling always helps, compare the single best model against the ensemble on the leaderboard. If the single model matches or beats the ensemble, the fold models may be too correlated or weak. Use the single model as baseline, then only add ensemble members that demonstrably improve over it.
rules.exceptions: When fold models are well-trained and diverse, ensembling almost always helps. This check is most valuable early in development or when training was resource-constrained.

rules.name: add_all_target_transform_variants_then_prune
rules.context: When pre-trained pipelines exist for a new model family with multiple target transformations (e.g., Cox, KM, Nelson-Aalen, rank-based) and the ensemble framework can handle additional columns.
rules.action: Add all available target-transform variants for the new model family at once rather than one at a time. Submit to check for improvement. Then prune members that don't contribute by removing them individually. Batch-adding is a good first step but must be followed by member selection, as including all without filtering can hurt.
rules.exceptions: If the gain from adding the entire family is marginal (<0.001), do not spend further iterations tuning that family (73937748:e20#1).

rules.name: test_new_backbone_as_swap_not_addition
rules.context: When the existing ensemble is already well-tuned and a new backbone has not been validated to be complementary.
rules.action: First test the new backbone as a swap for an existing member (not an addition) to isolate its contribution. If it does not improve or match the member it replaces, remove it and restore the previous member. Do not keep a new backbone that adds no measurable gain. Only after confirming standalone quality should you try adding it as an extra member.
rules.exceptions: When the ensemble is small (2-3 members), adding rather than swapping may be preferable since more members reduce variance.

rules.name: isolate_changes_one_at_a_time_in_ensemble_tuning
rules.context: When tuning ensemble composition by adding/removing members or changing blend weights, and leaderboard feedback is noisy (small test set or high variance metric).
rules.action: Iterate one change at a time to isolate effects — either add one member, remove one member, or change one weight. Submit after each change. When the LB test set is very small (e.g., ~7 rows), be skeptical of single-submission improvements and require consistent gains across multiple configurations before locking in a change.
rules.exceptions: When submissions are limited, batching complementary changes (e.g., adding a member + adjusting a preprocessing parameter to its known-best value) in one step can be more efficient (50496431:e43#2).

rules.name: remove_model_family_after_repeated_failure
rules.context: When a model family or modality has been added to an ensemble and tuned across 3+ iterations (different checkpoints, blend weights, hyperparameters) without ever improving the best score.
