rules.action: Remove the underperforming model family entirely from the pipeline. Verify by running the remaining ensemble and confirming the score matches or exceeds the previous best. Do not continue tuning the failing component.
rules.exceptions: If the model family was only tested with a single configuration or the failures were confounded with other simultaneous changes, more isolated testing may be warranted before removal.

rules.name: fold_ensemble_prefer_small_subset_same_architecture
rules.context: When ensembling fold checkpoints from the same architecture and adding more folds stops improving or worsens the score.
rules.action: For same-architecture fold ensembles, start with 2-3 members rather than all folds. If the full set scores worse than a subset, systematically drop the weakest member (swap each out one at a time). Test 3-4 representative fold indices individually to identify the strongest, then combine only the top performers.
rules.exceptions: Earlier in training when individual models are weaker, larger fold ensembles may still help (50376011:e39#1 showed adding more checkpoints helped). The optimal size depends on checkpoint quality and correlation.

rules.name: swap_one_ensemble_member_at_a_time
rules.context: When testing whether a new model checkpoint or variant improves a multi-model ensemble.
rules.action: Replace exactly one ensemble member with the new variant while keeping all other members and blending unchanged. If the score regresses, revert immediately. Do not simultaneously change preprocessing, weights, or other members, as this confounds the signal.
rules.exceptions: When you have automatic per-target weight optimization (e.g., Nelder-Mead) that can zero out bad models, adding without ablation is safer (7548275:e7#1).

rules.name: test_both_models_when_swap_regresses
rules.context: When replacing model A with model B in an ensemble causes a score regression, suggesting both capture different patterns.
rules.action: Instead of simply reverting, try including both models simultaneously. If the combined ensemble improves beyond the original, keep both; then selectively remove the weaker contributor to confirm complementarity.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: treat_small_toggle_effects_as_noise
rules.context: When toggling a single ensemble member on/off produces score differences ≤0.0002 with no consistent direction across 2+ trials.
rules.action: Treat the member's effect as noise. Fix it to whichever state and move on to higher-impact levers rather than continuing to toggle. Invest effort in adding architecturally diverse models or tuning higher-impact components instead.
rules.exceptions: If the metric is computed on a very small public test set (e.g., 7 rows), even larger differences may be noise (18837555:e1#2).

rules.name: prioritize_diversity_over_single_best_in_blend
rules.context: When blending predictions from multiple models and no single model outperforms the existing best ensemble.
rules.action: Prioritize architectural or methodological diversity (different transformer families, different input representations, different training objectives) over picking the single best checkpoint. Weight stronger standalone models more heavily but include weaker diverse models at reduced weight. Adding a third diverse model often beats a two-model blend even if individually weaker.
rules.exceptions: When components are too correlated (same architecture, same training setup), adding more doesn't help (53424936:e7#2).

rules.name: isolate_hp_changes_for_lb_attribution
rules.context: When validation scores diverge substantially from leaderboard scores, or when multiple hyperparameters are being changed simultaneously.
rules.action: Change only one or two hyperparameters per submission to isolate their effect on the leaderboard. When validation and LB diverge significantly, trust the LB score. Avoid bundling hyperparameter changes with bug fixes or feature changes, as it confounds the signal.
rules.exceptions: When wall-clock time is severely constrained, bundling 2-3 related changes (e.g., class imbalance + capacity) per submission can be acceptable as per 27656049:e3#1.

rules.name: sweep_depth_downward_from_default
rules.context: When using a GBDT model with a moderate default tree depth (e.g., 6-8) and suspecting overfitting.
rules.action: Sweep max_depth downward by 1 per step, submitting each. If the score improves or stays flat, continue reducing. Stop when you hit a new best. Even if an intermediate step regresses slightly, try one more reduction before reverting since small regressions can be noise.
rules.exceptions: 58130512:e20#2 warns against cutting depth too aggressively in one step (8→5) while also changing other params; incremental reduction is safer.

rules.name: dart_needs_more_iterations_and_specific_tuning
rules.context: When switching from GBDT to DART boosting in LightGBM.
rules.action: Significantly increase n_estimators (DART needs more iterations to compensate for dropped trees) and tune DART-specific parameters (drop_rate, skip_drop). Since DART doesn't support standard early stopping, sweep n_estimators manually in fixed increments (e.g., +500), tracking marginal LB gain per step. Stop when gain per step drops below ~0.0002.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: set_n_estimators_high_with_early_stopping
rules.context: When using a GBDT model with early stopping and n_estimators is set low enough that early stopping never triggers (e.g., n_estimators equals early_stopping_rounds).
rules.action: Set n_estimators to a large value (10-20x current) and rely on early stopping to find the right number of rounds automatically. When lowering learning rate, also increase early_stopping_rounds proportionally to allow enough rounds for convergence.
rules.exceptions: Does not apply to DART boosting where early stopping is unreliable.

rules.name: lr_n_estimators_tradeoff
rules.context: When GBDT training is too slow due to many boosting rounds at a low learning rate, or when you want to adjust capacity.
rules.action: Increase learning rate by 3-4x and reduce n_estimators proportionally (keeping lr × n_estimators roughly constant). Optionally increase num_leaves slightly to compensate for fewer rounds. Verify performance is maintained before further tuning.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: tune_hp_after_feature_engineering_plateaus
rules.context: When feature engineering improvements have plateaued (marginal gains < 0.001 over several iterations) and model hyperparameters have not been systematically tuned.
rules.action: Switch from feature engineering to hyperparameter tuning. Start with the highest-impact knobs: tree depth, learning rate, and subsampling. If using inherited/default parameters from a starter notebook, expect meaningful gains from the first round of tuning.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: add_subsampling_when_other_regularization_exhausted
rules.context: When L2 regularization, min_child_samples, and feature selection have already been tuned for a GBDT model but no column or row subsampling has been tried.
rules.action: Add both feature_fraction and bagging_fraction simultaneously at an aggressive value (e.g., 0.3) and increase early stopping patience proportionally. If this yields improvement, then try lowering learning rate and allowing more rounds to exploit the added regularization.
rules.exceptions: 27389424:e8#1 notes that lowering learning rate to 0.01 after adding subsampling caused regression, suggesting the combined change can overshoot.

rules.name: consistent_hp_across_ensemble_model_configs
rules.context: When an ensemble contains multiple instances of the same model type (e.g., two LightGBM configs) with shared structural hyperparameters.
rules.action: When tuning a structural hyperparameter (e.g., max_depth), apply the change consistently to all configs of the same model type rather than just one. If changing only one config yields a regression, try making all configs consistent before concluding the new value is worse.
rules.exceptions: When different configs target different loss surfaces (e.g., Cox vs. KM transforms), per-model specialization via automated search may be warranted as per 73937748:e5#1.

rules.name: scale_pos_weight_dampened_exponent
rules.context: When handling class imbalance in a binary GBDT model and is_unbalance or full inverse-frequency weighting seems too aggressive.
rules.action: Replace is_unbalance with scale_pos_weight set to (n_neg/n_pos)^(1/k) where k>1 (e.g., k=3 for cube root). Sweep the exponent k in small steps (1/2, 1/3, 1/4) around the current value, submitting each. Do not change other hyperparameters simultaneously during this sweep.
rules.exceptions: 60197293:e14#2 warns that scale_pos_weight is a binary classification parameter and should not be used for multi-class/ordinal tasks.

rules.name: reduce_n_estimators_geometrically_when_overfitting
rules.context: When validation performance does not degrade as you reduce n_estimators, indicating the GBDT model was over-complex.
rules.action: Halve n_estimators repeatedly (e.g., 900→450→225→100), checking validation after each step. If performance holds, keep reducing. Stop when validation degrades. This geometric reduction is faster than linear steps for finding the right order of magnitude. Submit only after confirming the direction over several steps.
rules.exceptions: 55987255:e27#1 notes that CV improvements from complexity reduction may not transfer to LB if there is distribution shift.

rules.name: tune_all_ensemble_gbdt_models_simultaneously
rules.context: When multiple GBDT models (e.g., CatBoost, LightGBM) contribute to an ensemble and none is individually well-tuned.
rules.action: Adjust hyperparameters across all GBDT models simultaneously in one submission: lower learning rates paired with higher iteration counts, moderate regularization, and increased tree depth/leaves. If the gain is very small (<0.05% of score), move to other levers like blending weights or feature engineering rather than continuing model-level tuning.
rules.exceptions: 73937748:e5#1 found only +0.00002 improvement from per-model HP specialization, suggesting marginal returns for well-tuned ensembles.

rules.name: l1_l2_regularization_direction_swap
rules.context: When a GBDT model has plateaued and current regularization uses mild L1 and moderate L2 (or vice versa).
rules.action: Try increasing L1 (reg_alpha) substantially (2-5x) while decreasing L2 (reg_lambda), and modestly increase n_estimators to compensate for the stronger sparsity penalty. If even a large jump yields only marginal gain (<0.001), declare regularization tuning exhausted and switch levers.
rules.exceptions: 55591012:e3#1 warns that 100x jumps in regularization are too aggressive; moderate jumps (2-5x) are preferred.

rules.name: bracket_capacity_with_large_steps_for_baseline
rules.context: When building an initial GBDT baseline with no prior leaderboard signal and needing to find reasonable tree complexity quickly.
rules.action: Start with moderate defaults, try a deliberately small model to check for underfitting (watch validation loss), then jump to a substantially larger model. Use large step sizes (4-10x changes in num_leaves) rather than fine-tuning, since the goal is to bracket the right capacity range before investing in CV or submission.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: conservative_tree_capacity_for_ordinal_objectives
rules.context: When using GBDT models with custom ordinal objectives (e.g., QWK) and moderate baseline tree params.
rules.action: Prefer conservative tree capacity (fewer leaves relative to depth). If increasing max_depth and num_leaves by 1 worsens the score, revert immediately rather than trying larger increases—overfitting on ordinal boundaries is likely the cause.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: match_inference_resolution_to_training
rules.context: When running inference with a pretrained CNN checkpoint (e.g., EfficientNet) and the inference image resolution may not match the resolution the model was trained at.
rules.action: Ensure the inference image decode/resize target exactly matches the model's trained input resolution (e.g., EfficientNet-B7 = 600px). Change both the image decoder target_size and the model's declared input_shape in the same edit. If the training resolution is unknown, try the canonical resolution for the architecture variant first. Derive resolution from model.input.shape programmatically when switching between checkpoints.
rules.exceptions: TensorFlow may auto-resize internally, so a mismatch may not be catastrophic (13702907:e4#1 still improved despite partial mismatch), but it is suboptimal.

rules.name: sweep_inference_resolution_in_small_steps
rules.context: When a CNN image classification pipeline is functional and you want to find the optimal inference resolution, especially for tasks with fine spatial detail (e.g., medical imaging with catheters/lines).
rules.action: Test 2–3 resolution values in ascending order around the canonical/training resolution (e.g., one step below, canonical, one step above). If a larger resolution regresses substantially (>0.5% on LB), revert rather than continuing upward. Stop when one step above and one below the current best are both worse. Re-sweep if the model architecture or training changes.
rules.exceptions: Diminishing returns are common; 13577502:e3#1 found 800px and 900px essentially tied. A single confirmation run may not distinguish signal from noise (13702907:e8#1 showed ~0.002 variance).

rules.name: do_not_change_resolution_and_architecture_simultaneously
rules.context: When modifying a CNN inference pipeline and considering both a resolution change and a model head/architecture change at the same time.
rules.action: Change only one variable at a time: test the resolution change first with the original architecture, then modify the head or architecture separately. Simultaneous changes confound the signal, making it impossible to attribute score changes. If a combined change regresses, revert both and re-test individually.
rules.exceptions: If a new checkpoint was trained with both changes together (new resolution + new head), they must be applied together to match training conditions.

rules.name: increase_resolution_with_matching_checkpoint
rules.context: When increasing inference resolution beyond the original training resolution for a pretrained CNN, and higher-resolution checkpoints are available.
rules.action: Pair the resolution increase with a checkpoint that was trained at or near that target resolution. Do not simply upscale input to a resolution the model never saw during training. Verify the pipeline runs (check for OOM) before submitting. Enable multi-GPU if the larger resolution causes memory issues.
rules.exceptions: Fully convolutional models with global pooling may tolerate resolution mismatches better than models with fixed-size FC layers (13577502:e3#1).

rules.name: conservative_augmentation_for_medical_images
rules.context: When training or augmenting medical images with standardized orientation and limited color variation (e.g., chest X-rays), and considering adding geometric or color augmentations.
rules.action: Start with minimal augmentation (e.g., small brightness adjustment with delta ~0.1). Avoid 90-degree rotations and keep color augmentation ranges narrow (±10% of identity). Add transforms one at a time, verifying each independently. If a combined augmentation regresses, remove the most aggressive transform first (geometric before color).
rules.exceptions: Some brightness augmentation does help (13542132:e1#1 improved with it); the issue is specifically with stronger/more diverse augmentation stacking.

rules.name: validate_spatial_augmentation_for_structured_inputs
rules.context: When considering spatial flip augmentation or TTA for inputs with fixed semantic channel/spatial ordering (e.g., EEG montages, medical images with standardized orientation).
rules.action: Be cautious applying spatial flip TTA or augmentation to inputs where spatial positions carry fixed semantic meaning (e.g., left/right hemisphere EEG channels, anatomical orientation in X-rays). Test with a single submission before committing; if it regresses, do not pursue further flip variants.
rules.exceptions: Horizontal flips may still help for chest X-rays if the model was trained with them (13542132:e1#1 used flips in baseline).

rules.name: avoid_scaling_and_ohe_for_gbdt
rules.context: When using XGBoost/LightGBM on tabular data and the preprocessing pipeline includes one-hot encoding of categoricals and/or standard scaling of numerics.
rules.action: Remove one-hot encoding and standard scaling for tree-based models—they add dimensionality without helping splits. Instead, use label encoding or native categorical handling. Aggregate multi-row records using groupby statistics. Impute missing values with median or let the GBDT handle NaNs natively.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: progressive_feature_set_expansion_for_gbdt
rules.context: When a GBDT model uses a small manually-selected feature subset (e.g., 30 out of 190 available features) and scores poorly, while feature importance analysis shows many unused features have high importance.
rules.action: Progressively expand the feature set: first add the next batch of important features and validate, then add more, and finally switch to automatic aggregation of all available features. Simultaneously simplify unnecessary preprocessing (imputation, scaling, outlier removal) that the GBDT doesn't need. Use importance-based ranking to prioritize which features to add first.
rules.exceptions: Adding all features without cleanup can slightly hurt (28093671:e8#1 v38→v39). Expanding beyond the top-N features shows diminishing returns (27656049:e4#1 v12→v13).

rules.name: ohe_handle_unknown_categories
rules.context: When OneHotEncoder is fitted on training data and the test set may contain unseen category values.
rules.action: Set handle_unknown='ignore' on the encoder as a safety net. Additionally, before transforming, map unknown test category values to the most common or most generic known category to avoid zeroing out rows entirely. Use debug prints to inspect encoder categories and identify unknowns. Do NOT use workarounds like transforming training data and slicing to test length.
rules.exceptions: If the OHE features have minimal importance, the handling method may not matter much (7823861:e2#2 showed barely any LB change).

rules.name: categorical_features_via_ohe_for_transformers
rules.context: When a pretrained transformer or embedding-based model needs to incorporate low-cardinality categorical metadata (e.g., category, domain) alongside text features.
rules.action: One-hot encode the categorical feature and concatenate it with the model's feature matrix (either as input or concatenated with transformer outputs before the final layer). Submit to verify the feature adds signal. Build incrementally: add one feature group, verify improvement, then add the next.
rules.exceptions: Improvement may be modest (+0.006 in 7240226:e3#1). Replacing token positions with one-hot values is unconventional and may not generalize.

rules.name: handcrafted_features_when_transformer_plateaus
rules.context: When a fine-tuned transformer model has plateaued on a text regression/ranking task and the targets include diverse quality dimensions (e.g., formatting, length, readability).
rules.action: Add scaled handcrafted text features (word/sentence counts, readability scores, spelling errors, paragraph statistics) as a separate input branch concatenated with transformer outputs before the final dense layer, or feed them to a GBDT alongside transformer embeddings. Scale numeric features with StandardScaler. Also consider sentence-level aggregations (mean, std) of readability metrics to capture within-document variance.
rules.exceptions: Gains from adding more textstat features at finer granularity show diminishing returns (59253662:e5#1 gained only +0.00098). The combined pipeline in 58527792:e3#2 was never submitted.

rules.name: pivot_to_new_feature_families_when_tuning_plateaus
rules.context: When hyperparameter tuning of a tree model on existing features shows marginal or no LB improvement, and expanding the number of selected features from the same pool doesn't help.
rules.action: Pivot to adding qualitatively different feature families (e.g., linguistic, syntactic, sentiment, embeddings) rather than continuing to tune the same feature set or expanding selection count. Introducing new feature families provides more uplift than squeezing the same features harder.
rules.exceptions: The first submission after adding new features may roughly match (not exceed) the previous best, serving as a correctness check (55591012:e8#2).

rules.name: isolate_preprocessing_changes_in_submissions
rules.context: When adding a new preprocessing step (e.g., notch filter, feature transform) at inference time that was not used during model training.
rules.action: Only add inference-time preprocessing that matches training-time preprocessing. If a filter or transform was not used during training, do not apply it at inference—it creates train-test mismatch. If you must test a new preprocessing step, isolate it as the sole change in one submission to measure its effect cleanly.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: bundle_complementary_small_changes
rules.context: When individual feature engineering changes (e.g., adding one aggregation, one interaction, one rounding) each have small or ambiguous effects based on prior experiments, and submission budget is limited.
rules.action: Bundle multiple complementary feature additions into one submission. Use local CV to pre-screen individual changes and only submit the combined package. If the bundle improves, keep it. However, avoid changing two untested things simultaneously without CV pre-screening, as this makes attribution impossible and regressions hard to debug.
rules.exceptions: Bundling makes it impossible to attribute gains to any single change (27836972:e6#1). The author in 27825577:e5#1 explicitly warns against stacking multiple untested changes.

rules.name: keep_all_features_in_regularized_gbdt
rules.context: When using a well-regularized GBDT (feature_fraction/colsample, early stopping, L1/L2) on tabular data and considering manually removing broad categories of engineered features or raising/removing arbitrary feature count caps.
rules.action: Do not manually remove broad categories of engineered features (e.g., max, min, shift aggregations) or aggressively truncate preselected feature lists. The model's built-in regularization handles irrelevant features. Start with the full feature set; only truncate if memory/runtime is a binding constraint. If a targeted exclusion regresses the score, revert immediately.
rules.exceptions: When using high-dimensional sparse text features (TF-IDF/count vectors with thousands of features), importance-based feature selection typically still helps even with regularized GBDTs (see 60197293:e7#2).

rules.name: importance_based_selection_for_sparse_text_features
rules.context: When feeding thousands of sparse text-derived features (TF-IDF, count vectors) into LightGBM/XGBoost models.
rules.action: Keep importance-based feature selection enabled. If disabled for debugging, always re-enable before final submission. Sweep the feature count cutoff in both directions from the current value (e.g., ±1000). If both directions degrade the score, the current value is near-optimal—stop and move to other levers.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: re_sweep_feature_selection_after_config_change
rules.context: When regularization, training objective, or feature composition has changed since the last feature-selection sweep (e.g., new regularization params, new embedding features added, or stacking features introduced).
rules.action: Re-sweep the feature-selection cutoff under the new configuration. When adding high-dimensional embeddings or stacking features, co-vary the feature-selection step: test (1) new features + old selection, (2) old features + dedicated selection, (3) new features + dedicated selection. If new features cause regression, re-enable or tighten feature selection before concluding they are harmful.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: sweep_feature_selection_ratio_monotonically
rules.context: When performing importance-based feature selection on hundreds of engineered features and each run yields a validation score.
rules.action: Start at a low fraction (e.g., 10%), sweep upward in increments (5-10 percentage points or doubling steps: 0.1→0.2→0.25→0.33→0.5→0.75). Stop when validation plateaus. If you change the objective or regularization, restart the sweep from the low end since the optimal cutoff may shift.
rules.exceptions: The optimal ratio may be near 1.0 for well-regularized GBDTs, making the sweep less informative (27389424:e6#1).

rules.name: trust_repeated_feature_removal_signal
rules.context: When a specific feature group (e.g., count aggregation) was previously shown to hurt LB performance and has been re-introduced alongside other changes.
rules.action: If removing a feature group previously yielded a clear improvement, and re-adding it doesn't show validation gains, remove it again. Trust the repeated signal over the hope that context changes (new hyperparameters, more folds) will make the feature useful. Submit only after confirming the removal still helps.
rules.exceptions: The effect size may shrink when other changes (regularization, fold strategy) partially compensate (27799930:e7#1 showed only +0.00035 vs original larger gain).

rules.name: prune_new_features_by_subcategory
rules.context: When a large batch of new engineered features (e.g., 50+ NLP/linguistic features) has been added in bulk and local validation is available.
rules.action: Add the full feature group first, then prune by removing entire sub-categories one at a time (e.g., sentiment, tense, paragraph stats), checking local validation after each removal. Remove features that duplicate signals already present in other feature groups first. Submit only after the pruned set stabilizes. If the entire group is net-negative, consider removing it all rather than continuing subcategory ablation.
rules.exceptions: If the entire group is net-negative (55987255:e14#1 scored worse than pre-episode best), group-level add/remove may be faster than subcategory pruning.

rules.name: remove_redundant_resolution_variant_features
rules.context: When a block of features represents the same underlying concept at multiple granularities or resolutions (e.g., matching scores at 6/8/10 loci, or one-hot categoricals that a transformer already encodes).
rules.action: Remove the entire block of redundant resolution-variant or implicitly-encoded features rather than selecting individual columns. For transformer models, remove broad one-hot categorical features from auxiliary inputs since the transformer likely already captures categorical distinctions through text. Verify with a submission.
rules.exceptions: The improvement may be confounded with other simultaneous changes (7613444:e4#2 also changed dropout and fold count).

rules.name: prefer_shap_over_native_importance_for_selection
rules.context: When choosing between SHAP-based and native tree split-count importance for feature selection in a GBDT model with many correlated features, and permutation importance has proven noisy.
rules.action: Prefer SHAP-based feature ranking over native split-count importance for feature selection. SHAP better accounts for feature interactions and correlated features. If native importance or permutation importance causes a regression, revert to SHAP. When permutation-importance-based removal hurts, regenerate importance with a different method or seed and only drop features consistently ranked unimportant across methods.
rules.exceptions: The SHAP advantage is inferred rather than cleanly isolated in both cases due to confounded changes.

rules.name: increase_depth_lower_lr_together
rules.context: When increasing GBDT tree depth substantially (e.g., doubling), especially after feature engineering has enriched the feature set beyond the original starter configuration.
rules.action: Proportionally lower the learning rate when increasing tree depth (e.g., depth 4→7 paired with lr 0.05→0.03). Add stronger regularization (lambda, gamma, min_child_weight, or reduced column sampling) to compensate for the increased capacity. Conversely, when reducing depth, allow a higher learning rate.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: stop_hp_sweep_at_plateau
rules.context: When tuning GBDT hyperparameters and the score matches or nearly matches the best known result, with micro-adjustments producing no further improvement.
rules.action: Make one final micro-adjustment (±1 on integer params, ±0.1 on float params) to confirm the plateau. If no improvement, stop the sweep and switch to a different lever (features, model architecture, ensembling) rather than continuing to search the same hyperparameter space.
rules.exceptions: If validation and LB diverge significantly, the plateau may be an artifact of one metric; verify on both before stopping.

rules.name: sweep_regularization_log_scale_then_narrow
rules.context: When sweeping a regularization parameter (reg_lambda, reg_alpha) for a GBDT model and the optimal range is unknown.
rules.action: Do a coarse log-scale sweep first (e.g., 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100) to find the order of magnitude, then narrow within the best bracket. If after many trials (10+) no clear optimum emerges, the regularization lever has low sensitivity—stop and switch to a different lever.
rules.exceptions: For high-dimensional sparse features (e.g., TF-IDF), smaller step sizes (20-30% increments) may be needed as per 60197293:e8#2.

rules.name: num_leaves_max_depth_compatibility
rules.context: When tuning num_leaves in LightGBM alongside max_depth.
rules.action: Keep num_leaves and max_depth compatible: num_leaves should not exceed 2^max_depth. Increase num_leaves in at most 2-3x steps. A large jump (e.g., 31→200 with depth=5, or 200→1000 with depth=25) risks overfitting. If a moderate increase already degraded performance, do not try a much larger value.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: sequential_model_load_predict_free_for_ensembles
rules.context: When running inference with multiple large models (transformers or vision) sequentially on a GPU with limited memory, such as Kaggle's environment.
rules.action: Load one model at a time, run predictions, then explicitly delete the model and call gc.collect() (and torch.cuda.empty_cache() for PyTorch). Accumulate predictions in CPU memory and average after all models finish. If OOM persists after deletion, also reduce batch size. Do not hold multiple models in GPU memory simultaneously.
rules.exceptions: For very small models, simultaneous loading may be fine. In 7823861, the root cause was multi-model loading rather than batch size, so fix memory management before adjusting batch size.

rules.name: dtype_downcast_and_gc_in_aggregation_pipelines
rules.context: When groupby aggregations on many numeric columns produce wide DataFrames (e.g., 100+ features × multiple statistics) and the pipeline runs in a fixed-RAM environment like Kaggle.
rules.action: Immediately downcast output columns after each aggregation step (float64→float32, int64→int32, counts→int8). Call gc.collect() after each major aggregation and after deleting intermediate DataFrames. If a single groupby().agg() call exceeds memory, split it into multiple calls with disjoint function lists, store results separately, then concatenate.
rules.exceptions: Removing DataFrame copies (X_train/X_test) to save memory can introduce indexing bugs—test carefully before committing (v44→v45 in 27799930).

rules.name: serialize_fold_models_to_disk
rules.context: When using K-fold GBDT or deep learning ensembles and keeping all fold models in memory simultaneously with test data would exceed memory limits.
rules.action: During training, save each fold's model to disk immediately after fitting (e.g., clf.save_model or torch.save). At inference, load one fold model at a time, accumulate predictions, then delete the model and call gc.collect() before loading the next. Average predictions after all folds.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: fallback_to_cpu_for_unproven_gpu_features
rules.context: When a GPU-accelerated library (e.g., CuPy) for feature computation introduces multiple import or runtime errors in the notebook environment and the feature it computes has not yet been proven valuable.
rules.action: Fall back to the CPU equivalent (e.g., SciPy instead of CuPy) to unblock experimentation. Do not submit until the pipeline runs cleanly end-to-end. If the feature doesn't improve the score once working via the CPU path, drop both the feature and the GPU dependency entirely.
rules.exceptions: If the GPU path is needed for speed (e.g., real-time inference constraints), invest in fixing it rather than falling back.

rules.name: match_inference_architecture_to_checkpoint
rules.context: When loading externally trained checkpoints into an inference notebook and the model architecture (head layers, pooling, fusion method, activation functions, dropout) may differ between training and inference code.
rules.action: Compare the inference model definition layer-by-layer against the training configuration that produced the checkpoint. Match dropout layers, activation functions, head input dimensions, pooling type, and fusion method exactly. If a mismatch is suspected (poor scores or errors), adjust the model definition to match the checkpoint, not vice versa. Test with a non-submitted run before submitting.
rules.exceptions: If the FC/head layer is small enough to train from scratch, a mismatch in the head may be tolerable while backbone weights still load correctly.

rules.name: prefer_simple_pooling_on_small_data
rules.context: When using a pretrained transformer for regression/classification on a small dataset (<5K samples) and considering complex learned pooling heads (attention pooling, weighted hidden layers) vs simple pooling (CLS, mean of last hidden state).
rules.action: Start with simple pooling (pooler output or mean of last hidden state). If trying complex pooling with learnable parameters, verify on CV that it outperforms the simple baseline before submitting. On small datasets, added head parameters tend to overfit. If complex pooling doesn't beat simple pooling after 2-3 attempts, revert to simple pooling and pursue diversity through ensembling different simple variants instead.
rules.exceptions: Complex pooling may still help if combined with proper regularization (e.g., multisample dropout) or if the ensemble of complex variants provides diversity gains (17371717:e2#2).

rules.name: head_architecture_diversity_for_ensemble
rules.context: When the backbone is fixed (e.g., same pretrained transformer) and individual models plateau on a small noisy dataset, but you can train multiple head variants.
rules.action: Train at least 3 head variants differing in pooling mechanism (CLS, attention, mean/max) and regularization (single dropout, multisample dropout, different rates). Keep backbone and training procedure identical. At inference, average all variants' predictions. Expect ~0.005 RMSE improvement from diversity alone on small noisy datasets. Individual head architecture matters less than diversity across heads.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: validate_new_architecture_in_isolation_before_ensembling
rules.context: When integrating a fundamentally different model architecture (e.g., 3D CNN, new backbone family) into an existing multi-model ensemble pipeline.
rules.action: Run inference with only the new model first and verify its standalone score is reasonable before blending it into the ensemble. If standalone performance is poor, fix the model weights or input preprocessing before blending. Do not blend a broken or untested model into a working ensemble, as it will regress the ensemble score.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: reduce_model_complexity_when_adding_folds
rules.context: When transitioning from a single-model training setup to k-fold CV with GBDT, and total training time becomes prohibitive.
rules.action: Reduce per-model complexity proportionally when introducing k-fold CV: cut boosting rounds (e.g., 5000→1000) and reduce tree complexity (fewer leaves). The ensemble effect of averaging k models compensates for weaker individual models. Fine-tune hyperparameters once the CV infrastructure is stable.
rules.exceptions: If the original model was already simple, further reduction may hurt more than fold-averaging helps (29588171:e5#2 shows that when blend weight is tiny, tuning is futile regardless).

rules.name: port_preprocessing_improvements_across_architectures
rules.context: When a preprocessing improvement (e.g., NER tagging, math normalization, text cleaning) was developed and validated on one model architecture but not yet tested with another architecture that previously showed promise.
rules.action: Port the preprocessing improvement to all available architectures and test each combination. Preprocessing gains often transfer across architectures. Combine the best preprocessing with each architecture variant and compare LB scores.
rules.exceptions: Preprocessing that is architecture-specific (e.g., tokenizer-dependent normalization) may not transfer.

rules.name: simplify_before_scaling_on_small_data
rules.context: When increasing model capacity (wider layers, more blocks, deeper networks) yields no improvement on a small dataset (<10K rows).
rules.action: Suspect the bottleneck is data volume rather than model expressiveness. Simplify the architecture (fewer layers, smaller hidden sizes) and ensure full training data is used. With small datasets, a single hidden layer often suffices and adding layers mainly adds overfitting risk. Only scale up capacity when you have evidence (e.g., underfitting on training loss) that the model is too small.
rules.exceptions: If offline training with a larger model shows clearly better per-fold validation scores, capacity was indeed the bottleneck (49524919:e11#1).

rules.name: keep_multi_input_fusion_when_validated
rules.context: When a multi-input fusion model (learned head concatenating features from multiple branches) consistently outperforms simple prediction averaging across single-input models.
rules.action: Treat the fusion head as load-bearing and do not remove it. Shift optimization to backbone choice, checkpoint selection, or input preprocessing instead. If disabling fusion causes regression across multiple tests, the learned cross-branch interactions are contributing meaningfully.
rules.exceptions: If the fusion head's FC layer doesn't match checkpoint weights (e.g., after switching concat vs average), scores will degrade regardless of fusion quality.

rules.name: concat_over_average_for_branch_fusion
rules.context: When a dual-branch model produces same-dimensional embeddings and you must choose between element-wise averaging and concatenation for fusion before the classifier.
rules.action: Prefer concatenation over averaging, as it preserves all information from both branches and lets the classifier learn cross-branch interactions. Double the input size of the final linear layer accordingly. If pretrained weights exist, ensure the fusion method matches training. Test both methods and expect the one matching training to win; if the alternative is worse, revert immediately.
rules.exceptions: Concatenation doubles the FC layer size, which may cause overfitting on small datasets or fail to load pretrained weights.

rules.name: ordinal_head_for_ordinal_metrics
rules.context: When the target is ordinal with few classes (e.g., 1-6) and the metric penalizes disordered predictions (e.g., QWK), and you have a working regression pipeline.
rules.action: Replace the regression output with K-1 sigmoid outputs summed to produce a continuous score in [0, K-1], then shift to match the label range. Use the same optimized rounding post-processing. This preserves ordinal monotonicity. However, do not assume ordinal-head benefits transfer across backbone sizes—test each head type with each backbone independently.
rules.exceptions: Ordinal head that scored 0.827 with large DeBERTa scored only 0.819 with small DeBERTa (55621328:e48#2), suggesting backbone-head interaction matters.

rules.name: bundle_infrastructure_upgrades_when_far_from_competitive
rules.context: When the baseline score is far below competitive range and multiple bottlenecks exist simultaneously (resolution, model capacity, data throughput, accelerator).
rules.action: Bundle infrastructure upgrade (accelerator, data pipeline), resolution increase, and stronger backbone into a single step rather than isolating each factor. This is justified when the baseline is clearly under-optimized on all fronts and the expected gain is large enough that attribution across factors is less important than rapid progress.
rules.exceptions: Bundling makes it impossible to attribute the gain to any single factor, which can mislead subsequent fine-tuning decisions.

rules.name: refactor_nn_training_pipeline_after_proving_value
rules.context: When a neural network component has demonstrated value in an ensemble but uses ad-hoc training code lacking proper fold-wise saving, DataLoaders, or consistent OOF/test prediction generation.
rules.action: Refactor to use proper fold-wise training with framework DataLoaders, save per-fold model checkpoints, and tune hyperparameters simultaneously. This consolidation step typically yields a small but reliable gain by ensuring OOF/test prediction consistency.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: switch_linear_to_gbdt_on_tabular_plateau
rules.context: Linear models (e.g., Cox PH, Ridge, logistic regression) have plateaued on a tabular dataset with many categorical or mixed features, and no further linear variant improves the score.
rules.action: Switch to gradient-boosted decision trees (LightGBM, XGBoost, CatBoost). Use label-encoded categoricals (not one-hot). Rank-average or blend predictions across CV folds. Expect a meaningful improvement from capturing nonlinear interactions that linear models miss.
rules.exceptions: If the dataset is very small or high-dimensional relative to samples, linear models with regularization may still be competitive.

rules.name: boosting_framework_swap_protocol
rules.context: The current gradient boosting framework (e.g., LightGBM) has been extensively tuned with diminishing returns, and you want to probe whether an alternative framework (e.g., XGBoost) performs better.
rules.action: Adapt the custom metric callback and early stopping to the new library's API. Reduce CV folds to speed iteration. Do a quick hyperparameter sweep (3-5 variants) using CV only. Submit to LB only after CV suggests competitiveness. If the first LB submission underperforms the best known score by a meaningful margin, revert to the original framework rather than continuing to tune the new one.
rules.exceptions: Neither author confirmed the swap helped on LB — both reverted or never submitted, suggesting framework swaps at the plateau stage rarely yield gains.

rules.name: same_target_different_gbdt_library_diminishing_returns
rules.context: You already have strong GBDT models in an ensemble and are considering adding another GBDT variant (different library, e.g., LightGBM vs HistGBM) trained on the same target and features.
rules.action: Check whether the new model uses a genuinely different target transformation or feature set. If it only differs in the GBDT library on the same target, expect diminishing returns. Test with a single LB submission before investing in weight tuning. Prioritize adding models with different targets, architectures, or feature sets for ensemble diversity.
rules.exceptions: In some cases (e.g., CatBoost alongside LightGBM with different preprocessing), cross-library diversity can help — especially if the libraries handle categoricals or regularization differently.

rules.name: sweep_seed_count_incrementally_and_stop_on_regression
rules.context: When using multi-seed averaging (NN or GBDT) and wanting to reduce prediction variance without changing the model architecture or hyperparameters.
rules.action: Increase the seed/repeat count by +1 or +2 increments while the score improves. When a step regresses, treat the previous count as optimal and stop. Do not change other hyperparameters simultaneously, as confounded changes make regressions uninterpretable. After major model architecture changes, re-probe with a single +1 increment; if it doesn't help, redirect effort elsewhere.
rules.exceptions: In 27799930:e8#3 the seed count effect was confounded with disabling DART, so the regression signal was ambiguous. In 77129691:e3#1 the author violated the single-variable rule by changing COLLAPSE and NREPEATS together.

rules.name: average_folds_then_seeds_for_transformer_ensembles
rules.context: When you have transformer (e.g., DeBERTa) checkpoints from K folds and S seeds, and want to improve predictions without changing the training recipe.
rules.action: Average predictions across all K fold checkpoints first (expect a meaningful variance-reduction gain). Then add checkpoints from additional random seeds to the average. Expect diminishing but positive returns from each seed addition, typically saturating around 3-5 seeds. Verify gains via CV rather than a tiny public leaderboard.
rules.exceptions: In 17371717:e6#2, earlier multi-seed averaging attempts did not always improve, suggesting checkpoint quality matters as much as the averaging itself.

rules.name: prefer_existing_backbone_seed_diversity_over_new_architectures
rules.context: When adding new transformer backbone types to an ensemble has been tried and failed (pruned due to regression), but existing validated backbones have untapped folds or seeds.
rules.action: Train additional seeds or folds of already-validated backbone architectures and add their predictions to the ensemble. Each addition should be verified via CV before submission. Expect diminishing but reliable gains. This is lower risk than introducing new architectures.
rules.exceptions: Gains may be very small (e.g., ~0.00016 RMSE) and indistinguishable from noise on small public leaderboards.

rules.name: verify_seed_variation_impact_before_scaling_on_small_lb
rules.context: When the public leaderboard has very few scoring rows (e.g., ~7) and you are considering multi-seed or multi-run averaging to improve score.
rules.action: Before scaling up the number of seed runs, verify on local CV that different seeds produce meaningfully different predictions. Do not trust a tiny public LB to detect small ensemble improvements. If two doublings of ensemble size show zero LB change, stop and switch to a different lever (e.g., blend weights, new backbones).
rules.exceptions: Lack of LB score change may reflect LB insensitivity rather than true ineffectiveness, so CV is the authoritative signal.

rules.name: offline_precomputation_for_pipeline_stability
rules.context: An expensive or non-deterministic pipeline component (e.g., model training, feature selection) is recomputed each run inside the submission notebook, causing instability, slowness, or interactions with other pipeline stages.
rules.action: Move the expensive component offline: run it once with proper validation, save its output (model weights, prediction files, selected feature lists) as versioned artifacts, and load them as fixed inputs in the submission notebook. This decouples the component from in-notebook changes, making the pipeline deterministic and faster. Re-run offline only when data or methodology changes significantly.
rules.exceptions: Loses adaptability if the underlying data or feature set changes significantly between runs, requiring the offline artifacts to be regenerated.

rules.name: align_cv_infrastructure_across_ensemble_members
rules.context: An ensemble combines multiple model components but one component lacks proper K-Fold CV structure and per-fold model persistence, while other components (e.g., GBDT models) already use proper CV pipelines.
rules.action: Refactor the weaker component to use the same K-Fold CV scheme as other ensemble members: iterate over folds, preprocess per fold, train, save each fold's model state, and generate aligned OOF predictions. This ensures unbiased OOF predictions compatible with stacking. The immediate LB gain may be small, but the infrastructure enables reliable future ensemble tuning and offline iteration.
rules.exceptions: Immediate score improvement may be negligible (e.g., +0.00003); the value materializes when combined with later ensemble weight tuning or offline model improvement cycles.

rules.name: debug_pipeline_not_postprocessing_on_bad_scores
rules.context: When a model produces unexpectedly poor scores (near-zero, negative, or large regression) after a code change, and the metric is rank-invariant or the regression doesn't correlate with the specific change made.
rules.action: Do not iterate on normalization, post-processing, or downstream transforms. Instead, trace the problem upstream: inspect raw model outputs for shape/alignment, check whether config or initialization calls silently override parameters (print effective config values), and verify data pipeline integrity. Disable the suspect change, re-run the baseline to confirm, then re-enable incrementally.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: incremental_activation_of_complex_additions
rules.context: When integrating a large or complex code change (multi-branch model, major preprocessing block) into a notebook, especially with limited debugging visibility (e.g., inference-only kernel).
rules.action: Activate complex components incrementally: wire up architecture or preprocessing first, fix runtime errors, test with minimal data/checkpoints and submit for early signal, then scale up. After inserting a large preprocessing block, re-read original data from disk in a subsequent cell to ensure downstream code has clean, unmodified inputs. Submit after each incremental step to isolate regressions.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: cleanup_new_model_before_abandoning
rules.context: A newly integrated model underperforms the existing best, and its code contains unused helpers, redundant configuration, or copy-paste boilerplate from rapid prototyping.
rules.action: Before abandoning the model, do an aggressive cleanup pass: remove unused helper functions, inline simple constants, simplify data/channel configuration, and verify pretrained weight paths. Dead code and misconfiguration can silently degrade predictions. Resubmit after cleanup to get a fair comparison.
rules.exceptions: Improvement may partly stem from fixing specific misconfigurations (e.g., wrong pretrained weights) discovered during cleanup rather than cleanup per se.

rules.name: simplify_preprocessing_for_tree_models
rules.context: A GBDT pipeline (XGBoost, LightGBM) includes scaling, imputation, or outlier removal, but the model natively handles missing values and is invariant to monotone feature transformations.
rules.action: Remove StandardScaler, median imputation, and z-score outlier removal from the pipeline. Let the tree model handle missingness natively, preserving informative patterns. Submit to confirm no degradation. Exception: post-aggregation NaN cleanup may still be needed when aggregation functions produce NaNs.
rules.exceptions: In 28093671 the author later re-added imputation of NaN aggregates, suggesting some post-aggregation cleanup is still needed. This rule applies specifically to tree-based models, not neural networks.

rules.name: consolidate_pipeline_into_single_composable_structure
rules.context: Preprocessing or model evaluation logic is scattered across manual operations outside the main pipeline (e.g., numpy shape ops outside albumentations, or repeated per-variant boilerplate), causing fragility and copy-paste bugs.
rules.action: Refactor all operations into a single composable pipeline: move shape/normalization ops into custom transform classes, or centralize variant configurations into a lookup dictionary so each variant is a single function call. This prevents inconsistencies with TTA/augmentation and eliminates copy-paste errors when switching variants.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: logit_rescaling_for_rank_metrics
rules.context: When a neural network's sigmoid outputs cluster near 0.5 with low discrimination, and the evaluation metric is rank-based (e.g., C-index, AUC) rather than calibration-sensitive.
rules.action: Multiply the pre-activation logits by a small constant (e.g., 2) to sharpen the sigmoid output distribution, increasing discrimination without retraining. Test a single reasonable value first; if it improves the ranking metric, keep it. Re-tune blend weights afterward since the NN's predictions are now more informative.
rules.exceptions: Only tested with factor=2; optimal value unknown. Diminishing returns when combined with other variance-reduction tricks (77129691 v20 did not improve further).

rules.name: avoid_clipping_for_rank_metrics
rules.context: When the evaluation metric is rank-based (e.g., Spearman correlation, AUC) and model outputs may extend beyond the nominal target range [0,1].
rules.action: Avoid clipping raw model outputs because clipping creates ties that degrade rank correlation. Use rank-preserving transformations (e.g., min-max scaling per column or quantile mapping) to map outputs into the required range. Only clip if the submission format strictly requires bounded values, using the widest bounds possible.
rules.exceptions: Even rank-preserving scaling needs careful implementation; MinMaxScaler scored poorly in one attempt (6803050 v10), suggesting execution matters.

rules.name: scaler_choice_for_ensemble_blending
rules.context: When ensemble component predictions have different scales and you are choosing a scaler (StandardScaler, RobustScaler, none) before weight optimization.
rules.action: If the weight optimizer searches over continuous weights at fine precision, explicit scaling (StandardScaler) is unlikely to help because the optimizer compensates for scale differences. When changing the scaler, always re-optimize ensemble weights from scratch since weights found under one scaler are not transferable. If scores remain similar across scalers, prefer the simpler option for stability.
rules.exceptions: When some models have heavy-tailed outlier predictions, RobustScaler may help. Other factors (e.g., OOF overfitting) may dominate scaler choice (75584724:e7#2).

rules.name: distribution_matching_caution_under_shift
rules.context: When the test set distribution may differ from training (known domain shift) and you are considering post-processing to align prediction distributions to training label frequencies.
rules.action: Be cautious with hard-coded distribution matching: if the test distribution differs from training, forcing the training distribution onto predictions will hurt. Prefer threshold-based rounding or make distribution alignment toggleable so you can A/B test. Validate on a held-out set or via LB before committing. Include optional flags (e.g., --do-scale) for easy toggling.
rules.exceptions: Earlier scaling attempts (v131-v134) produced worse scores, but text normalization (v105) improved scores, suggesting the interaction with preprocessing matters.

rules.name: monotonic_transform_on_sigmoid_probabilities
rules.context: When predictions are post-sigmoid (bounded [0,1]) and the metric is rank-based (AUC), and predictions may cluster near extremes compressing discriminative signal.
rules.action: Apply a concave power transform (e.g., square root, exponent < 1) to each model's sigmoid predictions before blending to spread values. Submit to check for improvement. Re-test after major pipeline changes (adding folds, new models) because the benefit may be fragile and context-dependent.
rules.exceptions: Benefit was fragile: reverted in v7 after adding fold-aware averaging, then re-added in v8 with new weights. Must be re-validated after structural changes.

rules.name: discretize_predictions_for_rank_based_metrics
rules.context: The evaluation metric is rank-based (e.g., Spearman correlation), the model outputs continuous predictions, and the ground truth labels take only a few discrete values (e.g., averages of crowd ratings).
rules.action: Post-process predictions by snapping/discretizing them to the known discrete target levels. Start conservatively with the most binary/sparse columns (e.g., clamp extremes near 0 or 1). Expand incrementally, one or a few columns at a time, verifying each batch improves the score. If a batch causes regression, revert entirely rather than partially fixing. Check for degeneracy (all values collapsed to one bin) and revert affected columns to continuous predictions.
rules.exceptions: Scaling/discretizing all columns at once can hurt (7548275 v24, 7823861 v22-v23). Binarizing near-binary columns may not help if the model already captures ranking well (6803050:e13#2). KBinsDiscretizer may be replaced by epsilon-based quantization for more adaptive results (7018718:e13#1).

rules.name: optimize_rounding_thresholds_for_qwk
rules.context: The evaluation metric is QWK (or similar ordinal metric), the model outputs continuous regression scores that must be mapped to discrete ordinal labels, and out-of-fold predictions are available.
rules.action: Use numerical optimization (e.g., Nelder-Mead via scipy.optimize.minimize) on OOF predictions to find rounding thresholds that maximize QWK, rather than using naive uniform midpoints (1.5, 2.5, etc.). Apply these optimized thresholds to test predictions. Naive thresholds can cost ~0.02 QWK. Fit thresholds on the data subset most representative of the test distribution.
rules.exceptions: Gain may be modest (~0.002) when the model is already well-calibrated (58130512:e6#1). Threshold optimization was sometimes removed in subsequent versions (58130512 v20), suggesting it doesn't always help.

rules.name: reoptimize_thresholds_when_model_changes
rules.context: The underlying model, checkpoint, or ensemble composition has changed (e.g., new architecture, new checkpoint, different number of folds averaged), and post-processing rounding thresholds were previously tuned for the old model.
rules.action: Always re-optimize rounding thresholds on local validation after any change to the model producing raw predictions. Do not reuse old thresholds. First submit with minimal/default post-processing to establish a new baseline, then incrementally re-tune. If two consecutive threshold/checkpoint combinations both regress, the issue is likely the model itself, not the thresholds—move on.
rules.exceptions: Threshold tuning alone may not recover a bad checkpoint (55621328:e28#2 v82 improved but didn't beat v80).

rules.name: conservative_incremental_postprocessing_expansion
rules.context: Applying column-specific or rule-based post-processing to multiple prediction columns, where each column may respond differently to discretization/thresholding.
rules.action: Add post-processing rules incrementally: start with the columns most likely to benefit (most discrete/binary distributions), verify improvement, then expand. Never add many new columns or aggressive intermediate bins simultaneously. If a batch causes regression, revert the entire batch rather than trying to fix individual rules incrementally.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: retest_rank_conversion_after_every_change
rules.context: When you have a cheap binary post-processing toggle (e.g., rank-based averaging vs raw probability averaging) and you have just made a substantive change to model architecture, backbone, checkpoint, image size, or fold count.
rules.action: Always test both states of the toggle (rank on and rank off) after every change. Do not assume the previous setting carries over—the optimal setting is configuration-dependent. Budget 2 submissions per change. If the gap is small (<0.002), prefer raw scores to preserve calibration for future ensembling.
rules.exceptions: When submission budget is very tight, the benefit is often small (≤0.003), so this may not justify the cost in all competitions.

rules.name: inference_dropout_match_training
rules.context: When loading pretrained transformer checkpoints for inference and considering whether to modify dropout settings at inference time.
rules.action: Keep inference-time dropout consistent with training-time settings. Default to dropout=0.0 for deterministic inference. If you must experiment, test at most one non-zero value; if it doesn't improve, revert immediately. Inference-time dropout changes are a weak lever when checkpoints were trained with fixed dropout.
rules.exceptions: MC-dropout for uncertainty estimation is a deliberate exception where non-zero inference dropout is intended.

rules.name: model_specific_inference_routing
rules.context: When integrating externally-trained models with different preprocessing, serialization formats, or prediction methods into a heterogeneous ensemble inference pipeline.
rules.action: Create dedicated conditional branches in the inference loop keyed by model name. Each branch applies model-specific preprocessing (imputer, scaler, feature engineering) that exactly replicates training-time transforms. For models saved as dicts or multi-component objects, reconstruct an sklearn Pipeline at load time for a uniform .predict() interface. Add debug prints and test end-to-end before submitting.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: serialize_full_pipelines_not_bare_models
rules.context: When saving pretrained models from a separate training environment for use in an inference notebook, especially when models require specific preprocessing steps.
rules.action: Serialize full sklearn-compatible pipelines (preprocessing + model) rather than bare model objects. In the inference notebook, load each pipeline and verify the return signature matches what the blending/ensemble code expects. For deep learning, prefer building architecture in code and loading weights separately rather than using full model serialization (e.g., load_model), which often fails with custom layers or TPU scopes.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: softmax_before_ensemble_averaging_for_kl
rules.context: When ensembling multiple folds/models whose outputs are logits and the evaluation metric is KL divergence or operates on probability distributions.
rules.action: Apply softmax to each fold/model's logits individually before averaging across folds, rather than averaging logits and applying softmax once at the end. Test both orderings empirically. Also verify whether models already output probabilities (softmax applied internally); applying softmax twice distorts distributions. Submit one variant to confirm.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: checkpoint_discovery_method
rules.context: When loading model checkpoints for ensemble inference and choosing between hard-coded paths vs. directory-based discovery (glob/listdir).
rules.action: If you need precise control over which folds/seeds are included (e.g., excluding specific folds based on validation scores), use a hard-coded list of file paths annotated with fold index and validation score. If checkpoints are organized by model type in separate directories with consistent naming, use sorted directory listing to reduce maintenance burden. Be aware that directory-based discovery can accidentally include unwanted files (optimizer states, etc.).
rules.exceptions: These two items recommend opposite approaches: hard-coded for control (18426209) vs. directory-based for convenience (50496431). Choose based on whether precision of ensemble composition or maintenance simplicity is the priority.

rules.name: config_checkpoint_architecture_match
rules.context: When switching to new model checkpoints that were trained under a different configuration than the default config, or deploying a new architecture that differs from the existing inference pipeline.
rules.action: Verify that inference config parameters (number of output labels, head type, special encodings, custom layers) exactly match what the checkpoints were trained with. Override mismatched parameters via command-line args rather than editing config files. If the architecture differs, add the new model class alongside the old one with a config flag for conditional instantiation. Keep the old code path for fallback. Test with a single submission before tuning weights.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: custom_inference_script_over_framework_default
rules.context: When the default inference path from a training framework produces inconsistent or suboptimal scores, and you suspect the black-box inference mechanics are unreliable.
rules.action: Write a dedicated inference script that explicitly restores model configs, loads weights, constructs the model, and runs batched prediction. Disable dynamic/adaptive features (dynamic input shapes, adaptive batch sizing) during non-standard inference modes. This gives full control over flags, preprocessing, and post-processing. Test against the previous pipeline; if it yields a new best, keep it as the stable foundation.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: retain_all_complementary_modalities
rules.context: When building a multi-input model for signal classification (e.g., EEG) where multiple views of the same underlying data are available (raw signals, spectrograms, derived images, text fields), and you are considering simplifying by dropping modalities.
rules.action: Retain all complementary modalities in the final model. Ablate one modality at a time rather than dropping to a single one. Expect that fundamentally different representations (e.g., raw EEG + spectrograms) carry substantial complementary information. If a modality consistently fails to help across multiple attempts, abandon it and invest in augmentation or ensemble diversity instead.
rules.exceptions: Adding low-signal fields or over-expanding vocabulary when concatenating text fields can cause regression (7676170:e2#1 counter_evidence). Mel-spectrogram branches may not add value if existing spectrograms already cover the frequency content (49576186:e8#2).

rules.name: add_modality_branch_when_tuning_plateaus
rules.context: When a multi-modal or single-modal model has plateaued and hyperparameter tuning, data sampling changes, or backbone swaps have been exhausted or are regressing.
rules.action: Add a new input branch (either a new modality or an alternative representation of an existing modality with different temporal resolution/normalization). Keep existing branches and preprocessing unchanged. Feed the new branch through its own backbone and concatenate embeddings before the classification head. Submit the structural change alone before adding augmentation or LR changes to attribute improvement correctly.
rules.exceptions: Preprocessing quality of the new branch matters—earlier mel-spectrogram attempts in 49576186 had mixed results, suggesting modality addition alone is not always beneficial.

rules.name: ensemble_diverse_input_representations
rules.context: When an ensemble already contains multiple models consuming the same input representation (e.g., spectrogram-based CNNs) and raw signal data or a fundamentally different input format is available.
rules.action: Train a separate model on the fundamentally different input representation (e.g., raw 1D EEG signal, possibly reshaped into 2D for pretrained CNNs) and add it to the ensemble by averaging softmax outputs. Expect the largest ensemble gains from combining models with different input modalities rather than from adding another variant of the same modality. The raw-signal model may be weaker standalone—its value is primarily as a diversity contributor.
rules.exceptions: The raw model alone may score worse than the combined ensemble (50496431:e33#2 counter_evidence), so it should not replace existing members but supplement them.

rules.name: test_multimodal_fusion_via_swap_before_adding
rules.context: When introducing a multimodal fusion model (e.g., EEG + spectrogram double-head) into an existing ensemble that already contains single-modality models covering those same modalities.
rules.action: First test the fusion model as a standalone replacement for the single-modality member it most overlaps with (swap test). If it doesn't beat the existing ensemble or the swapped member, try combining it with the best single-modality models rather than using it alone. Do not add it as an extra ensemble member until the swap test confirms it adds value.
rules.exceptions: Swap tests may not be conclusive on their own—further experimentation may be needed (50496431:e38#2 counter_evidence).

rules.name: custom_competition_metric_as_training_signal
rules.context: When the competition uses a non-standard metric (e.g., weighted Gini, custom capture rate) and you consider using it directly as the GBDT eval metric or as sample weights to align training with it.
rules.action: Probe the custom metric as eval_metric or sample weights in a single isolated experiment. If OOF/LB score does not improve over standard metrics (AUC, logloss), revert to standard metrics. Complex sorting-based or piecewise custom metrics often produce noisy early-stopping signals. Ranking-based metric components are frequently better served by the model's native ranking ability than by loss reweighting.
rules.exceptions: When the custom metric is smooth and differentiable (e.g., KL divergence), direct alignment with the loss can help (see 49576186:e11#2).

rules.name: bert_finetuning_lr_range
rules.context: When fine-tuning a BERT-base model on a small dataset (≤10K samples) with few epochs (3-5) and the learning rate needs to be chosen or adjusted.
rules.action: Start with 3e-5 as the default learning rate. If you try a lower rate (e.g., 1e-5) and validation does not improve, revert to 3e-5 rather than searching further downward. Going above 5e-5 (e.g., 1e-4) typically overshoots and requires additional stabilization (warmup, batch norm). Sweep upward in ~3x multiplicative steps and stop when validation degrades.
rules.exceptions: When switching loss function (e.g., softmax CE to sigmoid BCE), gradient magnitudes change and lr may need re-calibration outside the standard range.

rules.name: lr_reduction_requires_proportional_iteration_increase
rules.context: When reducing the learning rate of a GBDT or iterative model that uses early stopping, and n_estimators/epochs must be adjusted accordingly.
rules.action: When reducing learning rate, increase n_estimators/max epochs by at least the inverse ratio (e.g., halving LR should at least double n_estimators) to allow early stopping to find the right iteration. Verify via validation curves that the model has converged before submitting. Similarly for transformers: when lowering LR by a large factor (e.g., 10x), slightly reduce epochs to avoid overfitting.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: isolate_hyperparameter_changes_after_loss_switch
rules.context: When switching loss function or activation (e.g., softmax→sigmoid, CE→BCE, CE→focal loss) and simultaneously adjusting learning rate, dropout, or other hyperparameters.
rules.action: First make the loss/activation switch alone with minimal other changes to establish a baseline. Then tune learning rate and dropout separately, one at a time. Bundling loss changes with hyperparameter changes makes it impossible to attribute gains or regressions. Expect that BCE/focal loss may need higher LR (2-3x) to compensate for smaller per-output gradients.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: early_stopping_with_custom_objectives
rules.context: When using early stopping with a custom objective function in GBDT and the early stopping metric may not align well with the true competition objective.
rules.action: Test early stopping with moderate patience (50-100 rounds). If local CV does not improve or worsens, remove early stopping and use fixed n_estimators with regularization tuning instead. Custom objectives can cause the early stopping metric to misalign with the actual objective, leading to premature stopping.
rules.exceptions: When the eval metric is the same as the competition metric and is well-behaved (smooth, monotonic), early stopping is more reliable.

rules.name: custom_loss_scalar_tuning_strategy
rules.context: When a custom loss function has tunable scalar constants (e.g., label shift, scale parameters) and other levers have been extensively explored.
rules.action: Hold one constant fixed while sweeping the other. First probe an extreme value to gauge sensitivity. If validation degrades, make small perturbations (±0.01-0.03) around the current best. If tuned constants are very close to simple round numbers (e.g., mean≈3→use 3), test whether rounding simplifies the pipeline without hurting CV. Stop when two consecutive perturbations in opposite directions both degrade, bracketing the optimum.
rules.exceptions: This lever often has limited headroom; if two rounds of perturbation fail to beat baseline, move to a different lever.

rules.name: probe_alternative_then_revert_quickly
rules.context: When considering switching a well-tuned component (optimizer, booster type, loss function) to a trendy or fundamentally different alternative.
rules.action: Probe the alternative in a single submission with minimal other changes. If it regresses, revert immediately and invest time re-tuning the original component's hyperparameters rather than tuning the new alternative. Tabular models and short-training-run NNs are often less sensitive to component novelty than to hyperparameter tuning of a known component.
rules.exceptions: When the alternative fixes a fundamental mismatch (e.g., softmax→sigmoid for independent targets), it should be kept even if initial scores regress.

rules.name: lr_scheduler_for_short_training
rules.context: When training a neural network for only a few epochs (≤5) and using a cosine-warmup schedule that spends a significant fraction of training in warmup.
rules.action: Replace cosine-warmup with a step-decay scheduler (e.g., MultiStepLR) that keeps the initial LR for the first epochs and drops sharply near the end. Place milestones at roughly 60-75% of total epochs with a large gamma reduction (0.1). Alternatively, pair with KL/custom losses that benefit from stable early learning rates.
rules.exceptions: The improvement may be very small (+0.0002 range); only worth pursuing when other levers are exhausted.

rules.name: small_public_test_trust_cv_and_stress_test
rules.context: The public test set is very small (e.g., fewer than ~10 rows or essays), making public LB scores unreliable for measuring incremental improvements.
rules.action: Do not use small public LB score changes (<0.005) to guide model or ensemble decisions; rely on local CV/OOF scores instead. Additionally, stress-test inference by duplicating the test dataframe many times (e.g., 2000x) to verify the pipeline scales within time and memory limits on the hidden test set. Reserve LB submissions for confirming large directional improvements only.
rules.exceptions: Continued LB experimentation may still surface real improvements (17616127 eventually found a much better score through iteration), so the rule is about not over-indexing on small LB deltas, not avoiding submissions entirely.

rules.name: additive_boost_over_rank_offset_for_subset_adjustment
rules.context: When blending ensemble predictions with a binary classifier that flags a subset of records (e.g., high-risk), and you want to boost that subset's scores, and rank-space offsets are not translating into score improvements.
rules.action: Apply the classifier-based adjustment as a direct additive constant to the final continuous prediction values rather than manipulating intermediate rank vectors. Rank transformations compress the signal and lose the boost magnitude. Start with a round number (e.g., +1.0) and fine-tune from there.
rules.exceptions: 77347591 found the effect was not very sensitive to the exact boost value; 75145694 highlights that the new model's binary output must also be included in all conditional branches.

rules.name: match_spectrogram_preprocessing_train_inference
rules.context: When using pretrained model checkpoints at inference time and considering changes to spectrogram generation parameters (n_fft, hop_length, win_length, scaling, normalization, frequency cropping, log transforms) or EEG bandpass filter parameters (low/high cutoff).
rules.action: Do not change spectrogram preprocessing or bandpass filter parameters at inference time unless the checkpoint was trained with those exact parameters. Mismatched parameters silently degrade performance, often causing large regressions (>0.05). Widening the band (e.g., high cutoff from 20 to 40Hz) introduces out-of-distribution frequency content that hurts pretrained models. If a change regresses, revert preprocessing first. Only change preprocessing if you retrain with the new settings. If you must widen the bandpass, add a notch filter for line noise (50/60Hz) first. Prefer small perturbations around training-time values and test in isolation.
rules.exceptions: Some parameter changes at inference can help if they happen to match or approximate training-time settings (e.g., 50496431:e5#1 where halving n_fft/hop_length together improved score, possibly matching training). 50496431:e17#1 suggests coordinated multi-parameter changes can sometimes work. 50496431:e29#2 notes that v51 showed filter changes could yield a new best, suggesting it depends on whether training used similar settings.

rules.name: bandpass_filter_before_spectrogram
rules.context: When computing spectrograms from raw EEG signals for a CNN-based classification model and the current pipeline uses naive STFT without domain-specific filtering.
rules.action: Apply domain-appropriate bandpass filtering (e.g., Butterworth filters targeting clinically relevant EEG frequency bands) before computing spectrograms. Widen the bandpass to preserve low-frequency EEG content if the high-pass cutoff is too aggressive. Lower the spectrogram clipping floor to retain low-amplitude spectral information. These preprocessing changes can yield large gains (>0.03) without model architecture changes.
rules.exceptions: Widening the bandpass at inference time without retraining can hurt (50496431:e45#2). If widening, add notch filters for line noise (50/60Hz).

rules.name: keep_spectrogram_resolution_near_pretrained_input
rules.context: When using a pretrained CNN backbone (e.g., EfficientNet) on spectrograms and considering increasing frequency resolution (e.g., doubling n_fft or frequency bins).
rules.action: Prefer keeping spectrogram dimensions close to the pretrained backbone's expected input size rather than dramatically increasing frequency resolution. Higher resolution spectrograms may hurt if the backbone wasn't designed for them or if they introduce noise. If increasing resolution regresses, revert and improve other aspects (backbone choice, ensemble diversity).
rules.exceptions: 50496431:e21#1 showed that increasing the vertical crop (more frequency content) can sometimes help, suggesting the optimal resolution depends on the specific model and training conditions.

rules.name: one_spectrogram_param_at_a_time
rules.context: When tuning spectrogram or signal preprocessing parameters (frequency cutoff, FFT window, colormap, normalization) for a CNN-based model.
