rules.action: Change only one spectrogram parameter at a time and submit after each change to isolate effects. If a change regresses, revert immediately before trying the next parameter. Do not bundle preprocessing changes with model architecture changes, as it becomes impossible to attribute score changes.
rules.exceptions: 50496431:e17#1 argues that tightly coupled parameters (clipping + FFT + scaling) should be changed in coordinated groups rather than one at a time, since changing one alone can cause catastrophic regression that the others would compensate for.

rules.name: stop_tuning_validated_window_param
rules.context: When an input window/crop parameter has been validated across multiple prior submissions and the current value is at or near the best observed score.
rules.action: Do not continue tuning that parameter, especially not simultaneously with other modifications. If you must explore, change only the window parameter in isolation. Repeated tuning of an already-optimized parameter yields diminishing returns and risks regression.
rules.exceptions: 50496431:e21#1 showed that even after many prior tuning attempts, doubling the crop percentage still improved the score, so the parameter space may not be fully explored.

rules.name: ridge_as_default_stacking_meta_learner
rules.context: When combining multiple base model predictions via stacking and the meta-feature space is low-dimensional (handful of base model outputs) with a small training set (<10k samples).
rules.action: Use Ridge regression as the default stacking meta-learner. It outperforms or matches nonlinear alternatives (SVR, neural nets) and Lasso on small meta-feature sets. If Lasso (L1) drops score substantially (>0.5% absolute), revert immediately—L1 aggressively zeros useful ensemble members. Reserve nonlinear meta-learners for when Ridge clearly plateaus.
rules.exceptions: 73937748:e18#1 shows Ridge→Lasso swap failed twice in the same notebook, suggesting L1 is rarely better for moderate-sized ensembles. When base models number in the hundreds, L1 sparsity may help.

rules.name: oof_predictions_as_stacking_features_for_tree_models
rules.context: When a strong pretrained model (e.g., DeBERTa transformer) has OOF predictions available and the downstream model is a gradient-boosted tree ensemble (LightGBM/XGBoost).
rules.action: Load the OOF prediction matrix (per-class probabilities or regression outputs), add each as a separate column to the tree model's training features, and ensure the same model's test-time predictions are added to test features. This gives the tree model access to the transformer's learned representation without coupling inference pipelines. Verify the full pipeline runs before submitting.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: conservative_feature_addition_to_stacker_on_small_data
rules.context: When the stacking meta-learner operates on a small dataset (<5k samples) and you are considering adding handcrafted features, auxiliary-task outputs, or external prediction sources beyond base model predictions.
rules.action: Add features incrementally, validating each addition via CV. Aggressively prune any that do not clearly improve CV. If adding a batch of features degrades the score, remove them rather than tuning the meta-learner. Prefer the minimal feature set that improves over baseline. Introduce a configuration flag to systematically test feature-source combinations.
rules.exceptions: 17616127:e27#1 notes an earlier attempt with binned logits did help slightly (v44→v45), so the effect depends on meta-learner regularization and ensemble composition.

rules.name: cross_architecture_blending_on_top_of_stacking
rules.context: When a stacking meta-model from one backbone family (e.g., RoBERTa) is available and separate large models from a different architecture family (e.g., ALBERT, DeBERTa) exist with independent predictions.
rules.action: Compute the stacked prediction from the meta-model, then blend it with predictions from the different model family using a weighted average. Give the stacked output roughly equal or slightly higher weight. Typical starting weights: stacked ~3/8, each cross-architecture model ~2-3/8. Verify each model group's standalone metric before blending to ensure diversity.
rules.exceptions: Specific weights are likely competition-dependent and should be tuned on OOF.

rules.name: kfold_oof_blending_for_ordinal_and_regression_tasks
rules.context: When combining multiple diverse gradient boosting models (LightGBM + XGBoost) or multiple transformer checkpoints for regression or ordinal prediction tasks.
rules.action: Train each model variant in a stratified K-fold loop, collect out-of-fold predictions, then blend OOF predictions across model types (average or weighted). For ordinal targets, map continuous blended predictions to discrete scores using optimized thresholds tuned on the full OOF set. Use 5-15 folds for stability depending on dataset size.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: external_auxiliary_features_may_add_noise
rules.context: When external labeled data with richer annotations (sub-scores, different rubrics) is available and you plan to predict auxiliary features from it to add to the main model's stacking layer.
rules.action: Encode both external and target data with the same embeddings, train a regressor on external data→sub-scores, predict sub-scores for train/test, and append as features. However, if the LB score regresses, abandon the approach rather than tuning—domain shift between external and target data often makes these auxiliary predictions noisy. Adding handcrafted text statistics to a stacker on small data carries similar risk.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: km_survival_probability_as_regression_target
rules.context: When predicting survival outcomes with censored data using tree-based regressors (XGB, CatBoost, LGB) or neural regressors, and the competition metric is concordance-based.
rules.action: Compute Kaplan-Meier survival curves from training data and assign each patient their KM-estimated survival probability at their observed time as the regression target. This converts censored survival data into a continuous [0,1] target any regressor can handle. Train with k-fold CV and use OOF predictions for ensemble blending. Ideally fit KM per fold to avoid leakage. Combine with other survival transforms (Nelson-Aalen, Cox, rank-based) for ensemble diversity.
rules.exceptions: Using full training set KM curve rather than fold-specific introduces slight data leakage (77276039:e3#2). Diminishing returns when many target transforms already exist (73937748:e17#1).

rules.name: target_transform_diversity_in_survival_ensembles
rules.context: When building an ensemble for survival prediction and the pipeline already supports iterating over a list of target transformations (e.g., Cox, KM, Nelson-Aalen, rank-based).
rules.action: Add multiple survival-risk target transforms so each model family trains on several target variants, producing diverse ensemble members. Each transform yields a separate OOF prediction column for blending. When adding a new transform, keep the rest of the pipeline fixed and submit to verify improvement. If a transform underperforms, remove it to keep the ensemble lean. Stop adding transforms when marginal gains become negligible.
rules.exceptions: Gains from additional transforms diminish; 73937748:e17#1 saw only +0.00055 and did not surpass overall best.

rules.name: use_predict_proba_for_probability_metrics
rules.context: When the competition metric depends on predicted probabilities or ranking (e.g., Gini, AUC, capture rate) but the current pipeline uses hard class predictions or regressor outputs.
rules.action: Switch from predict() to predict_proba() and compute the competition's actual metric on probability outputs. Verify calibration by plotting OOF probability distributions. Do this before hyperparameter tuning, since tuning against the wrong output type wastes iterations. If using a regressor formulation, switch to the classifier variant for naturally calibrated probability outputs.
rules.exceptions: 28984551:e5#1 found only +0.00047 improvement from regressor-to-classifier switch, suggesting formulation alone may not be the dominant factor.

rules.name: horizontal_flip_tta_as_first_inference_boost
rules.context: When you have a trained image/spectrogram model and want a quick inference-time accuracy boost without retraining, and the input has approximate horizontal symmetry (e.g., chest X-rays, spectrograms with time axis).
rules.action: Add horizontal flip TTA: run inference on both original and flipped input, apply activation (sigmoid/softmax) independently, then average. This is a single on/off probe—submit to verify it helps before adding more augmentations. Expect small gains (0.1–0.5% of metric). If memory is tight, halve batch size to compensate.
rules.exceptions: In some configurations the gain is negligible (15372370:e4#2 showed ~0.001% change). For spectrograms, flip TTA may help more when combined with a full multi-model ensemble than for single models (50496431:e8#2).

rules.name: tta_toggle_per_checkpoint
rules.context: When switching to a new model checkpoint or changing ensemble composition, and TTA benefit was established on a previous configuration but is unknown for the current one.
rules.action: For each new checkpoint or ensemble configuration, test both TTA-on and TTA-off in isolation. Do not assume TTA that helped one model/ensemble will help another. If results are mixed across checkpoints, always test both variants for the best checkpoint before finalizing.
rules.exceptions: 52551258:e9#2 shows TTA hurt in one model version (v13→v14) but helped in another, confirming model-dependence. 53424936:e9#1 shows TTA may add noise for models not trained with shifted-window augmentation.

rules.name: apply_tta_consistently_across_all_inference_paths
rules.context: When an ensemble has multiple inference paths (e.g., single models and fold-averaged models) and TTA is applied to some but not others.
rules.action: Apply the same validated TTA (e.g., horizontal flip averaging) to every inference path in the pipeline. Inconsistent TTA across paths is a low-hanging-fruit fix that requires no sweep since the augmentation type is already validated on other paths.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: enable_tta_before_discarding_new_model
rules.context: When a new, larger backbone added to an ensemble with minimal inference augmentation produces a flat or slightly worse score.
rules.action: Before discarding the model, try enabling TTA (multiple crops/views averaged) and adjusting ensemble weights. A larger backbone may need multi-view inference to show its advantage. Only discard after these integration improvements also fail.
rules.exceptions: Sometimes the model genuinely adds little value even with TTA (53424936:e8#2 showed ViT-large with TTA scored the same).

rules.name: batch_local_iterations_before_submitting_postprocessing
rules.context: When refining post-processing or edge-case handling logic that can be validated by inspecting outputs locally (distributions, unique values, shapes).
rules.action: Make multiple local iterations checking outputs without submitting. Only submit once the implementation handles all detected edge cases and produces expected output characteristics. Reserve submissions for validating the overall approach, not debugging implementation details.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: chunked_processing_and_memory_management_for_large_inference
rules.context: When the test set or feature engineering pipeline exceeds available memory and you need to produce predictions, especially from multiple fold models or with expensive per-row transformations.
rules.action: First get an end-to-end pipeline working with reduced model capacity to minimize iteration time. Then split test data into N chunks by ID, process each chunk independently (read, feature-engineer, predict, delete), and average fold predictions. Move expensive transformations inside the chunk loop rather than applying globally. After each chunk's predictions are collected, delete chunk data and call gc.collect(). If OOM occurs, increase the number of chunks. For new feature sources (e.g., transformer embeddings), build a reusable batched extraction utility with explicit memory cleanup. Only after the full pipeline succeeds, restore model capacity and submit.
rules.exceptions: 15164527 uses model-level chunking (sequential model loading) rather than data-level chunking, but the principle of sequential processing with cleanup is the same. 28093671:e5 counter_evidence — running feature engineering globally before chunking failed; keep transformations inside the chunk loop.

rules.name: prefer_diverse_architectures_over_homogeneous_folds
rules.context: When building an ensemble and you have access to multiple backbone architectures, especially on small datasets where fold averaging of a single architecture yields diminishing returns.
rules.action: Prefer ensembling diverse architectures (different model families) over averaging folds of a single architecture. Fold averaging reduces variance but not bias; architecture diversity reduces both. Only replace a diverse ensemble with a single-architecture fold ensemble if the new folds individually outperform the diverse members.
rules.exceptions: On tiny public LBs (~7 rows), score differences may be noise rather than true signal about diversity benefit (17616127:e5#3).

rules.name: limit_followup_attempts_on_regressing_approach
rules.context: When a new approach or model integration causes a score regression but you believe the idea has merit and want to rescue it with modifications.
rules.action: Allow at most one follow-up attempt to rescue the regressing approach (e.g., enriching features, adjusting weights). If the second attempt also fails to match the previous best, abandon the approach and revert. Two consecutive failures on a noisy leaderboard are a strong signal the direction is wrong, not just under-tuned.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: treat_small_lb_differences_as_noise
rules.context: When the public leaderboard has very few evaluation rows (e.g., <20) or known high variance, and score differences between variants are very small.
rules.action: Treat score differences below a noise threshold (~0.001 on tiny LBs, or resubmit same config 2-3 times to estimate noise) as uninformative. Focus on adding diversity (more architectures, more folds) which is more likely to help on the larger private set. Do not revert changes based on sub-noise regressions. Resubmit identical configs to distinguish signal from noise before concluding a member helps or hurts.
rules.exceptions: Authors often do not actually resubmit to control for noise (50376011:e29#2), leading to ambiguous signals.

rules.name: conditional_early_exit_for_submission_runtime
rules.context: When full CV training is too expensive to run on the competition platform during submission, and the hidden test set size is detectable at runtime.
rules.action: At the start of the notebook, read the test file and check its size. If it is below a threshold (e.g., fewer than 10 rows, indicating a sample test), train only one fold and break early. This saves runtime for submission while still producing valid predictions. Keep the guard so full CV runs locally or when the real test set is larger.
rules.exceptions: Training fewer folds means a weaker ensemble at submission time, which could hurt the score if the hidden test is actually large.

rules.name: normalize_blend_weights_on_member_change
rules.context: An ensemble blend formula applies a single weight to a group of model predictions, and you are adding or removing members from that group.
rules.action: Always divide by the number of members in the group before applying the group weight. After any composition change, verify that effective per-model weights sum to 1 (or the intended total) before submitting. A catastrophic regression (scores far worse than any individual model) is a strong signal of weight normalization bugs.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: memory_management_upfront_in_constrained_environments
rules.context: Working in a memory-constrained environment (e.g., Kaggle kernels) and planning to add expensive NLP feature extraction or many engineered features.
rules.action: Add a reduce_mem_usage utility early and apply it to each intermediate DataFrame immediately after creation. Delete large intermediates and call gc.collect() after each feature block. Cast feature matrices to float16/float32 before training. Plan memory management upfront rather than retrofitting it after OOM errors, which wastes multiple iterations.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: revert_multi_change_regression
rules.context: A submission regresses significantly after changing multiple variables (hyperparameters, model, preprocessing, etc.) simultaneously, making it impossible to attribute the cause.
rules.action: Revert entirely to the last known-good configuration rather than attempting incremental fixes. Then re-apply changes one at a time, submitting or validating after each, to isolate which change caused the regression. Do not attempt to salvage the new combination by tweaking within it.
rules.exceptions: 50496431:e36#3 shows partial reverts (reverting preprocessing but keeping structural additions) can work when some changes are independently valid, though recovery may be incomplete.

rules.name: one_change_per_submission
rules.context: You are iterating on a pipeline and want to interpret leaderboard or validation feedback to guide next steps.
rules.action: Change only one variable per submission to maintain clean attribution. If you must change multiple things, ensure one has a clearly larger expected effect and track its direction across submissions. Reserve the secondary lever for isolated testing afterward.
rules.exceptions: 55591012:e10#3 notes that when one change is clearly dominant, bundling a minor change is acceptable if you attribute gains to the dominant lever.

rules.name: handcrafted_nlp_features_diminishing_on_rich_representations
rules.context: When a tree-based model already consumes high-dimensional text representations (TF-IDF with wide n-gram ranges and/or transformer embeddings), and you consider adding handcrafted linguistic features (sentiment, POS counts, readability indices, NER counts).
rules.action: Expect diminishing or negative returns. Test handcrafted features in isolation against a holdout/CV before adding to the full pipeline. Prioritize structural/meta-textual features (paragraph counts, essay segment statistics) that TF-IDF and embeddings miss, rather than semantic features they already encode. If a batch of handcrafted features was previously pruned for causing regressions, investigate the root cause before re-adding.
rules.exceptions: When the model lacks transformer embeddings and only has sparse TF-IDF, handcrafted features may still help (see 55987255:e6#1 where adding feature families to a non-embedding pipeline initially improved score).

rules.name: vocabulary_size_small_dataset_linear_model
rules.context: When using a bag-of-words vectorizer with a linear model (e.g., Ridge) on a small dataset (<10K rows) and the feature dimensionality is high relative to sample size.
rules.action: Sweep max_features downward aggressively (halving or more) until LB score stops improving. Keep max_features well below the sample count (e.g., 50-200 for ~6K samples). Once a coarse sweep brackets the optimum within a factor of 2, do a fine sweep with steps of ~3-5%. If three consecutive trials show <0.5% score variation, fix the parameter and move to a different lever.
rules.exceptions: When alpha range is also being tuned simultaneously, the two levers are confounded — vocabulary size and regularization strength interact.

rules.name: tfidf_countvec_ngrams_for_tree_models
rules.context: When using a tree ensemble (LightGBM/XGBoost) on text data and the current features are handcrafted statistics or low-dimensional embeddings only, without sparse n-gram features.
rules.action: Add character-level TF-IDF (e.g., 3-6 grams) and word-level CountVectorizer (e.g., 2-3 grams) features. Sweep min_df upward in multiplicative steps (0.05→0.1→0.2) while holding max_df moderate (~0.5). Separately vary ngram_range. Validate each vectorizer's inclusion/exclusion independently. Expect 4-6 iterations to bracket the optimum settings.
rules.exceptions: When the feature space is already dominated by thousands of TF-IDF features, adding more vectorizer variants yields diminishing returns.

rules.name: latent_topic_features_marginal_with_tfidf
rules.context: When adding latent decomposition features (LDA, LSA, NMF) to a tree-based pipeline that already has TF-IDF features at sufficient dimensionality.
rules.action: Add latent features one family at a time with a small number of components (5-10). Validate each addition independently via CV before combining. If CV doesn't clearly improve, remove rather than keep — these features often add noise when TF-IDF is already present. Ensure NMF max_iter is high enough to converge (400+), but validate that converged features actually help downstream, as partially-converged features are not always worse.
rules.exceptions: When TF-IDF dimensionality is very low or absent, latent topic features may provide unique signal (see 55987255:e1#1 where NMF contributed to initial ensemble).

rules.name: diverse_dense_representations_for_trees
rules.context: When a tree-based model on text data has plateaued and you want richer features beyond sparse TF-IDF.
rules.action: Combine multiple dense vectorization methods (SVD/LSA, NMF, Word2Vec) as they capture complementary signals. Ablate each representation individually to confirm it contributes before combining. Add features in batches by family (text statistics, then topic models, then sentiment, then readability). Submit after each batch to measure lift. If a batch helps, keep it and add the next.
rules.exceptions: Individual ablation results may be very close (within 0.003), making it hard to confirm each feature's contribution from LB alone. Gains from diverse features may be fragile across submissions.

rules.name: validate_new_feature_before_submission
rules.context: When adding a new hand-crafted or engineered feature to an existing pipeline with many features.
rules.action: Add the feature to the training set first and check local validation. Toggle it off and compare. Before submitting, ensure the feature is computed identically for both train and test to avoid feature mismatch. Only proceed to submission after confirming train/test parity and positive CV signal.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: structural_segment_features_for_essays
rules.context: When scoring essays with a tree-based model that already uses surface-level text statistics and TF-IDF, and the essays have structural elements (intro, body, conclusion).
rules.action: Split each document into structural segments (e.g., by paragraph position), compute the same feature set on each segment independently, and add segment-level aggregations (mean, std, min, max) as new features. These capture structural quality signals that whole-document TF-IDF and embeddings miss.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: match_inference_preprocessing_to_training
rules.context: When inference scores are unexpectedly low or degraded despite a strong model checkpoint, and the inference pipeline may use different preprocessing (resolution, normalization, text cleaning) than what the model was trained with.
rules.action: Before tuning architecture or ensembling, verify that inference preprocessing exactly matches training: check input resolution, normalization mean/std, dataset-specific transforms, and any text normalization. Fix all mismatches in one pass. Pair preprocessing changes with the corresponding checkpoint in a single submission to isolate the effect.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: align_tokenizer_vocabulary_with_training
rules.context: When a fine-tuned language model was trained with custom added tokens (e.g., newline tokens) and resized embeddings, or when switching between model variants that may have different tokenizer configurations.
rules.action: At inference time, add the same special tokens in the same order as training and resize embeddings to match. If the checkpoint was NOT trained with added tokens, do NOT add them—resized embeddings will have random weights for new IDs, degrading predictions. Verify tokenizer length matches the model's embedding dimension. Check training config or saved tokenizer to confirm which tokens were used.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: do_not_change_input_format_at_inference_without_retraining
rules.context: When you want to add domain metadata, benchmark references, or paired-input encoding to a model's input at inference time, but the model checkpoint was not trained with that input format.
rules.action: Do not change the tokenizer input format (e.g., adding sentence pairs, prompt templates with new metadata) at inference if the model was not trained with it—token_type_ids, positional embeddings, and learned representations will be misaligned. Instead, apply the idea as post-processing (e.g., subtract a benchmark prediction) or retrain with the new format. If adding a configurable prompt template, test plumbing offline before submitting.
rules.exceptions: 17371717:e10#2 shows that even post-processing normalization (subtracting benchmark output) may not help, suggesting the idea itself can be flawed for some tasks.

rules.name: add_diverse_architectures_over_weight_tuning
rules.context: When an ensemble of similar-architecture models has plateaued and weight tuning alone has not yielded improvements.
rules.action: Add one new architecturally distinct model family at a time (e.g., discriminative vs generative, 1D CNN vs 2D CNN, different backbone). Start with uniform or near-uniform weights and submit. Prioritize architecture diversity over weight optimization. If the new model regresses the score after 2-3 fix attempts, remove it rather than continuing to tune its weight.
rules.exceptions: 18523075:e4#1 counter_evidence: XLNet addition caused regression despite being architecturally distinct—individual model quality still matters. 52860091:e3#2: pseudo-labeled checkpoints of the same architecture also helped, suggesting checkpoint quality can substitute for architecture diversity.

rules.name: ensemble_equal_weight_diverse_variants
rules.context: When multiple model variants with similar individual scores but different architectures/heads/pooling strategies exist, and the dataset is small or noisy.
rules.action: Combine all existing model-head variants by loading each variant's fold checkpoints, running inference separately, and averaging predictions with equal weights. This requires no retraining and directly reduces prediction variance. Prioritize this before exploring new architectures.
rules.exceptions: 17371717:e2#1: A subsequent single new architecture replaced the ensemble and scored worse, but the ensemble's benefit was fragile. 7573212:e6#2: Non-uniform weighting of same-architecture folds hurt; equal weighting is safer when models are similar quality.

rules.name: test_individual_models_before_blending
rules.context: When you have multiple trained models loaded for ensemble inference but no reliable local validation, and you want to know each model's contribution.
rules.action: Before blending, submit each model's predictions individually (one-line change per submission) to establish per-model LB baselines. Use these to inform blend weights and identify broken models. When blending, assign higher weight to better-scoring models rather than using equal weights.
rules.exceptions: 49524919:e21#3: Time pressure may prevent testing every model individually before blending. 50496431:e28#1: The exact weighting scheme (inverse-error vs raw scores) matters less than giving better models more influence.

rules.name: continue_new_pipeline_if_within_range
rules.context: When a pipeline rewrite or major refactor produces scores close to (within ~2%) but not better than the previous best, and the new infrastructure enables capabilities the old pipeline lacked.
rules.action: Commit to the new pipeline and proceed to optimize (add more ensemble members, tune new features, exploit new capabilities). The payoff comes from capabilities the old pipeline couldn't support. Abandon only if scores are substantially worse across all checkpoint variants.
rules.exceptions: 49576186:e2#3: The subsequent submission scored much worse (0.42974), suggesting the direction may not always be productive. Validate with at least one more submission before fully committing.

rules.name: incremental_fold_training_with_separate_inference
rules.context: When total training time for all cross-validation folds exceeds the compute budget of a single session, or when training and inference have different resource requirements.
rules.action: Train folds incrementally across separate runs, saving model weights per fold. Create a dedicated inference-only notebook that loads all fold checkpoints, generates predictions for each, and averages them. This decouples training cost from submission cost and lets you scale fold count beyond single-session limits.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: bundled_refactor_then_isolated_feature_engineering
rules.context: When the codebase needs cleanup and you have multiple improvement ideas (new model, new features, pipeline refactor) to try.
rules.action: First, refactor infrastructure and add one new model variant simultaneously—submit to confirm no regression. Then, holding the model stack fixed, add a batch of engineered features and tune ensemble weights—submit to measure feature contribution. Limit to 2-3 such iterations before switching levers.
rules.exceptions: 73937748:e4#2: The bundled nature makes it impossible to attribute gains to any single change, which is a downside.

rules.name: defer_submission_until_pipeline_runs_cleanly
rules.context: When building or modifying an inference/feature pipeline that has multiple integration points (model loading, data processing, column alignment) and runtime errors are likely.
rules.action: Do not submit to the leaderboard until the pipeline runs end-to-end without errors. Fix bugs iteratively across multiple notebook versions, inspecting outputs (shapes, head, distributions) after each fix. Only submit once all components produce valid output. This conserves submission budget and avoids interpreting scores from broken pipelines.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: one_change_per_submission
rules.context: When testing risky or untested changes and leaderboard submissions are the primary feedback mechanism.
rules.action: Make only one substantive change per submission so you can attribute gains or regressions to that specific change. If the score regresses, revert before trying the next change. Never combine a new model addition with structural code refactoring and hyperparameter changes in a single submission.
rules.exceptions: When recovering from a failed experiment, bundling a revert with one promising change can be efficient (50496431:e43#3). Bundling complementary changes sometimes works when changes are low-risk (49576186:e9#1 counter_evidence).

rules.name: delete_models_and_gc_for_sequential_inference
rules.context: When running multiple large models sequentially on a single GPU with limited VRAM, and adding more models or folds causes OOM errors.
rules.action: After each model group finishes inference, delete model objects, call gc.collect(), and clear unnecessary variables. Keep only prediction arrays in memory. If OOM persists, reduce batch size or split test data into chunks processed independently.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: fix_one_bug_per_iteration
rules.context: When a large feature or code addition causes runtime errors and you cannot identify all issues at once from the traceback.
rules.action: Fix exactly one bug per notebook run. After each fix, attempt to run the full pipeline. Do not add new features or changes until existing additions run cleanly. Keep a checklist: variable references correct, objects initialized, feature lists match computed columns. Only submit once all errors are resolved.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: batch_infrastructure_changes_without_submission
rules.context: When changes are structural/infrastructure (seed, fillna strategy, metric implementation, early stopping) rather than single-knob tuning, and correctness can be verified via local validation output.
rules.action: Group related infrastructure changes into a non-submitted sequence of edits. Use debug prints (head, len, intermediate scores) to verify correctness locally. Only resume submitting once the infrastructure is stable and you return to single-variable tuning.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: catastrophic_regression_fix_data_pipeline_first
rules.context: When a large structural change (new modality, major refactor) causes a catastrophic score regression (e.g., score doubles or worse).
rules.action: Focus first on fixing the data preprocessing pipeline (transforms, shapes, scaling, normalization). Submit a fixed version using a single model's raw output to verify the pipeline works before adding complexity. The bug is almost always in preprocessing or data flow rather than model weights. Only then incrementally add models and blending.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: split_large_code_additions_into_runnable_pieces
rules.context: When working in a Kaggle notebook where each run is expensive and you want to add a large block of new code (feature functions, selection wrappers, new model types).
rules.action: Split large additions into independently runnable pieces: first add and verify the feature-extraction function alone, then wire it into train/test, then add the selection or model wrapper. Submit or validate after each piece works. Bundling causes a cascade of dependent bugs that take many iterations to resolve without any performance signal.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: keep_infrastructure_refactor_despite_noise_level_regression
rules.context: When a non-modeling change (infrastructure refactor, code cleanup, speed optimization) causes a score drop smaller than typical leaderboard noise (< 0.1% relative).
rules.action: Keep the change and continue. Do not revert infrastructure improvements for sub-noise-level regressions. The faster iteration speed will pay off over subsequent experiments. Only revert if the drop is clearly outside noise or persists across multiple submissions.
rules.exceptions: 50496431:e6#2 notes the small improvement could be from a subtle math change rather than a neutral refactor.

rules.name: local_validation_before_submission_for_encoding_bugs
rules.context: When a structural code change involves filtering or conditioning on categorical columns that may have been label-encoded earlier in the pipeline.
rules.action: Before submitting, check that filter conditions match the actual column encoding (strings vs. integers vs. floats). Inspect subset sizes or validation scores locally. If the local signal is clearly wrong or unchanged, fix the bug before spending a submission. Only submit once the local signal confirms the change is active.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: single_fold_pilot_before_full_experiment
rules.context: When a new inference setting (resolution, TTA, model variant) is untested and full multi-fold evaluation is costly in time or memory.
rules.action: Run the new configuration on a single fold first to verify it executes without errors and produces reasonable outputs. Fix any bugs found (indexing, memory, OOM). Only then scale to all folds for a proper submission. Do not submit the single-fold result as a serious attempt.
rules.exceptions: 15372370:e6#2 notes the author did submit the single-fold version, which scored poorly.

rules.name: stop_checkpoint_sweeping_switch_architecture
rules.context: When checkpoint sweeping with a fixed architecture shows high variance but no upward trend over many attempts (e.g., 5+ checkpoints), indicating the architecture is the bottleneck.
rules.action: Stop checkpoint sweeping. Switch to a structurally different architecture that better matches the task (e.g., multi-head for multi-output, classification vs regression). Deploy the new architecture with its best-CV checkpoint, then tune inference-time settings on top.
rules.exceptions: 15082684:e3#1 notes the new architecture alone didn't beat the best single-head result; gains came after combining with other adjustments. 55621328:e13#1 notes only single-fold checkpoints were tested.

rules.name: experiment_sequencing_prerequisite_first
rules.context: When two changes are coupled (one is a prerequisite the other depends on) and you want to understand individual effects without wasting submission budget.
rules.action: Make the prerequisite change first and check local validation (without submitting) to confirm it helps or at least doesn't break things. Then make the dependent change and submit. This saves submission budget while still giving signal on each change's contribution.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: submit_only_after_end_to_end_validation
rules.context: When building or refactoring a complex inference pipeline with multiple interacting components (model loading, data preprocessing, transforms, post-processing, output formatting) that may each harbor bugs.
rules.action: Run the full pipeline end-to-end locally/in-notebook before submitting to the leaderboard. Fix all runtime errors (missing imports, wrong column names, shape mismatches, output filename) in small separate commits. Only submit once the pipeline produces a valid output file. This avoids wasting submission quota on crashes or broken outputs.
rules.exceptions: When you have abundant submission quota and need LB signal to diagnose an issue that can't be reproduced locally (e.g., runtime timeouts).

rules.name: do_not_submit_intermediate_refactoring_steps
rules.context: When making multiple sequential infrastructure or pipeline changes (import fixes, path resolution, code restructuring) that are not individually expected to produce competitive scores.
rules.action: Iterate locally using notebook outputs (prints, shapes, CV scores) through multiple versions until the pipeline is complete and validated. Submit only the final stable version. This conserves submission budget and avoids misleading LB signals from broken intermediates.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: revert_after_persistent_regression
rules.context: When a new model component or major change causes a score regression, and 2-3 debugging/fix attempts fail to recover the prior best score.
rules.action: Abandon the new approach and revert to the last known best configuration. Keep the prior best submission as your fallback. Do not combine multiple untested changes (new architecture + new checkpoints) in one step. If the cleanup itself yields a new best, keep it.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: fix_infrastructure_before_modeling
rules.context: When a deep learning inference pipeline exists but has never been successfully submitted, or when a submission fails due to device placement, import errors, or output file issues.
rules.action: Before tuning any modeling choices, ensure the inference script runs end-to-end on the target hardware: move model and tensors to the correct device, verify imports and paths, confirm the output file has the exact expected name. Only after obtaining a valid baseline score should you begin model or hyperparameter exploration.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: isolate_infrastructure_from_modeling_changes
rules.context: When a substantive modeling change is bundled with infrastructure code that may fail on the execution environment (device settings, imports, paths).
rules.action: Isolate and fix infrastructure issues in a minimal follow-up edit before re-running. Do not change modeling code in the same fix commit so you can attribute any score change to the original modeling change. Keep each fix minimal (one path, one import, one setting) to isolate failures.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: verify_base_correctness_before_adding_modality
rules.context: When a new input modality or feature branch doesn't improve scores despite being theoretically sound, and the model architecture was recently modified with shape changes.
rules.action: Before concluding a new modality doesn't help, verify that existing tensor operations (concatenation axes, input dimensions, crop logic) are correct. Fix shape bugs and restore known-good hyperparameters first, then re-evaluate the modality. Toggle the new branch on/off only after the base model is verified correct.
rules.exceptions: 49576186:e7#1: Even after fixing bugs, mel-spectrogram still didn't help, suggesting the modality may genuinely not add value in some cases.

rules.name: resubmit_identical_code_to_diagnose_runtime_issues
rules.context: When a Kaggle inference notebook produces an unexpectedly poor score and you suspect a runtime issue (timeout, GPU OOM, incomplete inference) rather than a code bug.
rules.action: Re-submit the identical notebook without changes. If the score improves substantially, the prior run had a runtime failure. If the score is the same, the issue is in the code. This is a cheap diagnostic before reverting or debugging.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: submit_after_each_major_structural_change
rules.context: When making multiple structural changes to a pipeline (adding a new model type, changing data source, adding a feature block) rather than just hyperparameter tuning.
rules.action: Submit after each major structural change rather than batching many changes into one submission. If a regression appears, you can isolate which change caused it. Batching 10+ structural changes into one submission makes debugging the regression nearly impossible.
rules.exceptions: Runtime/quota constraints may force batching. When changes are interdependent (e.g., new target transform requires new features requires new model), batch them but validate via local CV before submitting (see 77276039:e3#1).

rules.name: gpu_memory_cleanup_between_stages
rules.context: When multiple large models must run sequentially in a single notebook with limited GPU RAM, and adding a new model component causes OOM crashes.
rules.action: After each GPU-heavy stage, call torch.cuda.empty_cache() and gc.collect(). Avoid aggressive explicit 'del model' if the variable may be referenced later—let garbage collection handle it. Add cleanup calls incrementally and verify the pipeline runs cleanly before submitting.
rules.exceptions: 58130512:e18#1: The author initially added 'del model, trainer' then had to remove it, showing premature deletion can cause downstream errors.

rules.name: staged_ensemble_member_integration
rules.context: When adding a new model to an existing ensemble requires both pipeline code changes and weight/config adjustments.
rules.action: Split the integration into two commits: first add the model to the weight/config dictionary and adjust surrounding weights (validate locally, do not submit). Second, implement the inference code path and submit. This isolates weight-tuning errors from inference bugs.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: isolate_changes_one_at_a_time
rules.context: When a multi-variable change (new model + preprocessing, new features + new architecture, etc.) produces an ambiguous or regressed score, and you need to identify which change is responsible.
rules.action: Revert to the last known-good state and re-introduce changes one at a time, submitting after each. Do not bundle architecture changes with preprocessing or feature changes. If you must bundle, expect multi-version debugging and budget extra iterations for stabilization.
rules.exceptions: Experienced practitioners with strong priors about each component's contribution can sometimes bundle changes effectively (50496431:e28#3 v91→v92 achieved new best despite bundling).

rules.name: revert_new_ensemble_member_on_large_regression
rules.context: When adding a new model to an existing ensemble causes a large score regression (>10% relative or several points absolute) on the leaderboard.
rules.action: Immediately remove the new model and restore the last known-good ensemble configuration. Do not attempt to debug the new component in-place. After recovering baseline performance, re-attempt the addition in isolation with careful validation. If it still underperforms after 2 attempts, abandon that model variant.
rules.exceptions: If the new model's standalone CV metrics are competitive, the regression may be a bug rather than a bad model—in that case, a targeted fix (not full revert) may be warranted (49524919:e25#1).

rules.name: temporal_crop_tta_requires_training_alignment
rules.context: When the model was trained on a fixed temporal crop from a longer signal and multiple shifted crops (left/center/right) are available at inference.
rules.action: If the model was trained with temporal crop augmentation (random or multi-crop), enable inference on all available crops, softmax each independently, and average. If the model was trained on center crops only, shifted crops are out-of-distribution—test TTA on one model group first and revert if no improvement. Do not combine TTA changes with other ensemble changes in the same submission.
rules.exceptions: Even with training alignment, gains can be very small (~0.07%) and may not justify 3× compute cost (53424936:e3#1).

rules.name: mc_dropout_inference_checkpoint_compatibility
rules.context: When adding MC-dropout or multi-sample dropout at inference time to a pretrained transformer model.
rules.action: Ensure model architecture changes for MC-dropout are backward-compatible with existing checkpoints. In eval mode, standard dropout is disabled—you must use explicit train mode or custom multi-sample dropout layers. Test the new inference code first with the exact checkpoints that produced your best score before trying new ones. Architecture mismatches between checkpoint and inference model silently degrade scores.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: exploit_domain_specific_symmetry_for_tta
rules.context: When the input modality has a known physical symmetry beyond simple image flipping (e.g., bilateral EEG leads with left-right hemisphere symmetry, spatial grid with anterior-posterior symmetry).
rules.action: Implement a modality-specific mirror transform that swaps symmetric channels (e.g., left and right hemisphere EEG leads, spatial grid axes), run a second inference pass with the mirrored input, and average predictions. This is distinct from image flipping and can provide additional gains on top of image-level TTA.
rules.exceptions: Gains are typically small (<0.001 in KL divergence). If negligible, do not invest further in TTA variants (52551258:e9#2).

rules.name: oom_ensemble_cleanup_then_prune
rules.context: Adding a new model component to an ensemble causes OOM or runtime failures on a resource-constrained inference platform (e.g., Kaggle notebooks with GPU memory limits).
rules.action: First add explicit memory cleanup (del variables, gc.collect, torch.cuda.empty_cache) after each model's inference. If still OOM, reduce seeds/folds for existing components. If still failing, remove the new component entirely and submit the simpler working ensemble rather than continuing to debug. Fragile components requiring exec() or cross-framework loading are especially high-risk and should be removed early.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: repurpose_failed_model_as_feature_extractor
rules.context: A major new model or approach (e.g., large LLM, new transformer) causes catastrophic score regression when used as a direct predictor, but a proven pipeline (e.g., tree-based model or existing ensemble) is already working.
rules.action: Rather than abandoning the failed model entirely, repurpose it as a feature extractor: strip the prediction head, add pooling, and produce dense embeddings as additional input features for the proven pipeline. Start with full candidate set, then prune based on resource constraints. Do not submit until the integrated pipeline runs cleanly.
rules.exceptions: Evidence is weak — in both cases the repurposed/added component did not clearly improve over the simpler baseline. The approach is speculative until validated by submission.

rules.name: incremental_build_complex_components
rules.context: A new pipeline component involves multiple interdependent code changes (data loading, model inference, integration, caching) that can each fail independently.
rules.action: Build in stages: first core logic, then integration/caching, then fix bugs revealed by execution in small commits. Run a no-op verification before submitting. Expect 2-3 bug-fix iterations after initial build. If resource constraints appear during integration, simplify or prune before attempting submission.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: revert_after_large_regression
rules.context: A submission regresses significantly (>10% relative) from the established best score, and multiple changes were made simultaneously.
rules.action: Revert to the last known-good state before trying additional new ideas. Do not push forward on top of a regressed baseline. Only after reverting, re-introduce changes one at a time to isolate the cause of regression.
rules.exceptions: 53424936:e4#1 — author chose not to revert despite regression, valuing cleaner architecture; 50496431:e53#1 — partial recovery after revert suggests multiple causes.

rules.name: stop_weight_tuning_add_new_model_family
rules.context: Several consecutive ensemble weight-tuning or member-toggling iterations (3+) produce sub-0.001 gains or regressions, indicating the current model pool's diversity is saturated.
rules.action: Stop reweighting existing members. Instead invest in building or integrating a structurally different model family (e.g., neural net alongside GBDTs, or a new backbone architecture). Train/validate it independently, then add it to the ensemble. A single well-chosen new model family can break through a plateau that many weight adjustments cannot.
rules.exceptions: 75145694:e20#2 — gain was still very small (+0.00010), suggesting the plateau may be fundamental. 73937748:e15#1 — NN contribution was sensitive to integration details.

rules.name: reduce_capacity_for_pipeline_development
rules.context: Building or debugging an inference/training pipeline where the training step dominates wall time and you need fast end-to-end iteration.
rules.action: Temporarily reduce model capacity (e.g., fewer boosting rounds, fewer epochs, smaller model) to get fast end-to-end runs. Once the pipeline is confirmed working, increase capacity back before submitting. Do not optimize hyperparameters and pipeline simultaneously.
rules.exceptions: 27799930:e3#2 — author only partially restored capacity (250 vs 1000 rounds), balancing speed against quality.

rules.name: withhold_submission_until_pipeline_verified
rules.context: After a major code addition, infrastructure change, or multi-component integration that introduces many new moving parts.
rules.action: Run the notebook without submitting first. Inspect outputs for errors, unexpected values, or shape mismatches. Fix any bugs found, then submit the corrected version. This avoids wasting submissions on broken code and ensures the LB signal reflects the true method.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: test_new_model_standalone_before_blending
rules.context: When integrating a new model family or modality into an existing ensemble, especially from a different source or framework.
rules.action: First verify the new model produces reasonable standalone predictions (submit alone or check output distributions) before blending into the ensemble. A large regression after adding a model signals a pipeline bug, not that the model is harmful. Only blend after standalone quality is confirmed.
rules.exceptions: 49524919:e27#1 — author added mel-spectrograms directly to blend without standalone test, making diagnosis harder.

rules.name: low_weight_for_weak_but_diverse_models
rules.context: A new ensemble member scores worse individually than existing members but uses a different input representation or architecture, suggesting potential diversity benefit.
rules.action: Assign the new model a small blend weight (e.g., 10-15%) while giving the bulk of weight to proven strong members. Submit the weighted blend. If it beats the previous best, the diversity benefit is confirmed. Do not use equal weighting when the new member is substantially weaker.
rules.exceptions: 50496431:e44#1 — improvement was marginal (0.22940→0.22895) and could be noise.

rules.name: escalate_after_incremental_tuning_plateau
rules.context: Three or more consecutive submissions show no improvement from incremental parameter changes (dropout, learning rate, blend weights), indicating the current configuration is near a local optimum.
rules.action: Stop incremental tuning and escalate to a structural change: swap out a model, add a new backbone, change the pooling/head architecture, or switch improvement axis entirely. Reserve incremental tuning for after the structural change succeeds.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: revert_new_component_after_failed_fix
rules.context: A newly added complex component (feature, model, preprocessing step) causes a score regression, and one targeted fix attempt also fails to recover performance.
rules.action: Revert the entire addition rather than continuing to debug. The base approach without the component is the stronger baseline. Only re-attempt the idea later with a fundamentally different implementation approach.
rules.exceptions: 55591012:e8#1 — author rebuilt the capability internally rather than simply reverting, which is a valid alternative.

rules.name: test_augmentations_one_at_a_time
rules.context: When testing multiple augmentation types or input modifications, and combining individually helpful augmentations produces a regression.
rules.action: Revert the augmentation that caused regression. Test augmentations one at a time against the best-so-far configuration. If combining two individually helpful augmentations hurts, keep only the one with the larger individual gain and re-test the other later with different parameters.
rules.exceptions: 13577502:e2#2 — the swap also changed epochs, so isolation was imperfect.

rules.name: improve_weakest_ensemble_component_infrastructure
rules.context: Ensemble score is plateauing and one member's training infrastructure (CV, saving/loading, hyperparameter tuning) is less rigorous than others.
rules.action: Invest in a single infrastructure rebuild of the weakest component (proper CV, deterministic saving/loading, consistent train/test pipelines) rather than micro-optimizing strong components. The payoff comes from better interaction with ensemble selection and post-processing in subsequent iterations.
rules.exceptions: 73937748:e22#2 — gain was only +0.00038, suggesting the ceiling may be near regardless.

rules.name: drop_features_after_two_failed_submissions
rules.context: A newly added feature set causes regression or stagnation across two or more submissions despite tuning its dimensionality or parameters.
rules.action: Remove the underperforming feature set entirely rather than continuing to tune it. Two consecutive submissions showing no improvement over the baseline without those features is sufficient evidence. Redirect effort to postprocessing or orthogonal improvements.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: optimize_each_model_before_combining
rules.context: When planning to combine two or more model families (e.g., 1D signal model + spectrogram model, GBDT + neural net) into an ensemble.
rules.action: First optimize each model family independently until returns diminish (scores oscillate within a narrow band across multiple attempts). Then combine them in one step. Do not attempt stacking prematurely before each component is reasonably tuned, as debugging two models simultaneously is harder than debugging one.
rules.exceptions: 49524919:e14#2 — the spectrogram model used an older checkpoint without re-optimization, suggesting full individual optimization of both components may not be strictly necessary.

rules.name: skip_submission_for_pure_refactors
rules.context: A change is purely structural (refactoring, cleanup, code reorganization) with no expected change to predictions.
rules.action: Skip submitting pure refactors to conserve submission budget. Only submit when the change includes new models, changed weights, or other substantive prediction differences.
rules.exceptions: 77450317:e2#1 — when migrating external scripts in-notebook, validation should confirm parity before submitting even if it's 'just' a refactor.

rules.name: verify_bugs_before_abandoning_feature
rules.context: A new feature idea degrades the score but the pipeline has known or suspected bugs (wrong merge keys, empty lists, incorrect variable references, inference loop scoping).
rules.action: Before concluding a feature idea is harmful, verify the pipeline is bug-free by checking data shapes, column counts, and sample values. If bugs are found, fix them and resubmit. Only abandon the idea after a clean run still underperforms.
rules.exceptions: 60197293:e17#2 — even after fixing all known bugs, the score was still below baseline, suggesting the feature may genuinely not help.

rules.name: continue_adding_models_while_gains_positive
rules.context: When each new ensemble member yields diminishing but still positive marginal gains, and more pretrained models are available.
rules.action: Continue adding models one at a time as long as each submission shows a non-negative delta. The cost per attempt is low (wiring + weight tuning), so even marginal gains are worth pursuing. Stop or switch strategy only when a new member causes a regression or no models remain.
rules.exceptions: Gains may be indistinguishable from LB noise, risking overfitting to the public leaderboard (75145694:e17#3).

rules.name: incremental_integration_with_isolation_for_complex_pipelines
rules.context: When integrating a new model component that has different preprocessing requirements (paths, transforms, variable scoping) into an existing multi-model inference pipeline.
rules.action: Create a dedicated feature-preparation function and inference branch for the new model. First add all new code but disable existing conflicting pipelines. Fix infrastructure issues (path conflicts, variable cleanup) one at a time. Test the new component in isolation (single fold/model) before re-enabling the full pipeline. Only after confirming it works alone, re-enable everything and blend.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: build_full_pipeline_before_tuning
rules.context: When starting a new competition notebook or converting a training notebook to inference, and no valid submission or leaderboard score exists yet, regardless of whether code is written from scratch, forked, or adapted from a training notebook.
rules.action: Prioritize getting the complete end-to-end pipeline working (data loading → preprocessing → model loading/training → prediction → submission file writing) before tuning hyperparameters, augmentation, or model architecture. Remove dead/duplicated code, consolidate parameters into named constants, and submit once the pipeline completes to establish a baseline LB score, even if the score is expected to be poor. Only then make targeted changes one at a time to measure isolated effects.
rules.exceptions: 53747598:e1#1 suggests deferring LB submission until all intended ensemble models are integrated, rather than submitting the first working single model. When bundling multiple changes early against a very weak baseline (49576186:e1#1), batching related changes in one submission may be acceptable since most changes are additive improvements.

rules.name: fix_one_bug_per_iteration_in_order
rules.context: When a notebook (especially one forked or adapted from another source) has multiple failure points and each run is expensive (GPU quota, time), with errors only visible after execution.
rules.action: Fix exactly one error per iteration in execution order: imports → data loading → model construction → inference → output writing. Re-run after each fix to discover the next error. Do not attempt multiple speculative fixes simultaneously, as this risks introducing new bugs and obscures which fix resolved which error.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: strip_training_code_when_adapting_to_inference
rules.context: When converting a training notebook into an inference/submission notebook, where training loops, CV evaluation, OOF scoring, and logging utilities are present but unnecessary for inference.
rules.action: First pass: strip out all training/evaluation code (fold generation, OOF scoring, training transforms, logging) and point to correct checkpoint paths. Second pass: run the notebook to catch runtime errors from leftover references or misplaced statements, fix those, then submit. For forked notebooks with many interacting components, also inline complex functions to inspect intermediate outputs and simplify to minimum viable logic before adding back complexity.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: runtime_device_detection_not_hardcoded
rules.context: When code must run across environments with varying GPU availability (e.g., local machine vs. Kaggle kernels), or when assembling multi-source notebooks with different hardware assumptions.
rules.action: Never hardcode device strings (e.g., 'cuda:0'). Always wrap device selection in a runtime availability check (e.g., torch.cuda.is_available()). When combining notebooks from multiple sources, search for all occurrences of 'cuda', 'gpu', 'GPU', 'device', '.cuda()' and unify them behind a single conditional device variable. Do not leave mixed device settings.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: debug_production_toggle
rules.context: When the pipeline has multiple expensive dimensions (folds, seeds, boosting rounds, preprocessing, multiple large models) that make full runs too slow for iterative debugging.
rules.action: Create a single global DEBUG flag that gates every expensive step (reduced folds, fewer seeds, smaller data). Prefer inferring the flag from the environment (e.g., test set size, presence of files) rather than hardcoding, to avoid accidentally submitting in debug mode. Use DEBUG mode to verify code changes quickly, then switch to full mode for final submission. The difference between debug and full scores quantifies the gain from additional compute (ensembling/averaging).
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: revert_to_working_config_on_upgrade_failure
rules.context: When a change (e.g., swapping a pretrained backbone, upgrading a library) causes the notebook to fail without producing a valid submission.
rules.action: Immediately revert to the last known-working configuration and submit to confirm it still works. Only then re-attempt the upgrade with verified assets (correct checkpoint paths, matching layer dimensions, compatible library versions). Do not spend time debugging a broken upgrade before securing a working baseline.
rules.exceptions: 50496431's pattern was comment-out/restore rather than full revert, suggesting the isolate-and-restore approach as an alternative to full revert.

rules.name: verify_ensemble_components_independently_first
rules.context: When building a multi-model ensemble pipeline from multiple contributors or sources, where each component has its own data pipeline, model architecture, and checkpoint.
rules.action: First integrate and verify each contributor's pipeline independently to confirm each produces a valid submission CSV. Then add a blending step with equal weights. Only after the full pipeline runs end-to-end, begin expanding ensemble membership or tuning blend weights. Before adding new models, prune weak or redundant existing models using offline validation scores.
rules.exceptions: These items are from the same kernel but different episodes; the pattern of verify-then-expand is consistent across both.

rules.name: infrastructure_stability_before_optimization
rules.context: When a complex assembled notebook has never been run end-to-end in the target environment, or when converting a training notebook to an inference/submission notebook for the first time.
rules.action: Prioritize fixing all execution blockers (wrong file paths, missing imports, variable name mismatches, read-only filesystem issues) before any model tuning. Make minimal changes per iteration targeting only blockers. Remove optional additions that complicate debugging. Submit only after the full pipeline executes without errors.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: clean_code_before_tuning
rules.context: When the notebook contains dead imports, unused cells, duplicated code, or debug artifacts before beginning an optimization campaign.
rules.action: Remove unused imports, dead cells, and debug artifacts before submitting the first baseline. This ensures subsequent changes are not confounded by extraneous code failures and establishes a reliable reference score. Interleave small cleanup commits between substantive model changes in complex multi-component pipelines.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: isolate_changes_revert_on_regression
rules.context: When two or more hyperparameters or components were changed simultaneously and the outcome worsened.
rules.action: Revert only one change (the more impactful or riskier one) and re-run to isolate which variable caused the regression. Avoid changing multiple things at once in future iterations. If bundled changes were made against a weak baseline and the score improved, keep all and continue; if it regressed, bisect.
rules.exceptions: Early in pipeline development when most changes are additive over a weak baseline, bundling may be acceptable (49576186:e1#1).

rules.name: pivot_after_repeated_no_improvement
rules.context: When 3+ distinct modifications to the same component (architecture, dropout, features, etc.) produce no measurable LB improvement.
rules.action: Stop micro-adjusting the current component, submit to confirm no improvement, then switch to a fundamentally different approach (e.g., new model family, different data representation, ensemble strategy). Do not continue iterating on the exhausted lever.
rules.exceptions: If modifications were confounded (changed simultaneously), first isolate individual effects before concluding the lever is exhausted.

rules.name: fix_kaggle_input_paths_first
rules.context: When setting up an inference notebook that depends on model artifacts or custom libraries stored as Kaggle dataset uploads.
rules.action: Verify that all config/weight file paths resolve correctly in the Kaggle ../input/ directory. Use 'cp -r' instead of 'mv' since input directories are read-only. Add path verification (print statements or assertions) before any modeling code. Submit immediately after fixing infrastructure to confirm the pipeline runs end-to-end.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: cache_expensive_intermediates
rules.context: When the notebook has expensive, deterministic preprocessing steps (model inference, feature extraction) that don't change between iterations.
rules.action: Pre-compute expensive intermediate artifacts in a separate run and serialize them (pickle, feather, etc.). In the main notebook, gate computation behind a flag: if cached files exist, load them; otherwise compute from scratch. This lets you iterate on downstream code (training, ensembling) without re-running upstream steps.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: incremental_multi_framework_integration
rules.context: When building a multi-model ensemble pipeline that combines models from different libraries (e.g., LightGBM + XGBoost) with shared custom functions.
rules.action: Add one model/library at a time. After adding each, run the notebook to verify no runtime errors before proceeding. Shared callback/eval functions must branch on input type (isinstance checks) because libraries pass arguments in different orders and formats. Do not submit until the full pipeline runs without errors.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: incremental_pipeline_debugging
rules.context: When building a multi-step pipeline (data loading, feature engineering, model inference, submission) where each notebook run takes significant time and intermediate outputs are not visible before committing.
rules.action: Build the pipeline skeleton first, then fix one bug per iteration by running and observing where it fails. Address bugs in execution order. Budget 3-5 debug iterations for a multi-stage pipeline. For file-loading/import wiring, budget 2-4 quick fix iterations checking: (1) all imports present, (2) file paths match filesystem exactly. Do not submit until the pipeline runs end-to-end without error.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: withhold_submissions_during_infrastructure_refactoring
rules.context: When making non-functional changes (memory fixes, code reorganization, feature-file swaps, pipeline restructuring) that haven't been validated end-to-end, and you want to avoid wasting submission slots or polluting leaderboard history.
rules.action: Withhold leaderboard submissions during pure infrastructure/refactoring episodes. Run the notebook to verify correctness via local output or runtime completion. Only submit once the full pipeline is stable and a meaningful modeling change has been made on top of the new infrastructure.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: rank_transform_placement_at_end
rules.context: When blending multiple model predictions in a pipeline that uses rank-based evaluation (e.g., concordance index, Spearman correlation) and rank transforms are applied per-component before blending.
rules.action: Blend component model raw predictions with weights first, then apply a single rank transform at the very end before submission. Do not rank-transform each component independently before blending, as this discards useful scale information about relative confidence.
rules.exceptions: Per-model ranking is not always worse—it depends on the specific weight configuration and model set (75145694:e8#1 counter_evidence).

rules.name: hierarchical_blending_for_meta_learners
rules.context: When combining a meta-learner (e.g., ridge stacking) with raw base model predictions, and the meta-learner was trained on different features than the raw outputs.
rules.action: Do not append meta-learner predictions into the same flat averaging pool as base models. Instead, average base models within their group first, then combine the group mean with the meta-learner output using a separate weighted average. Give the base model group slightly higher weight since it aggregates more diverse predictions.
rules.exceptions: The optimal structure may be more complex when adding additional components at the blend level (17616127:e10#2 counter_evidence).

rules.name: disable_rank_blending_for_single_model
rules.context: When the inference pipeline uses only one model/checkpoint rather than multiple diverse models, and rank blending is enabled.
rules.action: Disable rank blending for single-model inference. Rank averaging is designed for combining diverse predictions and can be neutral or harmful when applied to a single model's outputs. Re-enable it when adding a second model to the ensemble.
rules.exceptions: In a multi-model ensemble scenario, enabling rank blending is likely correct (7018718:e2#2).

rules.name: logit_space_averaging_for_probability_ensembles
rules.context: When component models output calibrated logits and the final metric rewards well-calibrated probability distributions (e.g., KL divergence, log-loss).
rules.action: Extract raw logits from each component model, compute a weighted average in logit space, then apply softmax to produce final probabilities. This preserves relative confidence magnitudes that softmax compression destroys. Verify the improvement is not confounded with simultaneous weight changes.
rules.exceptions: The improvement may be modest and confounded with weight changes (53747598:e4#1 counter_evidence).

rules.name: multi_scale_temporal_diversity_in_ensemble
rules.context: When models are trained on different temporal windows or resolutions of the same underlying signal (e.g., 50s, 30s, 10s spectrograms from EEG data).
rules.action: Include models from multiple temporal scales in the ensemble rather than choosing one. Average their predictions with equal or near-equal weights. The diversity from different temporal receptive fields provides complementary information. When existing models cover long and short windows, add an intermediate resolution and train both backbone families on it.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: diverse_model_families_and_target_transforms_for_survival
rules.context: When building an ensemble for a survival/concordance metric that rewards both accuracy and equity across subgroups, and you have multiple GBDT frameworks and survival target transforms available.
rules.action: Train each model family (XGB, LGB, CatBoost, HistGBM, NN) with every available target transformation (Cox, KM, Nelson-Aalen, rank, quantile). Cache OOF predictions for all variants and let a weight optimizer or stacking ensembler select which contribute. Also try the same architecture with and without feature engineering as separate pool members.
rules.exceptions: 73937748:e6#1 shows that adding target variants can regress if there are pipeline bugs (e.g., ID column issues); verify data integrity first. 77450317:e13#2 notes neural models may not immediately surpass GBDT-only ensembles.

rules.name: cross_framework_model_integration_isolation
rules.context: When adding a model trained in a different framework (e.g., TF/Keras model to a PyTorch ensemble) for inference-only blending.
rules.action: Build a self-contained inference block: import the framework, define a separate tokenizer and encoding function, build the model architecture to match training, load each fold's weights sequentially, average fold predictions, then blend with existing model predictions. Keep the new block isolated to avoid variable name collisions with the existing pipeline.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: rank_based_blending_with_anchor_swap
rules.context: When ensemble blend weight tuning has plateaued and all members are from the same model family (e.g., all GBDTs).
rules.action: Swap the seed/anchor model to one from a different model family (e.g., NN instead of GBDT), convert all member predictions to ranks before weighted aggregation, and re-use a previously validated weight dictionary. Submit to confirm improvement before adding more members.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: match_fusion_head_dims_to_heterogeneous_backbones
rules.context: When building a multi-branch fusion model with heterogeneous backbones of different output dimensions (e.g., ViT-small 384-dim and ViT-base 1024-dim) assigned to different input modalities.
rules.action: Ensure the fusion/classifier head input dimensions match each backbone's output exactly (e.g., 384*3 + 1024 for three small and one large ViT). Verify that pretrained checkpoints were trained with the same backbone-to-branch assignment; mismatches cause silent degradation rather than errors.
rules.exceptions: Even with correct dimension matching, the combination may still underperform simpler configurations if checkpoint compatibility is imperfect (53424936:e4#2).

rules.name: fp16_inference_caution_with_calibrated_postprocessing
rules.context: When switching from fp32 to fp16/mixed-precision inference and the pipeline uses precision-sensitive post-processing (e.g., optimized rounding thresholds, ordinal regression heads) or when run-to-run score variance under fp16 exceeds expected improvement margins.
rules.action: If optimized thresholds or post-processing were calibrated under fp32, do not switch to fp16 without re-calibrating. If repeated fp16 inference runs show high score variance that prevents reliable model comparison, disable mixed precision for inference. For simple regression (e.g., RMSE), fp16 may be safe—verify with a submission. Use autocast rather than blanket model.half() to avoid issues in precision-sensitive layers like LayerNorm.
rules.exceptions: In 17371717, model.half() worked fine for RMSE regression, but the author later switched to autocast as a safer approach. In 50376011, disabling AMP actually scored worse, suggesting AMP may sometimes help accuracy.

rules.name: attention_sweep_revert_threshold
rules.context: When replacing one spatial attention mechanism with another in a CNN and the new block underperforms the baseline at its initial configuration.
rules.action: Try 2-3 channel width configurations for the new attention block. If the best variant still underperforms the original block type by >0.5% AUC after the sweep, revert to the original block rather than continuing to tune. The block type itself is likely inferior for this task.
rules.exceptions: Confounding factors like backbone changes between versions can make the comparison unreliable (13848868:e6#2).

rules.name: revert_complex_inference_if_no_immediate_gain
rules.context: A more complex prediction method (e.g., KNN-augmented inference, SVR on frozen embeddings) scores worse than direct model outputs on the leaderboard.
rules.action: Revert to direct model outputs (softmax/logits) immediately. Complex inference layers (KNN retrieval, SVR on same-backbone embeddings) are sensitive to train-test distribution shift and often redundant with the model head. Invest effort in ensemble diversity across model families instead of augmenting a single model's inference pipeline.
rules.exceptions: If the complex method was tested with suboptimal hyperparameters (e.g., wrong K for KNN, untuned SVR C/gamma), one retry with tuned parameters may be warranted before abandoning.

rules.name: isolate_preprocessing_before_removing_models
rules.context: When a bundle of changes (new models, new scaler, new solver settings) causes a score regression in an ensemble.
rules.action: Isolate the preprocessing change (scaler type) and solver hyperparameters as likely culprits before removing new ensemble members. New diverse models are unlikely harmful individually. Try changing the scaler (e.g., to RobustScaler) and re-tune solver precision separately, then re-evaluate.
rules.exceptions: The scaler/precision tuning only partially recovered performance in the observed case.

rules.name: limit_threshold_tuning_submissions
rules.context: Tuning rounding thresholds via leaderboard submissions with limited submission budget, and CV-optimized thresholds are already available.
rules.action: Start with CV-optimized thresholds, submit once, then perturb in small steps. If two consecutive perturbations both degrade the score, stop tuning thresholds and change a different lever (model, ensemble). Do not spend more than 2-3 submissions on threshold tuning per model configuration.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: prefer_global_over_per_group_thresholds
rules.context: Ordinal regression with per-group (e.g., per-topic/prompt) rounding thresholds, where the group classifier is imperfect or per-group training distributions may not match the test distribution.
