rules.action: Prefer a single set of globally optimized rounding thresholds over per-group thresholds. Only use per-group thresholds if the group classifier is highly accurate and group distributions are stable between train and test.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: mel_spectrogram_from_raw_eeg_with_bipolar_montage
rules.context: When building spectrogram features from raw EEG data for a CNN ensemble, and you want control over frequency resolution and range beyond what precomputed spectrograms offer.
rules.action: Compute bipolar montage differences for standard EEG chain groups (LL, LP, RP, RR), then apply mel-spectrogram transforms with f_max matching the clinical frequency range of interest (e.g., 20Hz for EEG). Stack per-region spectrograms into a multi-channel image and feed to a standard image CNN backbone. Cache results to disk for efficiency.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: rank_transform_vs_raw_for_linear_meta_learner
rules.context: When using a linear meta-learner (Ridge/Lasso) over base model predictions and deciding whether to rank-transform predictions before stacking.
rules.action: Try both raw and rank-transformed base predictions. If base models already produce outputs on comparable scales, prefer raw predictions so the linear meta-learner can exploit magnitude differences. Reserve rank transformation for when base model scales are wildly different or the meta-learner is non-linear. The difference may be small (~0.001), so test once and move on.
rules.exceptions: Effect was modest (+0.0009) and may be confounded with other changes.

rules.name: do_not_change_stacking_head_and_membership_simultaneously
rules.context: When modifying a stacking ensemble and considering changes to both the meta-learner architecture and the set of base models in the same iteration.
rules.action: Change only one of {meta-learner type/architecture, ensemble membership} per submission. If both are changed simultaneously and performance degrades, you cannot attribute the cause. Test the meta-learner change first, then modify membership, or vice versa.
rules.exceptions: 73937748:e25#2 suggests bundling low-risk changes is acceptable when each is expected to be non-negative, but this is risky when either change could hurt.

rules.name: retune_target_transform_after_structural_change
rules.context: When a structural change to the target pipeline (e.g., stratified targets, new transform) has just yielded a new best score, and a target-transform scaling parameter was previously tuned.
rules.action: Re-sweep the target-transform parameter in small uniform steps (~2% of current value) from the current best. Submit each step. Continue in the improving direction as long as each step yields a new best. Stop when marginal gain drops below roughly half the previous step's gain, then move to a different lever.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: deterministic_over_stochastic_tta_for_spatial_tasks
rules.context: When applying TTA to models where spatial position is semantically meaningful (e.g., medical imaging with catheter positions, spectrograms with frequency axis).
rules.action: Prefer deterministic geometric TTA (horizontal flip with explicit averaging) over stochastic augmentation TTA (random rotations, shifts, scales). Stochastic augmentations at test time can corrupt position-dependent features. For spectrograms, only flip along the time axis; avoid flipping along the frequency axis.
rules.exceptions: More repetitions or milder stochastic augmentations were not explored and might work (15372370:e5#2).

rules.name: staged_multi_component_integration
rules.context: When adding a new model architecture or multiple new components (new backbone, restructured fusion, new weights) to an existing multi-model inference pipeline, especially when the new component requires changes to preprocessing, loading, or aggregation logic and components depend on each other for full benefit.
rules.action: First add the new model code/weights and verify standalone predictions (use strict checkpoint loading to surface mismatches). Then fix preprocessing/TTA/loading issues across 1-2 iterations. Finally re-enable existing ensemble members and tune blend weights. Build across 2-3 versions without expecting score improvement at each step; tolerate intermediate regressions and evaluate only after full integration is complete. Do not judge the new model's value until it is properly integrated alongside existing members. If the final combined score doesn't beat the baseline, revert.
rules.exceptions: 50496431:e30#1 — the final score didn't beat the prior best, and the author reverted, suggesting this strategy doesn't always pay off. 50496431:e33#1 suggests an A/B/AB pattern as an alternative when the new model is already properly loading. 50496431:e10#1 notes the intermediate regression was significant and persisted for two versions, so each step must be verified carefully.

rules.name: revert_after_regression_from_structural_change
rules.context: When a small isolated code change or pipeline refactor causes a clear score regression from a known best.
rules.action: Revert the specific regression-causing change. Optionally combine the revert with one additional small improvement to avoid wasting a submission on a pure revert. Do not keep iterating on the regressed code; return to the last best-scoring configuration and make smaller, isolated changes.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: abandon_exploration_after_repeated_failures
rules.context: When 4-5 consecutive submissions with a new approach or exploration direction all fail to beat the current best score, and the main configuration axes have been tried.
rules.action: Stop the current exploration direction. Return to the last best configuration and try a qualitatively different lever (e.g., different modality, different training strategy, or integrate the failed approach as a minor ensemble member rather than a replacement). Do not continue tweaking the same preprocessing or model family.
rules.exceptions: 55621328:e29#2 shows the author pivoted to blending the failed approach into the existing pipeline rather than fully abandoning it, which is consistent with the rule's integration suggestion.

rules.name: expand_ensemble_membership_before_weight_tuning
rules.context: When an ensemble of similar models has plateaued and incremental hyperparameter or weight tuning yields sub-0.001 improvements per iteration.
rules.action: Switch from parameter/weight tuning to adding diverse new members (different architectures, frameworks, or training pipelines). Keep aggregation simple (equal-weight average) while expanding membership. Submit after each addition to confirm non-negative impact. Defer weight tuning until membership is finalized.
rules.exceptions: 18837555:e3#1 confirms that premature weight adjustment regressed the score. 75145694:e11#1 shows diminishing returns when the ensemble already has ~27 members.

rules.name: diagnose_catastrophic_regression_as_pipeline_bug
rules.context: When adding a new component to an ensemble causes a score regression much larger than expected (e.g., worse than the new component's standalone score, or near-random predictions).
rules.action: Treat the regression as a pipeline/integration bug, not a model quality issue. Check checkpoint loading strictness (use strict=True), verify preprocessing alignment, prediction shape/scale compatibility, and weight normalization. Do not abandon the new component; isolate and fix the integration first.
rules.exceptions: 73671444:e3#1 suggests stripping out old code entirely rather than debugging interaction, which is an alternative when legacy code is the likely culprit.

rules.name: selective_revert_after_bundled_regression
rules.context: When a submission that bundled multiple changes (data processing, augmentation, model changes) causes a score regression and you need to recover but cannot tell which component hurt.
rules.action: Revert the most suspicious or speculative individual changes (especially data-level ones like sampling rate, normalization, or new modality/feature) while keeping minor infrastructure or structural improvements. Fix residual bugs from the partial revert, then resubmit. If the score recovers to near the prior best, the removed feature was likely harmful. If recovery is incomplete, the kept changes may also need reverting. Then re-introduce reverted changes one at a time in later iterations to see if they help in the improved context.
rules.exceptions: 49576186:e17#2 shows incomplete recovery (0.27844 vs 0.26921), suggesting kept changes may also have been suboptimal. 49576186:e11#1 notes the author still bundled multiple changes in later versions, so strict one-at-a-time was not always followed.

rules.name: pivot_from_augmentation_to_representation
rules.context: When 2-3 consecutive augmentation or preprocessing tweaks fail to beat the current best score, suggesting the feature representation is the bottleneck.
rules.action: Stop tuning augmentation details and pivot to changing the fundamental feature representation (e.g., switching spectrogram type, adding a new modality, changing the backbone, or implementing CV-driven feature selection). Bundle the representation change with compatible training adjustments.
rules.exceptions: 49576186:e25#3 bundled many changes making attribution unclear; 58130512:e11#3 notes the uncertain feature was later re-added in a different form.

rules.name: build_infrastructure_before_continuing_tuning
rules.context: When the competition metric differs from the training loss, fold quality varies, or the scoring function is a bottleneck during iterative search.
rules.action: Pause submissions and invest in infrastructure: implement the competition metric as a custom eval function, add per-fold quality weighting, and optimize scoring speed (e.g., numba JIT). Verify correctness via validation output before resuming submissions. Accept tiny score differences from numerical implementation changes.
rules.exceptions: 73937748:e23#1 shows a small score drop (0.00015) from the refactor, suggesting numerical differences can occur.

rules.name: test_new_member_with_ab_ab_pattern
rules.context: When a new model is available and you want to determine whether it complements or replaces an existing ensemble member.
rules.action: Test the new model as a replacement for the most similar existing member (A), test the existing member alone without the new one (B), then test both together (AB). If both together beats either alone, keep both. This isolates complementarity in 3 submissions.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: prioritize_least_optimized_ensemble_component
rules.context: When the ensemble contains components at different levels of optimization maturity and weight tuning alone shows diminishing returns.
rules.action: Prioritize improving the least-optimized component rather than further tuning already-strong ones. Clean up dead experimental code simultaneously. After achieving a small positive gain, move on to ensemble-level improvements rather than continuing to micro-tune the same component.
rules.exceptions: 75924487:e6#2 bundled infrastructure refactoring with ensemble changes, making attribution difficult.

rules.name: revert_complex_ensemble_to_simpler_approach
rules.context: When a structurally more complex ensemble (e.g., adding a meta-learner layer, stacking) scores worse than a simpler blend on the leaderboard.
rules.action: Revert to the simpler approach (e.g., simple average or weighted blend) rather than trying to tune the complex one. The added complexity may overfit CV folds or introduce train/inference distribution misalignment. Only revisit complexity after exhausting simpler improvements.
rules.exceptions: 17616127:e18#1 notes that earlier in history, adding more models did improve scores, so complexity is not always harmful—the issue may be specific to the meta-learner type.

rules.name: large_pipeline_build_without_intermediate_submissions
rules.context: When building a substantially new pipeline or inference script from scratch (new feature sources, new models, new inference logic) where intermediate broken states would waste submission quota and there are known unknowns (label alignment, weight calibration, output format).
rules.action: Build the full pipeline in stages without submitting: add feature extraction and model code, fix data flow and obvious bugs in follow-up edits, tune key parameters using offline validation (CV logs), add persistence and inference. Only submit once the pipeline runs cleanly end-to-end and is tuned. This conserves submission budget and avoids polluting the leaderboard with broken runs. Expect 2-4 debug iterations for a major refactor.
rules.exceptions: 58527792:e3#1 warns that building too long without external validation risks diverging from what works on LB.

rules.name: isolate_single_variable_changes_per_submission
rules.context: When making substantive changes to a pipeline (architecture, data processing, hyperparameters, ensemble composition) and leaderboard feedback is the primary signal.
rules.action: Make one structural change per submission to isolate its effect. If it improves, keep and proceed to the next change. If it regresses, revert before trying the next. Do not bundle architecture changes with preprocessing or ensemble weight changes in the same submission. Exception: when single-variable edits have plateaued and you have high offline confidence in multiple orthogonal changes, bundle them to save submission budget.
rules.exceptions: 7573212:e3#2 shows that when single-variable edits plateau and you have offline validation, bundling orthogonal improvements can be efficient. 50496431:e46#1 shows experts sometimes bundle when confident.

rules.name: incremental_debugging_without_submission
rules.context: When a large code refactor, data source change, or new feature addition introduces runtime errors, import failures, or variable mismatches and the error source is unclear.
rules.action: Make small targeted fixes across successive saves/versions without submitting to the leaderboard. Run cell-by-cell: fix stale debug code, then broken paths, then stale caches, then API/import issues. Only submit once the pipeline executes cleanly end-to-end. Budget 2-5 micro-fix iterations for a major structural change. This conserves submission budget and avoids confounding bug fixes with feature impact assessment.
rules.exceptions: 58130512:e12#2 notes that local debugging catches syntax/API bugs but not semantic ones (e.g., wrong filter condition).

rules.name: precompute_expensive_features_offline
rules.context: When the pipeline includes expensive deterministic feature extraction (embeddings, NLP features, spectrograms) that doesn't change between iterations, and the bottleneck is iteration speed on modeling/blending.
rules.action: Move expensive feature extraction into a separate preprocessing script that saves results as pickles or arrays. In the main notebook, load cached features and focus only on model training, CV, and blending. This decouples slow extraction from fast iteration. Rebuild the cache only when the feature set changes.
rules.exceptions: 59253662:e11#1 notes caching adds friction when the feature set is still evolving (new features require cache updates).

rules.name: staged_build_defer_submission
rules.context: When a major pipeline change (new model framework, new feature source, multi-step refactor) spans multiple code edits and intermediate states are incomplete or buggy, or when making multiple related infrastructure and hyperparameter changes (more folds, patience, code restructuring) from a working baseline where each intermediate state may not be submittable.
rules.action: Build in stages without submitting: implement, debug imports/paths/shapes, and verify end-to-end execution across 2-5 unsubmitted iterations, verifying locally via CV logs or execution output. Only submit once the full pipeline produces valid output and runs cleanly end-to-end. If an environment error blocks submission, fix it minimally and submit that version. This conserves submission quota and avoids misleading partial scores.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: kfold_cv_before_first_submission
rules.context: When you have a working single-holdout training pipeline that has never been submitted and you want a robust first submission.
rules.action: Switch from single holdout to k-fold stratified CV (k=5-10) with prediction averaging before submitting. Reduce per-fold training cost if needed to keep total runtime manageable. This gives both a more reliable validation signal and an implicit ensemble that typically scores better than any single model.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: incremental_ensemble_expansion
rules.context: When transitioning from a baseline to a multi-model ensemble, or when adding new model families to an existing ensemble, and each new addition yields a new best leaderboard score with gains not diminishing.
rules.action: Add one new model family per iteration and submit after each addition to confirm monotonic improvement. Build loading/prediction infrastructure first, then tune blend weights. Continue adding all available diverse model types or fold checkpoints as long as each submission yields a new best. When gains plateau, improvement reverses, or you run out of new model families, switch to optimizing ensemble weights or pruning redundant members rather than adding more.
rules.exceptions: When adding a correlated model family (e.g., another GBDT variant to a GBDT-dominated ensemble), naive addition can hurt before blend is properly tuned (73671444:e6#1 v17 regression). The author in 75145694 stopped after three additions despite accelerating gains, possibly due to running out of prepared model types.

rules.name: offline_training_load_for_inference
rules.context: When model training exceeds the submission notebook's compute budget (time or memory) but inference is fast, or when meta-models/stacking models need to be pre-fitted.
rules.action: Train the expensive model in a separate notebook, save the fitted model/predictor to a Kaggle dataset. In the submission notebook, install dependencies, load the pretrained model, run inference only, and feed predictions into the existing blend. This separates training cost from submission cost.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: ablation_by_removal_to_confirm_value
rules.context: When a multi-component change produces a large score improvement and you need to confirm which component is the key driver before investing further effort.
rules.action: Submit a version with the suspected key component removed while keeping other changes. If the score drops substantially, the component is confirmed valuable—refine it. If the score holds, the component was not the driver and can be deprioritized.
rules.exceptions: The ablation may not be perfectly clean if other confounding changes are present (7018718:e11#2 also changed experiment directory).

rules.name: keep_infra_change_if_regression_within_noise
rules.context: When a foundational/infrastructure change (seed fixing, refactoring, code cleanup) causes a score regression smaller than typical LB noise, and the change is prerequisite for planned future improvements.
rules.action: Keep the infrastructure change without reverting. Optionally re-run once to confirm the regression is within noise. Judge the infrastructure's value by the combined effect after the full planned sequence of improvements, not by its isolated LB delta.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: ensemble_diversity_via_feature_or_target_variants
rules.context: When the ensemble is dominated by one model family and adding new architectures is expensive, but the pipeline supports toggling feature engineering or target transformations.
rules.action: Duplicate an existing model pipeline with a different feature-engineering configuration or target transformation. Train both variants and add both as separate ensemble members. Evaluate OOF scores to confirm the new variant adds decorrelated signal before submitting.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: abandon_slow_feature_pivot_to_vectorized
rules.context: When a promising feature engineering idea requires Python-level loops over hundreds of thousands of groups and estimated full-data runtime is infeasible.
rules.action: Prototype on a small sample to verify correctness, then estimate full-data runtime. If infeasible, abandon the loop-based approach and pivot to a vectorized alternative (e.g., column-level transformations, groupby operations) rather than trying to optimize the loop. Do not submit the slow version.
rules.exceptions: If the feature can be reimplemented via vectorized groupby.diff or similar, the idea itself may still be valuable—only the implementation approach should be abandoned.

rules.name: do_not_revert_large_addition_on_first_regression
rules.context: When a large new code component (new model family, major feature pipeline) or a multi-change commit causes a leaderboard regression on its first submission, but the component is architecturally sound or has good standalone metrics (e.g., competitive CV scores or checkpoint loss values).
rules.action: Do not revert the entire change. Instead, systematically audit integration points: check variable references, remove duplicate code paths, verify input/output shapes and naming conventions, fix the most likely bug in the new code path (wrong input variable, missing preprocessing, shape mismatch) in a minimal follow-up commit, and resubmit. Treat the first submission of a large addition as a diagnostic baseline, not a final result. If the fix recovers most of the score, continue building on the new component.
rules.exceptions: If standalone metrics are not available, the regression is catastrophic with no clear bug hypothesis, or the component has no offline validation support, reverting may be safer (55591012:e6#1).

rules.name: isolate_new_model_before_ensemble_integration
rules.context: When adding a new model family or modality to an existing ensemble, where bugs in loading, transforms, or inference could silently corrupt predictions, and you want to assess its contribution before committing to a full blend.
rules.action: Submit the new model's predictions alone (via skip flags, index gating, or disabling existing models) to gauge its standalone LB score and verify it is reasonable. Use skip/continue flags rather than deleting code so reverting is trivial. Then re-enable all models, blend predictions, and submit the full ensemble. This two-step process catches integration bugs, isolates the new model's contribution, and lets you attribute score changes to each component.
rules.exceptions: Costs an extra submission; if submissions are very scarce, may need to skip isolation step. Solo scores may be worse than the ensemble yet still add diversity value—a model that is weak alone may still help in a blend, and vice versa (49524919:e35#1, 49524919:e24#1).

rules.name: combine_diverse_modalities_for_large_ensemble_gain
rules.context: When separately developed models on fundamentally different input representations (e.g., 2D spectrograms vs 1D time-series, or tree-based vs neural) have each been individually optimized to near their ceiling with diminishing returns.
rules.action: Combine predictions from models trained on different input modalities or architectures by averaging their outputs. Expect a large improvement because errors from different representations are weakly correlated. Implement as a single decisive integration rather than incremental blending, then iterate on component checkpoints afterward.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: dry_run_before_submission_on_new_model_integration
rules.context: When wiring new model checkpoints or pretrained artifacts into an inference/ensemble pipeline, especially when paths, preprocessing, or aggregation code are manually specified.
rules.action: Run the notebook end-to-end without submitting to verify paths load, predictions are produced (correct sign, scale, no NaNs), and aggregation executes without error. Print and inspect raw predictions for sanity. Only submit once the pipeline completes cleanly. After large refactors, submit immediately to catch silent bugs that degrade scores without raising errors.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: learned_stacker_vs_manual_blend_on_small_data
rules.context: When considering replacing hand-tuned ensemble weights with a learned meta-model (e.g., Ridge regression) and the training set is small or OOF predictions are limited.
rules.action: Verify on local CV that the stacker outperforms the manual blend before deploying. On tiny datasets, learned stackers can overfit OOF predictions. If the first stacker attempt regresses on LB, do not add more features to rescue it—revert to the simpler blend. Switch to a learned meta-model only when manual weight tuning has clearly plateaued across multiple submissions.
rules.exceptions: Ridge stacking can help when base models are sufficiently diverse (17616127 v34-v35 achieved a new best with ridge). Adding more inputs to the ridge can cause overfitting (17616127 v92).

rules.name: add_new_model_family_when_ensemble_plateaus
rules.context: When the current ensemble has stopped improving from reweighting existing components or tuning the meta-learner, and pretrained checkpoints from a new model family are available.
rules.action: Add a small number of folds/variants from the new model family blended at equal or modest weight with existing components. Submit to confirm a gain. If the first integration gives a large gain but subsequent variants of the same family yield near-zero improvement, stop refining that family after at most one additional variant and move to the next source of diversity.
rules.exceptions: Expanding from 2 to 5 folds of the same new family may not help on tiny public LBs (17616127:e21#1 v78).

rules.name: check_prediction_sign_and_pipeline_correctness
rules.context: When adding a new model causes a score drop far larger than its blend weight could explain, or when a complex inference notebook has multiple model families and blending steps.
rules.action: First check prediction sign/polarity by printing raw predictions and verifying their correlation with the target; negate if the convention is opposite. Also verify no stray 'continue' or 'skip' statements remain in model loops, and that the final submission references the intended blend column. Treat these as a checklist after every structural change—at least half the edits in a model-addition sequence will fix exactly these issues.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: one_change_at_a_time_when_adding_strong_model
rules.context: When integrating a strong new model into an ensemble that has many tunable weights, and prior multi-change submissions have sometimes regressed.
rules.action: Integrate the new model first as the primary addition and submit to confirm its value in isolation. Only after confirming a gain, make small additive changes (re-enabling disabled members, tweaking weights) one at a time. This isolates the signal from the new model and prevents confounding regressions from simultaneous changes.
rules.exceptions: When an automated stacker handles weighting (75924487:e3#2), adding all candidates at once then pruning can be more efficient.

rules.name: small_regression_resubmit_for_variance
rules.context: A structural fix (not a hyperparameter change) that you believe is correct causes a small score regression, and the platform has known non-determinism (e.g., TPU, random seeds).
rules.action: Re-submit 2–3 times with no code changes to estimate score variance. If the variance band overlaps with the previous best, keep the fix and move to the next optimization lever. If consistently worse, investigate whether the fix is truly correct.
rules.exceptions: 13702907:e5#2 shows that even after multiple resubmissions, the regression was partly real—don't use this as an excuse to ignore persistent drops.

rules.name: abandon_incremental_patching_on_failed_restore
rules.context: A targeted fix or restoration attempt scores worse than both the version being restored from and the version being restored to.
rules.action: Abandon incremental patching. Either fully revert to the known-good version or switch to a different lever entirely (e.g., feature engineering instead of fold logic). Do not spend multiple iterations debugging when the expected gain is small.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: inverted_predictions_check
rules.context: A rank-based metric (C-index, AUC) yields a score approximately equal to 1 minus the expected score (e.g., 0.29 when expecting ~0.69).
rules.action: Before tuning anything, negate the predictions and resubmit. If the score jumps to roughly 1 minus the original, the fix is confirmed. Always verify the sign convention of your target transformation against the metric's expected direction before any hyperparameter work.
rules.exceptions: Only applies to rank-based metrics where negation is meaningful; does not apply to RMSE or similar metrics.

rules.name: fix_bugs_before_experimenting
rules.context: A code change causes a runtime error or pipeline crash (no submission produced), visible from missing scores or error output.
rules.action: Fix the bug in the very next version with a minimal edit. Do not attempt further experimental changes (features, hyperparameters, new models) until the pipeline runs end-to-end and produces a valid submission. Keep bug-fix commits separate from experimental changes.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: sequential_model_loading_for_memory
rules.context: Inference pipeline loads multiple large models (e.g., transformers) for ensembling and crashes with OOM or memory errors.
rules.action: Instead of loading all models into memory simultaneously, load each model one at a time, run prediction immediately, store only the prediction array, then explicitly delete the model and call gc.collect() before loading the next. This trades compute time for memory.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: verify_pipeline_before_tuning
rules.context: Multiple plausible improvements (features, hyperparameters, post-processing) fail to move the leaderboard score, or score is far below a known baseline.
rules.action: Stop tuning inputs/post-processing. Instead, systematically verify the full prediction pipeline end-to-end: confirm model weights load correctly, inputs are shaped properly, outputs are in expected range, and submission file matches expected format. Fix pipeline bugs before resuming feature/hyperparameter work.
rules.exceptions: Some intermediate versions may not be submitted, making the stagnation pattern harder to observe in real time.

rules.name: incremental_debug_multi_dependency_changes
rules.context: A structural change (new model type, new CV scheme, external script integration) requires coordinated updates across multiple code locations (imports, variable names, data paths, feature lists) and produces cascading runtime errors.
rules.action: Before iterating through many small fix-and-rerun cycles, enumerate all locations the change touches and fix them in one version. If you must iterate, do not submit to the leaderboard until a local validation run completes successfully. Expect 2-3 debug iterations per new component. Fix failures in dependency order: imports first, then instantiation, then data alignment.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: update_all_hardcoded_references_on_param_change
rules.context: A parameter that determines feature shape or count (e.g., n_components, number of ensemble members) is changed in one place, but hardcoded references to the old value exist elsewhere (column name ranges, denominators, array shapes).
rules.action: After changing any shape-determining parameter, search the entire notebook for all hardcoded references to the old value and update them simultaneously. Use a single constant/variable rather than repeating magic numbers. For ensemble averaging, verify the denominator matches the actual count of terms before submitting.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: revert_on_catastrophic_regression
rules.context: An infrastructure or refactoring change (not a hyperparameter tweak) causes a >10% score drop or catastrophic regression, and one corrective attempt does not fully restore performance.
rules.action: Revert to the exact last working version immediately rather than continuing to patch forward. Diagnose the root cause offline before re-attempting. If a revert of a fix causes catastrophic regression, immediately re-apply the fix rather than exploring alternatives.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: submit_after_each_structural_change
rules.context: Making structural changes to the feature pipeline (column renames, new feature sources, changed merge keys, new data loading paths) without intermediate validation.
rules.action: Submit or run full local validation after each structural change, not after accumulating many. A batch of 10+ untested structural changes risks compounding errors that are hard to diagnose. When renaming columns, immediately verify consistency across all code paths (train, test, saved feature lists).
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: clean_single_model_before_ensemble
rules.context: Building an ensemble from multiple pretrained models or checkpoints, where dead/commented ensemble code or unavailable checkpoint paths exist in the notebook.
rules.action: First remove all dead/commented ensemble loading code to isolate a single-model pipeline. Confirm it runs and produces a valid score. Then add models one at a time, verifying each individually before combining. Do not attempt to debug multiple model integrations simultaneously.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: diagnostic_assertion_before_speculative_fix
rules.context: A bug location is suspected but not confirmed, and a wrong fix could waste a submission or debugging cycle.
rules.action: Insert a conditional assertion, raise statement, or debug print at the suspected failure point in a non-submitted run. Use the runtime output to confirm the hypothesis. Then make the targeted fix in the next version and submit. This two-step approach avoids wasting submissions on speculative fixes.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: feature_alignment_train_inference
rules.context: Training uses a subset of features (via saved selection list or model's feature_name()) but inference indexes with a different variable or the full feature set, causing a score regression.
rules.action: Verify that the prediction call uses the exact same column set the model was trained on (check model.feature_name() or the saved selection list). When porting training to inference, audit every feature-generation function's parameters—any parameter derived from labels must be replaced with a fixed default. Disable feature selection temporarily to isolate the issue if needed.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: remove_unused_imports_first
rules.context: Forking or adapting someone else's notebook and it fails to run due to missing optional dependencies that are not referenced downstream.
rules.action: Comment out or remove unused imports that cause errors before doing anything else. Verify the notebook runs end-to-end and produces a valid submission to establish a baseline score, then proceed to substantive changes.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: diff_against_exact_best_version
rules.context: Restoring previously beneficial code that was removed or broken in a cleanup step, and the restoration does not recover the original score.
rules.action: Before restoring removed logic, carefully diff against the exact version that achieved the best score. Verify column names and placement match exactly. If the restored version doesn't recover the original score, revert to the exact best version rather than patching forward, since other changes between versions may also have contributed.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: separate_infrastructure_from_modeling_changes
rules.context: When planning to make both infrastructure changes (library migration, I/O format, API wrappers) and modeling changes (features, hyperparameters, architecture) in the same iteration.
rules.action: Separate infrastructure migrations from modeling changes. Get the infrastructure change running and submitted first to confirm no regressions, then layer modeling improvements on top. Bundling them risks a long debugging cycle with no leaderboard feedback. If changes are truly interdependent (new architecture requires new inference code), batch them but accept you lose attribution ability if the result regresses.
rules.exceptions: 28093671:e7#2 notes the bundled approach eventually worked and produced a large score jump, so bundling is not catastrophic—just slower to validate. 18757376:e5#1 shows the batched submission regressed and the author could not attribute the cause.

rules.name: diagnose_before_reverting_on_failure
rules.context: When a new experiment variant or model integration causes either a submission failure or a regression much larger than expected from the change's scope.
rules.action: Do not revert entirely. Inspect notebook output for errors or pipeline bugs first. Apply minimal targeted fixes incrementally—fix the new component in isolation, then re-enable previously working components alongside it. Only revert if the fix doesn't resolve the issue within one or two attempts. Submit once the pipeline is at least close to the prior best.
rules.exceptions: In both cases the final score never beat the prior best, suggesting that sometimes reverting to a known-good config would be more time-efficient than extended debugging.

rules.name: pivot_to_data_fixes_when_model_tuning_stalls
rules.context: When model-level experiments (hyperparameters, loss functions, sample weights, custom metrics) yield no improvement or slight regression over multiple iterations.
rules.action: Pivot to data-level fixes: check whether input data has known artifacts (noise, precision issues, encoding problems) discoverable via EDA or community discussions. Revert unsuccessful model changes to a clean baseline, apply the data fix in isolation, and submit to confirm the gain before layering further model changes.
rules.exceptions: 27502740:e3#1 bundled denoising with metric removal, so individual contribution was not isolated. 58130512:e13#1 bundled a revert with a feature addition, also losing clean attribution.

rules.name: avoid_bundling_revert_with_new_addition
rules.context: When a single targeted change caused a score regression and you want to both revert it and add a new feature or component.
rules.action: Submit the revert alone first to confirm the baseline is restored, then add the new feature in a separate submission. Bundling a revert with an addition makes it impossible to attribute whether the new addition helped or hurt independently. Only bundle if submission budget is very constrained.
rules.exceptions: When submission budget is severely limited, bundling may be necessary despite losing attribution.

rules.name: revert_regressing_change_then_iterate
rules.context: A single identifiable change (weight shift, feature addition, architecture hyperparameter) caused a clear score regression on the leaderboard, and the prior best configuration is known.
rules.action: Immediately revert the specific change that caused the regression. You may bundle the revert with one small new improvement (e.g., enabling TTA, adding a validated component) to avoid wasting a submission, but keep the revert as the primary action so attribution remains clear. Use the restored baseline as the platform for further experiments.
rules.exceptions: Bundling a revert with another change (53747598:e6#1, 50496431:e16#1) makes attribution ambiguous—recovered scores sometimes don't fully match the prior best. When multiple interacting changes caused cumulative regression, a compound revert plus re-optimization may be needed (53762022:e6#1).

rules.name: one_change_per_submission_for_attribution
rules.context: When exploring multiple hyperparameters, preprocessing factors, or structural pipeline changes and each submission costs a leaderboard evaluation.
rules.action: Change only one conceptual element per submitted version. If a change regresses, revert it before trying the next change. Maintain a fixed baseline configuration and measure each change against it. Do not stack untested changes—if two things changed and the score dropped, you cannot attribute the cause. When you must iterate without submitting, keep a stable baseline you can diff against.
rules.exceptions: 49576186:e20#3 notes bundling is sometimes acceptable when changes are complementary (e.g., mel-spectrogram + loss function). 27799930:e6#1 argues for batching orthogonal improvements when individual fixes are too small to measure, but acknowledges attribution loss.

rules.name: batch_orthogonal_fixes_when_individual_gains_unmeasurable
rules.context: When a single change caused a small regression or no gain and the codebase has several known issues (memory bugs, code bugs, feature inconsistencies, untested feature ideas) where individual fixes are unlikely to each yield measurable LB gains.
rules.action: Do not continue probing changes one at a time. Batch several orthogonal improvements (memory optimization, code bug fixes, feature refinements, multiple promising feature ideas) guided by local validation and debug locally without submitting intermediate broken versions. Submit only when the accumulated changes show clear validation improvement. This avoids wasting submission quota on uncertain individual changes.
rules.exceptions: Conflicts with one_change_per_submission rule. Apply batching only when individual changes are too small to measure on LB and changes are truly orthogonal, not for structural changes. 27799930:e6#1 acknowledges attribution is lost when batching.

rules.name: fix_bugs_minimally_before_experimenting
rules.context: When a submission fails or produces invalid results due to a bug (wrong column names, skipped model loops, broken code paths) during an experimental change.
rules.action: Make the minimal fix in the next version and submit immediately rather than combining the fix with additional experimental changes. Verify submission column assignments match the intended prediction source before submitting.
rules.exceptions: 49524919:e28#3 counter_evidence: v130 combined bug fixes with checkpoint changes yet still produced a useful result.

rules.name: revert_and_isolate_on_catastrophic_regression
rules.context: When a multi-component change (architecture + ensembling, model class + blend weights, etc.) causes a large or catastrophic score regression and the cause is ambiguous.
rules.action: Immediately revert to the last known-good configuration or strip back to a minimal working setup. Then re-introduce changes one at a time, submitting after each to verify no regression. Do not attempt to fix a catastrophic result by adding more complexity. Budget 2-3 submissions for disambiguation.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: isolate_component_change_in_ensemble
rules.context: When modifying one model component (e.g., backbone upgrade) in a multi-model ensemble where toggling members causes large score swings.
rules.action: First establish a clean baseline by testing the component in isolation or a minimal ensemble. Then re-add it to the full ensemble. Attribute regressions to ensemble composition before concluding the component change itself failed. Accept temporary score regressions during isolation steps.
rules.exceptions: Intermediate regressions during isolation waste submissions; directly swapping in the full ensemble might reach the answer in one step if submission budget is tight (50496431:e31#1 counter_evidence).

rules.name: ablate_ensemble_members_individually
rules.context: When an ensemble has regressed after adding or removing members and you need to identify which members are beneficial or harmful.
rules.action: Remove or add one member at a time and submit to measure its marginal contribution. Never strip multiple members at once—a large regression from bulk removal is uninformative about individual contributions. If no single model beats the best ensemble, restore the best-known ensemble configuration rather than continuing to test individuals.
rules.exceptions: 50376011:e4#1 notes the author never successfully re-composed a better ensemble from ablation findings, suggesting ablation is diagnostic but not always sufficient for improvement.

rules.name: prune_before_adding_after_consecutive_regressions
rules.context: When two or more consecutive additions (new ensemble members, new feature sources, new model components) each degrade the leaderboard score relative to a known-good baseline.
rules.action: Reverse direction: instead of adding more components, aggressively prune recently-added models, features, and complexity. Remove the weakest ensemble members and heaviest feature extractors first. Submit to verify recovery before adding anything new. If 3-4 recombination attempts still fail to recover the best score, invest in genuinely new model diversity rather than re-tuning stale components.
rules.exceptions: 55987255:e16#1 notes pruning alone may be insufficient—the best configuration may be from an earlier, simpler pipeline that cannot be recovered by pruning the current one.

rules.name: restore_features_or_modalities_after_removal_regression
rules.context: When a regression is clearly caused by removing features or modalities (confirmed by the score drop coinciding with the removal).
rules.action: Immediately restore the removed features/modalities. Then iteratively refine their preprocessing or representation one or two changes at a time, submitting after each to confirm direction. If a refinement regresses, revert that specific change rather than the whole restoration. Only move to the next lever (e.g., hyperparameter tuning) once the feature/modality set is stabilized.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: keep_inference_pipeline_constant_when_swapping_architecture
rules.context: When swapping model architecture or model family and the new variant requires retraining or new checkpoints.
rules.action: Keep the ensembling, postprocessing, and inference pipeline identical when swapping architecture so the leaderboard delta isolates the architecture effect. If you must change multiple things (new architecture + new checkpoints + different ensembling), plan follow-up submissions that re-add dropped components. If the alternative partially recovers but doesn't beat the original baseline after 2-3 attempts, revert to the original family.
rules.exceptions: 28984551:e3#1 notes that model-switching only partially worked; real recovery came via ensembling rather than single-model swaps.

rules.name: toggle_preprocessing_factors_individually_on_large_regression
rules.context: When a new inference pipeline has multiple preprocessing differences from a known-good one and produces a large regression.
rules.action: Toggle each changed preprocessing factor one at a time, submitting or checking validation after each. Start by enabling the factor most likely to match training conditions. If a factor consistently hurts across multiple checkpoints, disable it permanently. Limit to 3-4 experiments before deciding.
rules.exceptions: 55621328:e10#1 notes v19→v20 changed two factors simultaneously, making attribution harder; sometimes practical constraints force bundling.

rules.name: near_random_score_debug_pipeline_not_model
rules.context: Submission score is near random baseline (e.g., AUC ~0.5, Spearman ~0, C-index ~0.5 inverted) despite a model with strong CV, or score does not respond to any modeling change across multiple submissions.
rules.action: Stop tuning the model. Systematically check the inference pipeline in order: (1) correct checkpoint loaded and paths resolve, (2) model in eval mode, (3) correct input normalization, (4) predictions mapped to correct IDs, (5) submission file writes the intended variable. Add assertions at each stage. Fix the earliest broken stage before resuming model work.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: large_regression_diagnose_bugs_before_reverting
rules.context: A structurally sound code change (e.g., ensemble restructuring, new architecture, sorting for efficiency) causes a large score regression far beyond normal variance.
rules.action: Do not revert immediately. Inspect for implementation bugs: type errors, arithmetic mistakes (weights not summing to 1), data alignment issues (reordered predictions not mapped back by ID), and variables referencing wrong names. Fix bugs incrementally, one per version. Only revert if the score still regresses after all bugs are resolved.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: fix_one_bug_per_iteration
rules.context: A new code block or pipeline has multiple interacting failure points, where the first error halts execution and hides subsequent bugs.
rules.action: Fix one bug per run, starting from the earliest failure point. After each run, read the error or output, fix only the next issue, and re-run. Do not attempt to fix all issues simultaneously. Continue until the block runs without errors and produces sensible output. Do not submit until the full pipeline runs end-to-end.
rules.exceptions: If bugs are clearly independent and all visible at once (e.g., from static analysis), fixing multiple in one pass is acceptable per 7573212:e1#1.

rules.name: verify_submission_variable_wiring
rules.context: Ensemble or post-processing code stores results in a temporary variable before writing the submission file.
rules.action: After computing final predictions, verify that the exact variable written to the submission dataframe columns is the one containing the intended output. Search for mismatches between the variable holding processed results and the variable assigned to output columns. Also check for typos in attribute names (e.g., 'odel' vs 'model') in custom prediction classes.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: verify_checkpoint_paths_resolve
rules.context: An inference pipeline loads external model checkpoint files by path, and scores are unexpectedly low or do not change across model swaps.
rules.action: Before tuning post-processing or hyperparameters, verify all model checkpoint paths resolve correctly and intended weights are loaded. Check for naming convention issues (dots vs hyphens, trailing slashes, directory structure). Make one small path change per commit and check error output. A path that silently fails can cause random-weight predictions without raising an error.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: audit_code_correctness_before_tuning
rules.context: Score has plateaued or is stagnant across multiple submissions, and the pipeline includes custom ensemble/blending code or preprocessing that was added incrementally.
rules.action: Before tuning hyperparameters or adding features, audit the prediction pipeline end-to-end for bugs—especially in custom classes combining model outputs, preprocessing mismatches per model type, and silent fallbacks from wrong file paths. Fix correctness issues first; a single well-tuned model often outperforms a buggy ensemble.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: reorder_data_merge_by_id
rules.context: Data is reordered for batching efficiency (e.g., sorting by sequence length) before inference.
rules.action: Always track reordered IDs explicitly and merge predictions back to the submission by ID rather than relying on positional alignment. If a catastrophic regression occurs after adding sorting, check alignment first before reverting the sorting change.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: debug_mode_for_fast_iteration
rules.context: Fixing bugs in feature handling, inference code, or pipeline plumbing that don't require full training to validate, and full CV is too slow.
rules.action: Add a conditional early-exit after the first CV fold or reduce estimators/epochs to speed up iteration. Do not submit these debug runs. Once the fix is confirmed working, remove the early exit, restore full hyperparameters, and submit the production run. Be careful to remove debug shortcuts before submitting—leftover breaks can produce misleadingly good or bad scores.
rules.exceptions: 55987255:e7#1 shows that removing a debug shortcut can cause regression if the single-fold result was luckily well-calibrated.

rules.name: silent_failure_fix_may_regress
rules.context: A bug fix corrects a silent failure (e.g., wrong file path causing fallback, missing feature set) and makes the pipeline behave as originally intended, but the leaderboard score regresses.
rules.action: After fixing a silent failure, immediately submit to check whether the 'correct' behavior helps. If the score regresses, consider that the fallback behavior may have been accidentally better. Disable the fixed component or revert to the fallback rather than debugging the loaded artifact, since it may be stale or suboptimal.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: abandon_after_consistent_underperformance
rules.context: 3+ variants or checkpoint versions of a new approach all score substantially worse than the established baseline, with no improving trend across iterations.
rules.action: Abandon the approach and pivot to a qualitatively different idea (different model family, modality, or data source) rather than continuing to iterate on the same failing concept. The consistent underperformance signal means the approach is fundamentally unsuited, not just poorly tuned.
rules.exceptions: If the new approach has a clear architectural advantage (e.g., multi-modal fusion) and obvious untuned configuration knobs remain, spend 2-3 more iterations tuning before abandoning (50496431:e39#2).

rules.name: declare_lever_exhausted_on_plateau
rules.context: A sweep of 3+ variants of a hyperparameter or feature subset produces scores within noise range of each other (e.g., within ~0.001).
rules.action: Declare the lever exhausted. Pick the best or simplest variant and switch to a qualitatively different lever (model architecture, new feature family, ensemble method). Continuing to search a flat region has diminishing returns.
rules.exceptions: If the public leaderboard has very few samples (e.g., ~7 rows), apparent insensitivity may be an artifact of the evaluation set rather than true insensitivity (18851026:e2#2 counter_evidence).

rules.name: smoke_test_before_submitting_major_refactors
rules.context: You are making structural changes to the pipeline (removing modalities, changing control flow, switching model APIs, or restructuring data loading) that affect the inference path.
rules.action: Before submitting, run the full inference pipeline end-to-end locally or in a dry run. Verify all model loops execute, output shapes are correct, and submission files are valid. Budget at least one non-submitted version for smoke-testing. Parameterize variables you plan to sweep so changes require editing only one line, not toggling commented blocks.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: rerun_to_verify_before_interpreting_regression
rules.context: A submission regresses unexpectedly and the inference pipeline involves checkpoint loading, shell commands, file renaming, or stochastic operations where silent failures are possible.
rules.action: Before changing your modeling approach, re-run the exact same configuration at least once and inspect intermediate outputs (file existence, shapes, prediction values). Only after confirming the pipeline executed correctly should you interpret the LB score as a signal about model quality. Budget 2-3 verification runs before acting on a surprising result.
rules.exceptions: When submission budget is very tight, a single re-run may be all you can afford. Prioritize re-running when the regression magnitude is implausibly large.

rules.name: stop_pruning_switch_to_diversification
rules.context: 2-3 successive feature removal attempts produce regressions or scores within noise range, and the score is plateauing.
rules.action: Stop pruning features and instead add qualitatively different feature types (e.g., topic models, sentiment, embeddings). Diminishing returns from subset selection signal that the feature space needs expansion, not contraction. Submit the combined version to confirm the additions help.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: revert_buggy_feature_rather_than_debug
rules.context: A newly engineered feature involves non-trivial data manipulation (cross-referencing train/test, datetime parsing, per-group merges) and you spot a potential bug (e.g., referencing wrong DataFrame).
rules.action: Remove the feature entirely and submit the clean version rather than spending iterations debugging. Only re-add it after verifying correctness offline. Prioritize pipeline reliability over marginal feature additions, especially when the expected gain is small relative to existing features.
rules.exceptions: If the feature is expected to be a major contributor (not marginal), iterative simplification may be worth the cost, though 27836972:e3#1 counter_evidence shows this can still fail to beat baseline.

rules.name: diagnose_ensemble_regression_with_individual_submissions
rules.context: An ensemble regresses after changing or adding multiple component models simultaneously, and you cannot tell which component is responsible.
rules.action: Submit each individual model's predictions separately to identify which models are strong and which are weak. Compare individual scores to the blend score. Then restore the blend using only confirmed-good components. This costs a few submissions but quickly reveals whether the regression comes from a specific model or from blend weights.
rules.exceptions: Costly if submission budget is tight. Individual model LB scores may not perfectly predict blend contribution due to diversity effects.

rules.name: revert_sensitive_hyperparameter_after_failed_alternatives
rules.context: You have tried 2-3 alternative derivations or computations of a sensitive hyperparameter (adaptive, distribution-based, etc.) and all underperform a known good setting.
rules.action: Restore the original proven value and stop searching that dimension. Redirect effort to orthogonal levers like ensemble weighting, postprocessing, or new model families. Do not continue exploring the same parameter space.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: ensemble_member_swap_revert_on_consecutive_failures
rules.context: Two consecutive single-member swaps in an ensemble both regress from the best known score.
rules.action: Stop the membership search and consider a qualitatively different approach (adding a new model family, changing the blending method, or adjusting training rather than inference). Do not persist with the regressing configuration; revert to the best known ensemble composition first.
rules.exceptions: If the new member has a clear architectural advantage and obvious untuned knobs, spend 2-3 iterations tuning it before discarding (50496431:e39#2).

rules.name: blend_over_stack_for_single_external_prediction
rules.context: You have a small number of strong external predictions (e.g., one model's OOF + test preds) and stacking them as a feature into the main model yields only marginal improvement.
rules.action: Switch to post-hoc blending: keep external predictions separate, run a fine grid search over blend weights using OOF scores on the full training set, select the weight maximizing the competition metric, and apply it to test predictions. If many diverse meta-features are available and the meta-learner is powerful, stacking may still be preferable.
rules.exceptions: Stacking can outperform blending when multiple diverse meta-features are available and the meta-learner is powerful enough to leverage them (27502740 counter_evidence).

rules.name: bracket_small_changes_with_reruns_to_estimate_noise
rules.context: Leaderboard scores show high variance across identical re-runs (noise floor comparable to the effect size of changes being tested), such as single model swaps, threshold tweaks, or adding one ensemble member.
rules.action: Bracket each small configuration change with at least one no-code re-run before and after to estimate the noise floor. Only trust an improvement that exceeds the observed re-run variance. If the change's effect is within the noise band, revert to the simpler configuration.
rules.exceptions: When submission budget is very limited, a single confirming re-run may be all that's feasible (50376011 counter_evidence).

rules.name: isolate_infrastructure_from_modeling_changes
rules.context: You want to change multiple aspects of the pipeline simultaneously — infrastructure (GPU enablement, device settings, artifact paths), CV logic, and model hyperparameters or ensemble composition.
rules.action: Isolate infrastructure changes first and verify they produce equivalent scores before making modeling changes. Bundling infrastructure with hyperparameter/ensemble changes makes it impossible to attribute regressions. If a bundled set of changes regresses significantly and you cannot isolate the cause, abandon the bundle and return to the last known-good configuration.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: gauge_new_model_standalone_before_ensembling
rules.context: New model checkpoints or artifacts from a different codebase are available and you want to test whether they improve an existing ensemble, but their standalone LB quality is unknown.
rules.action: First submit the new models alone (or as a small blend) to gauge standalone quality on the leaderboard. If substantially worse than the existing ensemble, do not expect them to help much. If reasonable, add with small weight and increase only if LB improves. If the expanded blend cannot beat the previous best after 2-3 weight adjustments, abandon the new members.
rules.exceptions: When the new models are known to be highly diverse (different modality or architecture), they may help even with lower standalone quality.

rules.name: lock_in_upstream_gains_then_tune_postprocessing
rules.context: Re-running the same code produces significantly better scores than before, indicating upstream model checkpoints or data pipelines have improved.
rules.action: First lock in the gain with re-runs to confirm it's real. Then try applying normalization (e.g., softmax) to raw predictions if not already done — test per-fold vs. after ensembling and keep the better placement. Then try expanding the ensemble one model at a time. If adding models doesn't consistently beat the improved single-model baseline, keep the simpler configuration.
rules.exceptions: When one model dominates, adding models may not help (50376011 counter_evidence: two-model ensemble did not consistently beat single model with softmax).

rules.name: pivot_after_repeated_failures_on_same_lever
rules.context: When 3-5+ consecutive submissions varying the same lever (e.g., blend strategy, inference-time config, post-processing variant) all fail to beat the established best score.
rules.action: Stop iterating on that lever and pivot to a qualitatively different approach (e.g., different model architecture, different preprocessing pipeline, different meta-learning method). The search space for the current lever is likely exhausted or it is not the bottleneck. Revert to the known-best configuration first, confirm it reproduces, then make the structural change.
rules.exceptions: If the lever has known unexplored sub-regions (e.g., untested model families), a few more attempts may be warranted before pivoting (73937748:e10#3 counter_evidence: author took 7 attempts before pivoting).

rules.name: one_change_per_submission
rules.context: When exploring multiple pipeline components (features, CV strategy, blending, preprocessing, checkpoints) in a sequence of submissions and you need to attribute score movements to specific changes.
rules.action: Change at most one lever per submission. If you change multiple things and get a regression, you cannot attribute the cause and may discard a good setting along with a bad one. Keep one anchor configuration (your best score) and return to it as a control between experiments. Never simultaneously switch a precomputed artifact and the CV/splitting logic.
rules.exceptions: When submission budget is very limited, pairing a high-confidence improvement with a neutral cleanup is acceptable (58130512:e35#3). Also, 7018718:e10#1 notes that exhaustive single-variable search may not be worthwhile if the breakthrough requires a fundamentally different approach.

rules.name: revert_to_known_good_after_regression
rules.context: When an experimental change (ensemble composition, configuration tweak, feature addition) produces a score below the established best.
rules.action: Immediately revert to the exact configuration that produced the best known score, submit to confirm it reproduces, then make one incremental change at a time from that baseline. Do not stack multiple untested changes on top of a regressed configuration.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: ensemble_expansion_quality_gate
rules.context: When adding more models to an ensemble causes the blended score to drop instead of improve over 2+ iterations, despite weight optimization.
rules.action: Stop adding members. Verify with a minimal 2-model ensemble that any new member improves over the best single model before including it. Curate members by individual OOF quality and only include those above a threshold, or switch to a regularized stacking method (e.g., Ridge) that can shrink weak members toward zero. Do not invest in larger ensembles until a minimal ensemble shows improvement.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: ablate_ensemble_members_via_isolation
rules.context: When an ensemble has accumulated many model families over time and recent additions may be degrading performance.
rules.action: Test individual model groups in isolation by disabling all others, compare standalone scores to the full blend, then try the full blend minus suspected harmful members. The drop-one-out test is more informative than standalone scores alone, since individual ablation scores may all be worse than the full blend without revealing which member to drop.
rules.exceptions: Individual isolation scores alone may not reveal which member to drop (49524919:e28#1); the full-blend-minus-one test is needed to confirm.

rules.name: remove_underperforming_additions_cleanly
rules.context: When a recently added component (feature set, augmentation, model member) fails to improve the score across 3+ tuning attempts after its introduction.
rules.action: Remove the component entirely in a single edit while keeping everything else fixed, and submit to confirm the baseline is restored. Do not simultaneously change other variables (fold count, embedding source) in the ablation edit, as this confounds the signal. If the score doesn't recover, the regression has another cause.
rules.exceptions: 58130512:e29#3: the author changed fold count simultaneously with removing augmentation, confounding the result. 58130512:e35#1: removal scored worse than the version with features, suggesting marginal value or confounding from other changes.

rules.name: freeze_ensemble_weights_for_reproducibility
rules.context: When ensemble weight search has converged and you need reproducibility for final submission, but the runtime optimizer introduces variance across runs.
rules.action: Save the best weights found by the optimizer into a fixed dictionary, add a flag to bypass runtime search, and verify the frozen configuration reproduces the same OOF score before submitting. If the frozen version regresses, the runtime search may have been overfitting to OOF noise—revert to the dynamic version.
rules.exceptions: 75584724:e7#1: frozen weights scored worse (0.69376 vs 0.69419), possibly because a concurrent scaler change invalidated the weights.

rules.name: refactor_then_verify_baseline_before_new_experiments
rules.context: When refactoring a complex multi-model pipeline (renaming, reorganizing, fixing bugs, removing dead code) and the current best score is known from prior submissions.
rules.action: Submit the refactored pipeline to verify it reproduces the pre-refactor baseline score before making any new algorithmic changes. Fix imports and minimal dependencies first, then re-enable full inference, then confirm the score matches. Keep refactoring and experimentation in separate submissions. Do not tune weights or add new components until the baseline is recovered.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: prune_ensemble_components_that_consistently_hurt_or_dont_help
rules.context: When an ensemble component or modality has been tested across 3+ submissions without improving the best score, or has been empirically shown to hurt the blend.
rules.action: Remove the unhelpful component entirely, including all associated code (loading, transforms, prediction loops, imports). Redistribute freed ensemble weight to remaining strong components. Remove dead code to reduce runtime, memory, and cognitive overhead, and prevent accidental re-inclusion. Verify on leaderboard after removal.
rules.exceptions: 52200959:e5#1 argues against dropping weak individual components if they contribute diversity in an ensemble that already works — the disagreement is explained by whether the component has been shown to help in the blend (keep) vs. shown not to help or hurt in the blend (remove).

rules.name: record_standalone_scores_when_decomposing_ensemble
rules.context: When decomposing an ensemble into individual components for debugging, refactoring, or weight tuning, and each component can be submitted independently.
rules.action: Record each component's standalone LB score. Use these scores as quality signals for weighting (e.g., inverse error). Verify the reassembled ensemble matches the original score before proceeding to new experiments. Components with standalone scores much worse than the target (>10% worse) should be tested carefully for blend contribution before keeping.
rules.exceptions: Whether to keep or drop a weak standalone component depends on whether it demonstrably helps the blend — see prune_ensemble_components rule.

rules.name: isolate_one_change_per_submission
rules.context: When you have 2+ independent levers to test (e.g., new features, preprocessing, hyperparameters, ensemble members, model swaps) and leaderboard submissions or evaluation cycles are the primary evaluation signal.
rules.action: Change at most one conceptually distinct variable per submission or evaluation cycle. Fix all other variables and submit to isolate the effect. If you bundle multiple changes and get a regression, you cannot attribute it and must waste iterations unwinding. Only after each lever's marginal value is known should you combine them. Hold the model checkpoint fixed when testing preprocessing changes, or submit the checkpoint-only change first before layering preprocessing changes on top. Limit to 2-3 unsubmitted versions before getting evaluation feedback.
rules.exceptions: When levers are inherently coupled (e.g., a checkpoint was trained with specific preprocessing), joint changes may be unavoidable. Also, when reverting a known-bad change, bundling the revert with a new change can work (7676170:e3#1 v17). When local validation is cheap and you plan an add-then-prune strategy with many candidate features, adding all at once then pruning can be faster (27799930:e4#1).

rules.name: revert_first_on_large_regression
rules.context: When a change (especially a compound one) causes a score regression relative to the previous best, and you have a clear record of which configuration produced that best score.
rules.action: Immediately revert all changes to the last known-good full configuration (ensemble membership, weights, settings) rather than trying to fix the regression by tuning other hyperparameters on top. Confirm the baseline score is restored. For large regressions (>~10-15% relative), revert within 1-2 iterations—do not persist for more than one follow-up attempt. Then re-introduce changes one at a time to test if a variation improves on the restored baseline. If a multi-change version regressed, isolate by reverting the suspected harmful change while restoring the suspected beneficial setting. After reverting, try a smaller variation of the same idea if desired.
rules.exceptions: If the regression is tiny (e.g., <0.0001) and CV improved, the drop may be noise—consider a complementary fix rather than full revert (75145694:e16#1). When the regression is small (<0.2% absolute) and you have high-confidence orthogonal improvements queued, layering additional changes may be viable (27799930:e8#2). When you believe the approach is architecturally correct and the regression is from integration bugs, debug first before reverting (49524919:e26#2).

rules.name: simplify_pipeline_when_scores_oscillate
rules.context: Multiple recent incremental changes (model additions, data augmentation, feature selection) have caused scores to oscillate around or regress from a previous best, and it is unclear which change is responsible.
rules.action: Strip out the most suspect volatile components (e.g., oversampling, newly added models, complex caching) in one batch. Replace them with fixed, precomputed artifacts from the best-performing configuration. Fit models on original unmodified data. Submit once to check if the simplified pipeline recovers. If only partial recovery, fine-tune remaining hyperparameters individually.
rules.exceptions: Bundling multiple removals makes attribution impossible; the score may only partially recover if a beneficial component was also removed (55431616:e3#1 counter_evidence).

rules.name: test_ensemble_members_individually_before_blending
rules.context: When adding new model families or backbones to an existing ensemble, especially when each has its own preprocessing or checkpoints.
rules.action: First test each candidate model individually (standalone submission or single-model prediction) to verify it produces reasonable scores. Then combine all verified models into the blend. If the blend regresses despite individually-working components, suspect a code/integration bug (merge logic, output columns) rather than model incompatibility.
rules.exceptions: When individual models are too weak to produce meaningful standalone scores, skip individual testing and focus on integration debugging.

rules.name: batch_infra_changes_submit_only_when_complete
rules.context: When a new approach requires coordinated changes across multiple pipeline components (e.g., new dependencies, data loading, model architecture) and intermediate states are broken or meaningless.
rules.action: Batch all prerequisite infrastructure changes without submitting. Use intermediate versions to inspect outputs (display dataframe heads, list directories, check shapes) to confirm correctness. Only submit once the complete pipeline is assembled and locally verified. This avoids wasting submission quota on uninformative broken states.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: abandon_failing_exploration_after_repeated_regressions
rules.context: When 2-3 submitted variants of the same idea (e.g., new feature family, new architecture, new aggregation) all regress relative to the pre-change baseline.
rules.action: After 2-3 consecutive regressions from variants of the same lever, abandon the entire line of exploration and revert to the known-good baseline. Do not continue permuting the same options. Pivot to a fundamentally different approach or lever. Budget at most 4-6 submissions before deciding.
rules.exceptions: If the regressions are small and you have strong theoretical reason to believe the idea should work, one more attempt with a substantially different configuration may be warranted.

rules.name: ensemble_swap_one_member_at_a_time
rules.context: When you have multiple candidate models for an ensemble and want to find the best combination via leaderboard feedback.
rules.action: Swap or toggle one ensemble member at a time against the current best blend and submit. If the score improves, keep the change and try the next swap. If it regresses, revert that member and try a different candidate. Use configuration flags rather than deleting model files. Stop when consecutive swaps regress.
rules.exceptions: 50496431:e8#1 shows that sometimes two things were changed at once (re-added TTA and removed model groups), making attribution harder. Strict one-at-a-time is ideal but not always followed.

rules.name: batch_unsubmitted_iterations_with_local_validation
rules.context: When compute or submission budget is limited and multiple incremental changes are planned (features, CV folds, hyperparameters).
rules.action: Make several non-submitted iterations, using local CV validation to filter changes. Pull back changes that hurt validation. Only submit once the accumulated package shows a clear validation improvement over the last submitted best. This conserves submission budget but risks confounding which change helped.
rules.exceptions: 27799930:e10#2 notes that bundling prevents attribution of gains to specific changes. If you need to understand which change helped, submit more frequently.

rules.name: diagnose_ensemble_regression_as_bug_before_abandoning
rules.context: When adding a new model to an ensemble causes an unexpectedly large regression (much worse than the member's expected standalone performance).
rules.action: Suspect an infrastructure or configuration error rather than concluding the model is harmful. Revert to the known-good baseline to confirm it still works. Then re-enable the new member after checking for config/data issues (row count mismatches, wrong output columns, skipped loops). Only after confirming correct execution should you evaluate the member's contribution.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: keep_both_architectures_when_replacement_regresses
rules.context: When replacing one model component with a new architecture variant causes a regression, but both have reasonable standalone performance.
rules.action: Instead of choosing one architecture, keep both as separate ensemble members. Re-introduce the removed component alongside the new one so the ensemble benefits from architectural diversity. Individual backbone regressions do not disqualify a model from the full ensemble—diversity matters more than solo performance.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: ablate_new_technique_by_disabling_it_in_isolation
rules.context: When a new technique is introduced alongside other changes (new checkpoints, hyperparameters) and the score improves, but causation is unclear.
rules.action: After observing improvement, disable only the new technique while keeping other changes fixed, and submit. If the score worsens, the technique is confirmed beneficial. Then re-enable it and continue iterating. Do this within 1-2 submissions to avoid wasting budget. When a multi-variable change yields a good score, remove one change at a time to isolate which lever drove the improvement.
rules.exceptions: 17371717:e12#2 notes the ablation was not perfectly clean due to a confounded checkpoint path change.

rules.name: expand_then_prune_ensemble_membership
rules.context: When you have many candidate models for an ensemble and noisy evaluation signal (small test set or noisy LB).
rules.action: First expand the ensemble aggressively by adding multiple diverse models. If the expanded ensemble improves, keep it as baseline. Then prune one model at a time, removing the most suspect member. Use CV scores as primary signal; treat small LB movements as noisy. Stop pruning when removing any remaining member worsens CV.
