rules.exceptions: 18550705:e2#1 shows pruning steps did not recover the best expanded score, suggesting aggressive expansion may be better than subsequent pruning on very noisy LBs.

rules.name: refactor_inference_for_heterogeneous_models
rules.context: When you need to ensemble predictions from models with different architectures, training configurations, or checkpoint formats, and the existing inference code hardcodes a single model path.
rules.action: Refactor inference so each checkpoint specifies its own architecture class. Instantiate, load, and run each model independently, collecting per-model predictions into a list, then average externally. First get loading mechanics right with a single checkpoint before scaling to multiple models. Accept a temporary score regression from reduced ensemble size during the build phase.
rules.exceptions: 77450317:e12#1 — the refactored notebook scored 0.69547 (regression from 0.69702), suggesting refactoring can introduce bugs; verify carefully before submitting.

rules.name: scaffold_new_component_then_enable_incrementally
rules.context: When adding a complex new component (custom model class, new feature source, new inference pipeline) to an existing working pipeline.
rules.action: Scaffold the entire new code in one commit but keep it disabled. Submit using existing predictions to confirm nothing else broke. Only after that baseline holds, enable the new component's predictions incrementally. If the first submission regresses, disable the new code (comment out rather than delete) and debug before iterating further.
rules.exceptions: 17616127:e14#1 — the author never actually submitted predictions from the new component, so the staged approach was not fully validated.

rules.name: precompute_and_cache_expensive_features
rules.context: When the notebook's iteration cycle is too slow because expensive preprocessing (feature engineering, TF-IDF, embeddings) reruns every time, but most iterations only change model hyperparameters or downstream code.
rules.action: Serialize expensive intermediate results (feature matrices, labels) to pickle/parquet files in a separate utility notebook. In the main notebook, add a boolean flag (e.g., SUBMIT or DEBUG) that gates the expensive code. When the flag is off, load cached files instead. Test the fast path before moving on to modeling changes. Budget 2-4 iterations to fix import and path bugs.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: staged_development_with_incremental_submission
rules.context: When building a complex multi-component pipeline (new features, embeddings, models, blending) across several edits, especially when structural changes could interact unpredictably.
rules.action: Submit after each major component addition rather than batching all changes into one long unsubmitted sequence. This lets you attribute score changes to specific components. If you must batch, limit to 2–3 development iterations before a leaderboard check. If a batched submission regresses, you cannot identify which addition helped or hurt.
rules.exceptions: If strong local CV is available and trusted, it can partially substitute for intermediate submissions (55987255:e30#3 counter_evidence). Also, when submission budget is very limited, batching may be necessary (7670859:e2#2).

rules.name: switch_from_tuning_to_feature_enrichment_at_plateau
rules.context: When hyperparameter tuning, blend-weight sweeps, or architecture tweaks have plateaued (scores oscillating without improvement over 3+ attempts), and the dataset is small or the metric rewards diversity.
rules.action: Stop tuning existing parameters and instead add new feature families: extract dense embeddings from pretrained models, add handcrafted features (similarity, linguistic metrics, topic decompositions), and train lightweight models on these features. Blend with existing models via rank-averaging. If the enriched pipeline scores below baseline, abandon the new features rather than tuning them further.
rules.exceptions: Feature enrichment does not always help—55987255:e30#1 saw the enriched pipeline score below the simpler baseline (0.81128 vs 0.81508), and 7670859:e2#1 saw only modest improvement (+0.00725) before reverting to end-to-end BERT. Noisy or redundant features can hurt.

rules.name: ablation_test_when_score_plateaus
rules.context: When an ensemble or multi-component system has plateaued and you are unsure whether each component contributes positively.
rules.action: Test removing one component at a time (or replacing the ensemble with a single variant) via submission or local CV. If the score regresses, restore the component. If it doesn't regress, permanently remove it to reduce complexity. Then try expanding the surviving components' pool. Use one submission per ablation for definitive signal.
rules.exceptions: CV rankings may contradict LB rankings (52200959:e3#1 counter_evidence), so ablation via submission is more reliable than CV-only ablation when CV-LB correlation is poor.

rules.name: debug_pipeline_when_score_invariant_to_changes
rules.context: When the leaderboard score does not change across 3+ substantively different modifications (model swaps, post-processing toggles, ensemble additions) that should clearly affect predictions.
rules.action: Stop tuning and verify the end-to-end data flow: check that test data is loaded correctly, predictions have expected shape and variance, and the submission file actually contains the new predictions. Print checksums or summary statistics of predictions at each pipeline stage to locate where outputs stop changing.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: revert_broken_model_swap_before_continuing
rules.context: A model or backbone swap causes a large score regression (>2x degradation or catastrophic drop) compared to the last known-good configuration.
rules.action: Immediately revert to the last known-good model/backbone. Do not attempt to fix the broken swap in-place. If the new architecture has merit, add it as a separate ensemble member with its own config rather than replacing the working model. Validate recovery before exploring further.
rules.exceptions: If the baseline architecture is fundamentally mismatched to the problem and competitive solutions use a different approach entirely (52551258:e2#1), a wholesale replacement may be warranted instead of reverting.

rules.name: revert_failed_change_before_new_experiment
rules.context: A recent change caused a score regression and you want to try a different improvement idea on the same pipeline.
rules.action: Revert the failed change to restore the last-best configuration before layering the new idea. Do not build on top of a regressed state, as confounding effects make it impossible to evaluate the new idea. Optionally batch the new idea with other planned improvements and submit them together.
rules.exceptions: When the refactor introduced both harmful and valuable components, a compound recovery (simultaneous revert of bad + addition of new) can save iterations (59253662:e9#1).

rules.name: stop_pruning_ensemble_after_consecutive_regressions
rules.context: Two or more consecutive attempts to prune or simplify an ensemble each cause score regressions from the prior best.
rules.action: Stop pruning and revert to the last best ensemble configuration. The removed components are likely complementary. Instead of further pruning, try adding a new diverse model to the ensemble.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: add_new_model_incrementally_not_replace
rules.context: You want to explore a new model architecture in an ensemble-based pipeline, especially when evaluation is noisy (small public test set or high variance).
rules.action: Never fully replace a working model with an untested one in a single step. Instead, add the new model to the ensemble at low weight first. If the score improves or holds, gradually increase its weight. This bounds downside risk from noisy evaluation or checkpoint mismatches.
rules.exceptions: When the baseline is fundamentally weak and a known-strong architecture exists, wholesale replacement may be justified (52551258:e2#1).

rules.name: recover_from_refactor_regression_incrementally
rules.context: A multi-component refactor causes a large score regression and the root cause is ambiguous among several interacting changes.
rules.action: Do not simply revert everything. Re-add valuable components from the failed version one at a time, fixing bugs between submissions. Submit periodically to track recovery. Once the score exceeds the pre-regression best, move on to new levers. Alternatively, in a single recovery step, simultaneously revert the clearly harmful elements while introducing one new complementary component.
rules.exceptions: When the regression is clearly attributable to a single change (e.g., one backbone swap), a full revert is faster than incremental rebuild (18423958:e3#1).

rules.name: restore_accidentally_removed_component
rules.context: A score regression coincides with a refactor or cleanup that removed or disabled a previously contributing component (e.g., post-processing, feature set, ensemble member).
rules.action: Identify which removed component was responsible by comparing before/after code. Restore that component first (even if reimplemented), verify the score recovers, then continue iterating. Do not explore new model variants until the regression is explained and reversed.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: equal_weight_averaging_for_same_architecture_folds
rules.context: Ensembling multiple checkpoints from the same architecture trained on different CV folds, and ad-hoc manual weighting regresses compared to simpler averaging.
rules.action: Use simple equal-weight averaging across all K folds rather than cherry-picking subsets with manual weights. Load one model per fold, predict independently, and average. This is more principled and scales naturally.
rules.exceptions: When models are from different architectures, tuned weights may outperform equal averaging (17616127:e4#1 counter_evidence shows 2-model weighted blend beat 4-model equal mean).

rules.name: ensemble_pruning_one_at_a_time
rules.context: When a large ensemble (6+ members) has reached a good score and you suspect some members are redundant or harmful, especially when the evaluation metric is noisy or the public LB has few samples.
rules.action: Remove one ensemble member at a time and submit to isolate each member's contribution. If the score improves, keep the removal. Do not prune multiple members simultaneously, as you cannot attribute regression to specific removals when evaluation is noisy. After pruning is settled, try non-equal weighting; if weighting regresses, revert to equal weights on the pruned set.
rules.exceptions: 18550705:e5#1 counter_evidence: the author pruned 4 at once, making attribution impossible. One-at-a-time is costlier in submissions but more informative.

rules.name: refactor_then_verify_before_submitting
rules.context: When the notebook has grown complex with accumulated code (inline feature engineering, dead code, repetitive blocks) and a major structural refactor is needed to speed iteration.
rules.action: Refactor in small incremental steps. After each structural change, do a verification run with no other changes to confirm outputs/validation metrics match pre-refactor levels before submitting or tuning further. Bundle housekeeping with a small low-risk improvement (e.g., adding a checkpoint, toggling a model) so the submission also tests a hypothesis rather than being wasted on pure refactoring.
rules.exceptions: 73937748:e13#1: author never fully recovered pre-episode best, suggesting refactoring can inadvertently change ensemble composition. 7670859:e3#1: no submission was made during refactoring episode, so LB impact was unconfirmed.

rules.name: consolidate_winning_components_after_plateau
rules.context: When many incremental experiments have been tried with mixed results and scores have plateaued, and the pipeline has accumulated complexity/technical debt from patching.
rules.action: Consolidate all winning components discovered across experiments into a single clean rewrite. Remove dead code and unused feature pipelines, replace expensive runtime computation with precomputed artifacts, and combine the best model types and training procedures. Submit the consolidated version. This avoids compounding bugs from incremental patches and often yields a larger gain than any single tweak.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: parameterize_before_variant_iteration
rules.context: When the notebook works for one model/backbone and you plan to iterate over multiple variants (pretrained checkpoints, architectures).
rules.action: Before experimenting with new model variants, refactor inference/training functions to accept model name/path as a parameter rather than hardcoding. Bundle this refactoring with a small substantive change so the submission also tests a hypothesis, avoiding a wasted submission on pure refactoring.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: abandon_weak_ensemble_member_quickly
rules.context: When adding a new model to an existing ensemble causes a score regression, and 1-2 quick fix attempts (weight retuning, post-processing) don't fully recover the previous best.
rules.action: If adding a new ensemble member regresses the score and a quick fix doesn't recover it within 2-3 submissions, abandon that member entirely and try a qualitatively different model type instead. Don't spend more than 2-3 iterations trying to rescue a weak addition.
rules.exceptions: 75145694:e19#1: partial recovery was observed (0.69329→0.69348), suggesting cleanup has some value even if it doesn't surpass the previous best.

rules.name: revert_batch_size_after_model_upgrade
rules.context: When switching to a heavier model (e.g., end-to-end fine-tuning vs. frozen embeddings) on a fixed-resource environment like Kaggle notebooks.
rules.action: After switching to a larger model, revert inference batch size to the smallest previously-working value rather than debugging larger sizes. Optimize batch size only after the pipeline is stable and submitted.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: isolate_factors_after_compound_regression
rules.context: A multi-factor change (base model, weights, post-processing, new modality) was committed simultaneously and caused a score regression, making it impossible to attribute the cause to any single factor.
rules.action: Isolate and test one factor at a time. Prioritize checking post-processing transforms and data pipeline bugs before re-tuning weights. Submit each isolated fix to confirm its effect before combining fixes. If catastrophic (e.g., score jumps from 0.28 to 1.02), first revert the most suspicious changes together to recover a working baseline, then isolate sub-changes individually.
rules.exceptions: Some authors prefer bundling revert with a new component to save submissions (53747598:e6#1), trading attribution clarity for submission efficiency.

rules.name: restore_ensemble_after_single_model_regression
rules.context: A previously strong multi-model ensemble was replaced or partially disabled (e.g., for a single-model experiment or modality swap), causing a large score regression, and the prior ensemble code still exists in the notebook.
rules.action: Restore the full ensemble by re-enabling all prior model definitions, tokenizers, data loaders, and blend logic. When introducing a new model modality, never remove existing strong models—add the new one alongside them. Fix any variables overwritten during the failed experiment. Submit only after verifying all components are active.
rules.exceptions: Restored scores may not perfectly match the prior best due to subtle differences (18423958: 0.45975 vs 0.45939). Adding the new modality back alongside the old may still not improve over the original ensemble (52551258: 0.29324 vs 0.28137).

rules.name: batch_fixes_before_submitting
rules.context: Restoring or fixing a complex pipeline requires multiple interdependent code changes (uncommenting models, setting missing variables, fixing syntax), and submitting intermediate broken states would waste quota.
rules.action: Make all necessary code fixes across successive edits without submitting. Verify syntax (matching quotes, parentheses, string arguments) and run the notebook locally to check for errors between fixes. Submit only after the final fix when the pipeline is believed to be complete.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: do_not_panic_revert_intentional_ablation
rules.context: You intentionally disabled components for diagnostic purposes (e.g., per-fold probing, feature flag toggling) and received a catastrophic score that is an expected artifact of the debug setup.
rules.action: Do not panic-revert. Complete the diagnostic sweep to gather the information you need, then restore the full pipeline in one step. Keep the pre-ablation code intact (commented out or behind flags) so restoration is trivial. Use the diagnostic information (e.g., per-fold scores, per-component contributions) to inform subsequent optimization.
rules.exceptions: The diagnostic detour may not immediately yield a score gain (15164527: restored 0.96797 vs prior best 0.96811); the benefit is informational for future tuning.

rules.name: suspect_data_alignment_on_catastrophic_drop
rules.context: A catastrophic score regression (e.g., from 0.82 to 0.57, or from 0.28 to 1.02) occurs immediately after changing how external predictions or features are joined/concatenated to the feature matrix.
rules.action: Suspect row misalignment or corrupted predictions first, not modeling issues. Replace positional joins (pd.concat) with explicit key-based merges (pd.merge on shared ID). Disable new features to confirm the base pipeline still works, then re-enable with corrected merge logic. Verify shapes and alignment locally before submitting.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: toggle_ensemble_members_to_diagnose_regression
rules.context: A rank-average or blended ensemble includes multiple model submissions and the score has regressed after changing ensemble composition, but you don't know which member is responsible.
rules.action: Systematically toggle individual submissions in/out of the ensemble one at a time, submitting after each change. If removing member X or adding member Y improves the score, keep that configuration. Leave placeholders for future members to test incrementally. For fold-averaged models, isolate each fold's predictions and submit individually to identify weak folds.
rules.exceptions: Recovery may be partial (77276039: 0.69188 vs 0.69244), suggesting ensemble member swapping alone may not fully explain the regression.

rules.name: abandon_single_probe_regression_and_pivot
rules.context: A single-variable probe (hyperparameter tweak, preprocessing change, or new technique) produces a regression on the leaderboard, and there are qualitatively different ideas in the backlog to try.
rules.action: Abandon the probed variant after one negative result. Do not iterate further on the same lever. Pivot to a structurally different approach (different model family, different feature set, different pipeline stage). Only revisit the abandoned lever if all other options are exhausted.
rules.exceptions: If the regression is tiny (within noise) and there is an obvious missing piece (e.g., normalization mismatch), allow one refinement iteration before abandoning (49576186:e4#2). If local validation was positive but LB regressed, suspect metric misalignment rather than the idea itself (29588171:e4#2).

rules.name: single_probe_for_binary_structural_change
rules.context: You have a discrete, binary structural hypothesis to test (e.g., single model vs ensemble, boosting type swap, per-group vs global target, on/off toggle) and a competitive baseline.
rules.action: Implement the change, submit once, and evaluate. If the leaderboard score improves, retain the change and move to a different lever. Do not spend multiple iterations on a binary choice. If it succeeds, do not iterate on the same lever—move to the next most promising one.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: retest_postprocessing_after_model_change
rules.context: The upstream prediction pipeline has changed (new model, new backbone, new ensemble composition, different fold count) and post-processing parameters (rounding thresholds, rank conversion, calibration) were tuned for the previous pipeline.
rules.action: Treat post-processing parameters as dependent on the upstream model. Re-optimize them on validation data after any model or ensemble change before submitting. Do not assume post-processing preferences transfer across model changes. Test both on/off states for toggleable post-processing with each new model.
rules.exceptions: If the metric is purely rank-based (e.g., Spearman), monotonic post-processing is invariant and need not be re-tuned.

rules.name: revert_before_layering_after_catastrophic_regression
rules.context: A single change (backbone swap, data source swap, ensemble member swap) caused a large regression on the leaderboard, and you want to recover while possibly testing a new idea.
rules.action: First revert the change that caused the regression to restore the proven pipeline. If you want to test a new idea simultaneously, layer it on top of the revert in one submission. If the combined result is still far from the best, abandon both the revert-variant and the new idea. Do not submit a broken configuration to the leaderboard without reverting first.
rules.exceptions: 28093671:e10#1 shows that combining revert with HP changes can prevent reaching the prior best, so ideally revert cleanly first. 29588171:e4#2 shows that not reverting and stacking further changes on a regressed config leads to further regression.

rules.name: stop_weight_tuning_seek_model_diversity
rules.context: Tuning ensemble blend weights or composition among existing models yields diminishing returns, and the blend cannot beat the best single model or the score has plateaued across several weight-tuning iterations.
rules.action: Stop tuning blend weights after one or two probes. Invest effort in adding a structurally different model (different architecture, different input representation, or different framework) to the ensemble instead. Keep the blending infrastructure but change what you blend.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: ensemble_member_toggle_one_at_a_time
rules.context: You have a multi-model ensemble and want to determine whether adding or removing a specific member improves the blend.
rules.action: Add or remove one member at a time with no other changes, then submit to measure the effect. If adding a member with noticeably worse validation loss worsens the score, remove it immediately without trying to tune its weight. If removing a suspected weak member improves the score, keep the removal. Do not bundle a member toggle with other changes (feature changes, preprocessing) in the same submission.
rules.exceptions: 50496431:e15#1 notes the author violated this by simultaneously disabling a model and adding features, making attribution impossible.

rules.name: avoid_bundling_changes_unless_one_dominates
rules.context: You have multiple changes to test (e.g., feature cleanup + hyperparameter overhaul, or new model + training recipe improvements) and limited submission budget.
rules.action: Bundle changes only when one is expected to dominate the effect (e.g., major HP shift vs minor feature removal). Record the combined result. If the combined result is negative or ambiguous, isolate individual effects before abandoning. If budget allows, prefer single-variable probes for attribution clarity.
rules.exceptions: Bundling prevents knowing which change helped; if the result is negative, you won't know which to revert (27836972:e13#2). 18550705:e3#2 notes this sacrifices attribution but saves experiments.

rules.name: sequential_isolation_of_compound_changes
rules.context: You introduced multiple configuration changes at once (e.g., fold count + model index, or new backbone + new preprocessing) and the combined result is ambiguous or unsubmitted.
rules.action: After introducing a compound change, isolate by reverting one variable to its known-good value and submitting. Use that result as a baseline, then adjust the second variable in the next step. This lets you attribute score changes to specific levers even without local validation.
rules.exceptions: 50376011:e28#2 notes the author still changed two things at once in the follow-up, so isolation was incomplete in practice.

rules.name: restore_production_settings_before_tuning
rules.context: You have been iterating with reduced settings for speed (fewer folds, cached preprocessing, subset of data) and now have a working pipeline with a baseline score.
rules.action: Before tuning new levers, restore all settings you weakened for iteration speed (fold count, data size, ensemble members). Submit to confirm the restored setting matches or exceeds your baseline. This establishes the true baseline before further optimization.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: verify_checkpoint_model_compatibility_before_submit
rules.context: You are swapping in a new pretrained backbone or checkpoint into an inference-only pipeline.
rules.action: Before submitting, verify that the checkpoint weights were actually trained with the same architecture and hidden dimensions you are loading. Check that the checkpoint name/provenance matches the model config. If a backbone probe degrades score catastrophically (>2x worse), abandon immediately and revert rather than debugging—the issue is likely a weight mismatch or fundamentally undertrained model.
rules.exceptions: 18423958:e2#1 notes the catastrophic score may have been caused by a checkpoint mismatch rather than the backbone being inherently worse.

rules.name: submit_alternative_pipeline_quickly_then_revert_if_worse
rules.context: An alternative data source or pipeline (precomputed features, different framework, different model family) is available and you already have a strong baseline.
rules.action: Submit the alternative pipeline quickly to get leaderboard signal. If it regresses substantially, immediately revert to the proven pipeline rather than debugging the new one. When reverting, restore the exact configuration that produced the best score—do not layer additional changes on top of the revert.
rules.exceptions: 28093671:e10#1 shows the author combined reverting with HP changes, preventing full recovery to the prior best.

rules.name: probe_simpler_method_before_complex_tuning
rules.context: You have a complex ensemble method (learned meta-model, multi-step blending) and want to test whether a simpler alternative (weighted average, power-mean) can match or beat it.
rules.action: Try the simpler method in one shot. If it improves, keep it. If it regresses, allow at most one refinement iteration (e.g., relaxing constraints or adjusting the formula). If it still underperforms after 1-2 iterations, revert to the original method and pursue a different lever entirely.
rules.exceptions: 15203842:e3#1 only tried one exponent; the approach may not generalize beyond the specific pair of submissions.

rules.name: oof_predictions_stored_before_postprocessing
rules.context: OOF predictions are being stored after transformations (clipping, rounding, offsets) that should only apply to final submissions, potentially corrupting CV evaluation.
rules.action: Before tuning any post-processing step, ensure OOF predictions are stored in their raw form immediately after model prediction, before any clipping or rounding. This is a prerequisite for trusting calibration experiments and CV metrics.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: infrastructure_change_verify_parity_then_revert_quickly
rules.context: You want to make a purely infrastructural change (mixed precision, data loading format, fallback path removal) on an already-optimized pipeline that should be score-neutral.
rules.action: Make the infrastructure change in isolation and submit to verify score parity. If the score regresses even slightly, suspect numerical precision or config mismatches rather than tuning further. Revert within 1-2 attempts if parity is not achieved. Remove any debug/fallback code paths that could silently override the intended output.
rules.exceptions: 7548275:e5#2 notes the gain from removing the fallback was only +0.00006, suggesting it may not have been triggering.

rules.name: isolate_one_variable_per_submission
rules.context: When testing multiple independent changes (e.g., preprocessing + model hyperparameter, feature + architecture, or infrastructure + experimental change) and each could independently cause a regression, especially near a personal best score where you want to attribute any score change to a specific change.
rules.action: Change only one lever per submission so regressions or improvements can be attributed. Separate infrastructure changes from experimental changes: submit infrastructure-only first to confirm parity, then layer the experiment. If you bundled multiple changes and regressed, partially revert the most suspicious change first or bisect to isolate the cause. If two consecutive bundled submissions regress, revert fully before trying something else. Do not continue stacking on a regressed state—unbundle.
rules.exceptions: When all pending changes are independently low-risk (e.g., bug fixes + infrastructure), bundling is acceptable to conserve submission budget (77450317:e8#2). When local CV is reliable and changes are minor, bundling for local evaluation is fine (60197293:e9#2). When you have high confidence that multiple changes are each independently correct (e.g., matching known training settings) and submission budget is limited, bundling is acceptable (15082684:e4#2, 59253662:e3#2).

rules.name: revert_to_best_baseline_between_probes
rules.context: When a failed experiment needs reverting and you want to test a second independent idea, or when you also have new improvement ideas you want to try after a regression.
rules.action: Always revert cleanly to the last-best configuration and confirm the score is restored before testing the next independent change. Only then layer on new changes in a separate submission. Stacking a new change on a regressed baseline confounds signals—you cannot tell if the second change helps or hurts. Bundling revert + new changes makes it impossible to diagnose whether the new changes help or hurt relative to the true baseline.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: catastrophic_regression_signals_bug_not_bad_idea
rules.context: When a submission produces a catastrophic regression (score 2x+ worse than baseline), especially when multiple changes were bundled.
rules.action: If the regression is catastrophic (>50% worse), suspect a bug rather than a fundamentally bad modeling choice. Inspect implementation details (shapes, initialization, preprocessing alignment) before reverting the ideas entirely. If a single fix partially recovers, continue debugging. If no recovery after one fix attempt, revert entirely and pivot to a different lever.
rules.exceptions: 50496431:e49#1 shows recovery was still worse than baseline after fixing, suggesting some bundled ideas may genuinely be inferior even after bug fixes.

rules.name: single_probe_then_abandon_speculative_additions
rules.context: When testing a speculative addition (SMOTE, handcrafted features for transformers, SVR on embeddings, external data) whose value is uncertain and the base pipeline is already well-tuned.
rules.action: Run one experiment with reasonable defaults. If the leaderboard score worsens, abandon the idea immediately rather than sweeping parameters—if the direction is wrong, parameter tuning won't save it. Move on to a different lever.
rules.exceptions: 18757376:e3#1 notes that a different feature subset or scaling might have helped, so single-probe abandonment could be premature for feature engineering with many possible configurations.

rules.name: retune_blend_weights_after_ensemble_composition_change
rules.context: When ensemble members have changed (added/removed models, swapped checkpoints, retrained components) but blend weights remain from the old composition.
rules.action: Re-probe the blend weight by shifting it moderately from the previous best (e.g., ±0.10). If the first probe improves, accept it; if not, try the opposite direction. One or two probes usually suffice since the optimum rarely shifts dramatically after composition changes.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: stop_tuning_after_plateau_or_oscillation_and_pivot
rules.context: When small incremental blend weight or hyperparameter adjustments have been oscillating around the same score for several submissions (4-5 probes) with diminishing returns and no consistent improvement over the best found.
rules.action: Stop tuning the same parameter. After 2-3 consecutive steps yield progressively smaller gains or oscillation, pivot to a structurally different lever (e.g., adding a new model, changing architecture, different post-processing). The search space is likely exhausted or the parameter's effect is dominated by noise at this resolution. Accept the best value found so far and invest effort in structural changes instead. Avoid over-investing in one dimension of the search space.
rules.exceptions: If other pipeline components have changed since the parameter was last tuned, re-test one or two values near the old optimum (77347591:e3#1).

rules.name: checkpoint_and_move_to_orthogonal_lever_after_new_best
rules.context: When a single probe yields a clear new best score and there are other promising orthogonal directions to explore.
rules.action: Record the result, checkpoint the code with version logs documenting the baseline score, and move on to the next orthogonal lever (e.g., new features, different architecture) rather than immediately grid-searching around the new hyperparameters. Return to fine-tuning later if needed.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: ablation_test_component_after_ensemble_changes
rules.context: When a pipeline component (post-processing step, feature group, model member) was added earlier and the ensemble or model composition has since changed.
rules.action: Comment out or remove the component in a single submission to measure the LB delta. If the score drops substantially, keep the component; if neutral or negative, remove it permanently. Do this as a one-shot probe and revert immediately after observing the result.
rules.exceptions: Small deltas may be within leaderboard noise (53424936:e1#1 saw only 0.00014 improvement from restoring a feature).

rules.name: test_new_model_standalone_before_ensemble_integration
rules.context: When a new model variant or modality is available and its quality relative to existing ensemble members is unknown.
rules.action: First test the new model in isolation to get its standalone leaderboard score. If standalone quality is far worse than the ensemble, it is unlikely to help when blended. Limit checkpoint sweeps to 2-3 variants before deciding to abandon or integrate. If standalone is reasonable, add it to the full ensemble and submit.
rules.exceptions: 52551258:e8#1 notes weak standalone models can still improve ensembles via diversity, so don't discard solely based on standalone score.

rules.name: diagnose_experiment_setup_before_concluding_lever_ineffective
rules.context: When a probe improves over the last run but not over the global best, and the experimental setup involved multiple dependent parameters.
rules.action: Check whether the experimental setup is internally consistent (e.g., all dependent parameters updated, no config mismatches). Fix configuration mismatches first, then re-evaluate whether to continue the sweep or pivot. Do not conclude a lever is ineffective until the setup is verified correct.
rules.exceptions: 17371717:e3#1 shows that even after fixing bugs, the architecture change may still not be beneficial, so bug-fixing is necessary but not sufficient.

rules.name: use_local_cv_to_gate_leaderboard_submissions
rules.context: When leaderboard submissions are limited and local validation is a reliable proxy for leaderboard performance.
rules.action: Use local validation output to gate leaderboard submissions. If a probe does not show local improvement, skip the submission entirely and pivot to a qualitatively different approach. Only submit to the leaderboard once you have a configuration that clearly improves local CV.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: multiple_reruns_to_estimate_noise_before_concluding
rules.context: When leaderboard scores show high variance across identical or near-identical submissions, making single-submission comparisons unreliable.
rules.action: Before concluding a code change helped or hurt, submit the same code 3-5 times to estimate the noise range. Only trust improvements that exceed this noise band. Do not revert a change based on a single worse score if it falls within the observed noise range.
rules.exceptions: Time pressure may override thoroughness; 13848868:e5#3 suggests always testing both states of a cheap toggle rather than relying on noise estimation.

rules.name: swap_checkpoint_family_rather_than_debug_regression
rules.context: When you have multiple offline-trained model variants available and the current checkpoint/config combination is underperforming after a configuration change caused regression.
rules.action: Rather than debugging the regressed configuration, switch to a different pre-trained checkpoint family entirely. Bring along its own optimized post-processing thresholds from offline CV. Submit once to probe whether the variant improves, then move on to the next variant if it doesn't beat your overall best.
rules.exceptions: Single-probe swaps can be wasteful if not combined with further tuning (55621328:e37#1).

rules.name: staged_config_changes_comment_then_activate
rules.context: When preparing a multi-step configuration change, especially after many prior edits have left the notebook in an uncertain state.
rules.action: First commit new candidate configurations as comments without changing runtime behavior. Then re-run the existing baseline to confirm it works and record its score. Only then activate the new configuration and submit. This two-step approach isolates config errors from model quality changes.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: ensemble_member_pruning_for_weak_contributors
rules.context: When one ensemble member has a history of poor standalone performance or caused regressions when given high weight.
rules.action: Drop the suspected weak member entirely and redistribute its weight among remaining members. Submit once to confirm improvement. If the score improves, keep the pruned ensemble. If not, restore the member at a low weight.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: do_not_bundle_data_subsetting_with_other_changes
rules.context: When you suspect training distribution doesn't match test distribution and want to subset training data, while also having other pending changes.
rules.action: Test data subsetting in isolation first. If subsetting removes a large fraction of training data, verify on CV before submitting to check for underfitting. If bundled with other changes and a large regression occurs, revert entirely rather than debugging which component failed.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: selective_revert_bundled_changes
rules.context: When a multi-change commit causes a regression and one component is clearly beneficial (e.g., a bug fix) while another is speculative (e.g., new optimizer, new technique).
rules.action: Revert only the speculative component while keeping the clearly correct fix. If the revert recovers or exceeds the previous best, confirm the speculative component was harmful and move on. If it doesn't recover, investigate the next most suspicious component.
rules.exceptions: When the regression is very large and multiple speculative changes were made, it may be faster to revert all and re-add one at a time.

rules.name: gate_submissions_with_local_validation
rules.context: When you have a local validation metric that correlates well with the leaderboard and submission budget is limited.
rules.action: Run experiments locally first and check the validation metric. Only submit changes that show local improvement. Revert negative probes without submitting to conserve leaderboard submissions for promising changes.
rules.exceptions: When local validation is noisy or the metric doesn't track LB well, leaderboard probing may be necessary (29588171:e7#2).

rules.name: ablate_technique_before_investing_further
rules.context: When a technique (e.g., TTA, flip augmentation) was added alongside other changes and its isolated marginal contribution is unknown.
rules.action: Disable the technique while keeping everything else constant, submit, and compare. If the score change is negligible or positive (technique was hurting), remove it permanently. If removal causes clear regression, keep it. Limit ablation to one submission per technique.
rules.exceptions: TTA effects can be context-dependent—a technique that hurts in one ensemble configuration may help in another (52551258:e8#2 shows TTA regressed then later helped).

rules.name: standalone_probe_before_ensemble_integration
rules.context: When a new model variant or backbone is available and you want to decide whether to add it to an existing ensemble, or when one ensemble component appears dominant after a blend improvement.
rules.action: Test the new model's or strong component's predictions in isolation first (disabling all other models) to get its standalone score. If it scores substantially worse than the ensemble (e.g., >2-5% relative), keep the ensemble and instead tune blend weights to increase that component's contribution. If it is competitive, try blending it with the existing ensemble as the next step. Do not iterate on the single-model path if it clearly underperforms the blend.
rules.exceptions: A weak standalone model can still improve an ensemble through diversity, so rejecting it based solely on standalone performance may be premature (18423958:e6#1 counter_evidence, 52551258:e10#1). Consider testing the blend anyway if the model is architecturally diverse from existing members.

rules.name: increase_ensemble_members_progressively
rules.context: When single-model scores have plateaued and multiple diverse checkpoints exist from different folds or seeds.
rules.action: Progressively increase ensemble size by adding fold checkpoints one batch at a time (e.g., 2→4→5 members). After each expansion, verify the gain is real. Also verify all trained fold checkpoints are referenced with correct filenames and the inference loop iterates over all of them. Stop expanding when marginal gain diminishes or GPU memory is near capacity.
rules.exceptions: Ensemble gains are not guaranteed—specific checkpoint combinations can regress (50376011:e23#1 counter_evidence shows 4-model ensemble regressing).

rules.name: prioritize_backbone_diversity_over_weight_tuning
rules.context: When blend weight re-tuning across similar-architecture models produces negligible or oscillating improvement.
rules.action: Stop tuning weights and instead swap the weakest-contributing member for a backbone from a different model family (e.g., replace a RoBERTa variant with DeBERTa or T5). Architectural diversity typically yields larger gains than optimizing blend coefficients among similar models.
rules.exceptions: After a structural change to the ensemble, one re-probe of blend weights near the old optimum is warranted (55591012:e7#2).

rules.name: rerun_to_separate_noise_from_signal
rules.context: When a principled change produces a small regression within the observed leaderboard noise band (established by prior identical re-runs showing score variation).
rules.action: Re-submit the identical code once without any changes. If the re-run improves past the previous best, accept the change. If both runs regress, revert. Do not make further changes between verification runs.
rules.exceptions: Only applicable when you have empirical evidence of leaderboard noise magnitude from prior identical re-runs. If noise is low, a single regression is informative.

rules.name: retest_previously_rejected_settings_after_pipeline_changes
rules.context: When a previously rejected feature, hyperparameter value, or technique exists in commented-out code and the pipeline has changed substantially since it was last tested.
rules.action: Re-enable the feature or re-test the old parameter value in isolation, since the optimal setting can shift after other pipeline changes. Submit and compare to the current best. Do not spend more than one iteration on re-testing a single previously-rejected setting.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: limit_diagnosis_of_failed_bundle
rules.context: When a multi-change commit regresses and the individual contributions are unknown.
rules.action: After a bundled change regresses, try at most one or two targeted probes modifying the most suspicious component. If those also fail, revert all bundled changes to recover the baseline score, then pursue a completely different lever. Do not spend more than two submissions diagnosing a failed bundle.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: cleanup_debug_output_before_submission
rules.context: When preparing a modified pipeline for leaderboard submission and the code contains verbose logging or debug prints inside inference loops.
rules.action: Comment out verbose logging and debug prints in inference loops before submitting. This prevents timeouts and makes the submission cleaner. Treat the cleanup as a separate micro-commit so the experimental change itself is isolated.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: probe_infrastructure_change_without_submitting
rules.context: When testing a change that affects model loading, code structure, or infrastructure rather than model quality, and the current pipeline is known to work.
rules.action: Run the change without submitting first. If the notebook execution fails or outputs look wrong, revert immediately. Do not spend multiple iterations debugging an infrastructure change that doesn't promise a score improvement. Confirm the original approach still works by submitting it if needed.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: single_variable_ensemble_substitution
rules.context: When you have a candidate replacement for one ensemble member and want a clean signal from the leaderboard.
rules.action: Replace exactly one ensemble member while holding all others fixed. Update all downstream references (CSV names, column names, fallback logic) consistently. Submit to get a clean A/B comparison. If it improves, lock it in and move to the next component.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: reduce_cv_folds_for_slow_exploratory_runs
rules.context: When trying a slow algorithm variant (e.g., DART boosting) that may not pay off, and you have per-fold metrics available.
rules.action: Reduce CV folds to 2 for a quick probe. Inspect per-fold validation scores. If the idea doesn't clearly beat the baseline on those folds, revert the risky change while keeping any ancillary improvements. Then restore full CV folds and submit.
rules.exceptions: 2-fold CV is noisy; the quick probe may misjudge the idea's potential due to high variance.

rules.name: revert_on_large_regression
rules.context: When a single exploratory change (architecture swap, feature replacement, model substitution) causes a large score regression clearly outside the range of recent competitive scores.
rules.action: Immediately revert to the last known-good configuration. Do not attempt to tune or fix the failing approach further unless strong offline evidence (e.g., CV) suggests the LB result is noise. One large regression is sufficient signal to abandon the direction.
rules.exceptions: If the regression is within the noise band of identical-code reruns (e.g., <0.001), cross-reference with CV before reverting (see marginal_regression_keep_and_move_on rule).

rules.name: isolate_multi_change_regression
rules.context: When multiple changes were bundled in one submission and the result is a regression or ambiguous outcome, making it impossible to attribute the effect to any single change.
rules.action: Revert the most disruptive or uncertain change (e.g., architecture modification) while keeping changes with stronger prior justification (e.g., regularization, hyperparameter tweaks). Submit the partially-reverted version. If it recovers, the reverted component was harmful. Then probe the reverted changes individually later. Avoid bundling architectural changes with hyperparameter changes in a single experiment.
rules.exceptions: If the author can diagnose the issue through notebook outputs (e.g., error logs, prediction distributions) without needing LB feedback, systematic rollback may be unnecessary.

rules.name: single_shot_probe_new_idea
rules.context: When testing a new idea (loss function, preprocessing parameter, postprocessing transform, data cleaning) that is cheap to implement and has one natural default setting, and the baseline is already established.
rules.action: Implement the idea with one reasonable default, hold all other settings fixed, and submit. Use the LB delta to decide keep or discard. If the gain is positive, keep it provisionally. If it regresses, abandon immediately rather than sweeping variants—unless you have strong prior reason to believe a different setting would reverse the result.
rules.exceptions: A single probe may miss the correct value (e.g., the tested setting was wrong but another could help). Counter-evidence from 50376011:e12#1 notes the author did not try alternatives after one regression.

rules.name: toggle_postprocessing_after_every_model_change
rules.context: When a zero-cost binary postprocessing toggle (e.g., rank conversion, sqrt transform) has shown inconsistent direction across different model configurations.
rules.action: After every substantive model or config change, test both with and without the toggle. Do not assume the direction from previous experiments carries over. Submit whichever scores better. Always re-test the toggle on the new best before moving on.
rules.exceptions: This consumes extra submissions; only worthwhile when submission budget is not the bottleneck.

rules.name: reoptimize_postprocessing_with_new_checkpoint
rules.context: When switching model checkpoints in a pipeline that has checkpoint-specific post-processing (e.g., rounding thresholds, discretization, label shifts).
rules.action: Always re-optimize post-processing parameters (thresholds, scaling constants) whenever you switch the model checkpoint, and submit them as a single combined change. Never reuse old post-processing settings with a new model, as the prediction distribution shifts with each checkpoint. Strip old post-processing back to defaults, then re-tune for the new checkpoint's outputs.
rules.exceptions: In 55621328:e15#2, co-optimization of checkpoint + thresholds still sometimes regressed, so it doesn't guarantee improvement.

rules.name: switch_lever_on_diminishing_returns
rules.context: When successive iterations on the same lever (e.g., feature engineering, hyperparameter tuning, checkpoint selection) yield progressively smaller gains (e.g., from +0.01 to +0.002 to +0.001).
rules.action: Lock in the current best value for the diminishing lever and switch to a qualitatively different lever (e.g., from feature engineering to model stacking, from post-processing tuning to architecture upgrade, from checkpoint iteration to model capacity increase). Do not over-optimize one parameter when gains per step are an order of magnitude smaller than gains available from other levers.
rules.exceptions: In 77347591:e6#2, the subsequent switch to a different lever caused a large regression, suggesting the new lever may be riskier than continued incremental tuning.

rules.name: marginal_regression_keep_and_move_on
rules.context: When a probe yields a marginal LB regression (within noise range, e.g., <0.001) and either CV scores are available as a second signal or higher-impact levers remain untapped.
rules.action: Do not automatically revert a sub-noise-threshold regression. Cross-reference with CV if available; if CV is neutral or positive, keep the change. If no CV is available but larger gains are available from other levers, accept the marginal regression without reverting and move on to higher-impact experiments. Reserve reverts for clear regressions visible in both CV and LB.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: avoid_aggressive_ensemble_pruning
rules.context: Recent additions to an ensemble have degraded performance and you suspect over-complexity, but both adding and removing members have regressed from a known best.
rules.action: Remove members one at a time rather than pruning multiple simultaneously, to identify which specific members are net-positive. If both adding and removing consistently regress from the known best, stop iterating on ensemble composition and focus on improving individual member quality instead.
rules.exceptions: 60264017 counter_evidence: aggressive multi-member pruning produced the worst score, confirming incremental removal is more informative.

rules.name: revert_structural_change_first_on_bundled_regression
rules.context: A submission bundled two or more changes (e.g., a structural/novel change and a hyperparameter tweak) and the score regressed, making it unclear which change caused the drop.
rules.action: Revert the structural or more novel change first while keeping the familiar hyperparameter change, then submit. If the score recovers, the structural change was the culprit. This is faster than reverting everything and re-testing individually. If recovery is incomplete, also probe the hyperparameter change.
rules.exceptions: When both changes are entangled (e.g., 27389424 where LR also shifted during revert), the isolation is imperfect and partial recovery may be coincidental.

rules.name: stop_single_model_probes_return_to_ensemble
rules.context: Multiple consecutive submissions of individual model variants or single components each score worse than a known-best ensemble baseline (2-3+ consecutive regressions from simplifying).
rules.action: Stop testing individual components in isolation. Restore the full ensemble pipeline and probe ensemble-level levers (blending weights, member composition, post-processing). Use the ensemble score as a floor; only submit a single model if local validation strongly suggests it exceeds that floor.
rules.exceptions: If the goal is to find a strong single model to later include in a better ensemble, continued single-model probing may be justified (17616127:e2#2 counter_evidence).

rules.name: isolate_ensemble_member_contribution_before_tuning
rules.context: An ensemble regresses after modifying or adding one member, and you need to determine whether the problem is the changed component or the blend interaction.
rules.action: Submit each ensemble member individually (or disable others) to measure standalone quality. If the isolated member scores far worse than the ensemble, the ensemble diversity is load-bearing — fix the member rather than the blend. If the member is strong alone but hurts the blend, adjust weights or remove it. Treat isolation runs as diagnostic probes, not final submissions.
rules.exceptions: Isolation costs submissions; prefer local validation when available. Isolation may conflate backbone quality with lost ensemble diversity (50496431:e13#1).

rules.name: remove_regressing_ensemble_member_try_replacement
rules.context: Adding a new member to an ensemble caused a score regression compared to the previous ensemble composition.
rules.action: Immediately remove the regressing member and try a different backbone or model variant in the same slot. If the replacement improves, also audit remaining members by disabling suspected weak contributors one at a time. Submit after each atomic change to isolate effects.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: pivot_lever_after_repeated_failures
rules.context: 4+ consecutive iterations tuning the same lever category (e.g., augmentation parameters, checkpoint swaps, a single hyperparameter) show no improvement or persistent regression.
rules.action: Abandon the current lever entirely and switch to a fundamentally different one (e.g., from augmentation to loss function, from checkpoint selection to ensembling, from hyperparameter tuning to adding model diversity). One or two probes on the new lever should clarify whether it has higher upside.
rules.exceptions: If the repeated failures are due to a confound (e.g., model size difference in 17616127:e13#1), fixing the confound on the same lever may be more efficient than pivoting.

rules.name: reestablish_baseline_before_architectural_pivot
rules.context: A regression has occurred and you are considering a large architectural restructuring or disabling multiple proven components simultaneously.
rules.action: First revert the specific change that caused the regression to re-establish the known-best baseline. Only then make one structural change at a time. Never combine a large infrastructure refactor with introducing a new component in a single submission — catastrophic regressions from large diffs are nearly impossible to debug.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: compensate_regression_via_orthogonal_ensemble_expansion
rules.context: A config or hyperparameter change caused a regression on a single model, but you have untried ensemble combinations available.
rules.action: Rather than debugging the regression in isolation, keep the change but add more diverse models to the ensemble. If the combined score exceeds the previous best, the change was not harmful in the ensemble context. If it still regresses, revert the change.
rules.exceptions: Attribution is unclear — the improvement may come entirely from ensemble expansion, not the config change (50376011:e13#2 counter_evidence).

rules.name: verify_pipeline_with_repeated_runs_before_config_restore
rules.context: After many exploratory edits you have lost track of which configuration was best, and the code has accumulated changes.
rules.action: Re-run the current (suboptimal) configuration 2-3 times to establish a reliable baseline and confirm the pipeline works. Clean up dead/commented code. Then switch back to the known-best configuration. This separates infrastructure issues from configuration issues.
rules.exceptions: If leaderboard noise or non-determinism is high (50376011:e5#1 showed ~0.3pt variance between identical runs), repeated runs may not provide reliable signal.

rules.name: limit_simultaneous_inference_hyperparameter_changes
rules.context: You suspect inference configuration (token length, seed, batch size) may be a bottleneck and want to probe it.
rules.action: Change at most one lightweight inference hyperparameter per submission to maintain attribution. If the score does not improve after 1-2 probes, revert and return to the primary lever (model selection or ensembling) rather than sweeping further.
rules.exceptions: When submission budget is very limited, bundling two small changes may be acceptable if you plan to unbundle on the next step.

rules.name: combine_best_individual_models_into_equal_weight_ensemble
rules.context: Two or more individual model variants each produce competitive but inconsistent scores, and single-model swaps have plateaued.
rules.action: Combine the best-performing individual model variants into an equal-weight ensemble. Start with uniform weights rather than tuning weights, since diversity benefit of averaging typically dominates weight optimization at small ensemble sizes.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: isolate_signal_from_noise_before_acting_on_score_changes
rules.context: When a score change (improvement or regression) is observed after a single modification, but the pipeline may contain stochastic elements or the change magnitude is small relative to historical score fluctuations.
rules.action: Before reverting or committing a change, establish the noise floor: either use a clean A/B probe where the change is the only variable (making attribution unambiguous), or re-submit identical code 2-3 times to estimate run-to-run variance. Only trust score differences that clearly exceed the noise floor. If attribution is unambiguous and the change clearly regresses, revert immediately; if variance is comparable to the observed difference, do not act on it. Use the noise estimate as a threshold for future decisions—only accept changes that consistently outperform across multiple runs.
rules.exceptions: When a catastrophic score drop occurs (e.g., pipeline failure producing wildly out-of-range scores), treat it as a bug rather than normal variance. Bundling a revert with other improvements can introduce confounds about what actually helped. Authors often act on single-run results despite knowing about noise (50376011:e25#1 counter_evidence). Only one re-run gives a weak variance estimate; ideally 2-3 re-runs are needed.

rules.name: revert_regressing_change_before_iterating
rules.context: A recent change (feature selection method, preprocessing step, post-processing branch, configuration change, or ensemble member swap) caused a leaderboard regression confirmed across one or more consecutive submissions, especially when two or more consecutive submissions regress from a known-good configuration.
rules.action: Revert the suspected regressing change entirely and restore the exact last-known-good state. Submit to confirm recovery before making any additional modifications. Do not combine the revert with new untested changes (hyperparameter tweaks, data reordering, new features) in the same submission, as this confounds diagnosis and risks compounding regressions. Then move to a qualitatively different lever rather than continuing the same line of exploration.
rules.exceptions: 27656049:e6#1 — revert only partially recovered performance, possibly because the author simultaneously changed hyperparameters and fold count, confounding the revert signal. 55621328:e25#1 — author combined the revert with an incremental improvement (updated checkpoint) to maximize submission value, which worked but adds confounding.

rules.name: revert_all_on_multi_variable_regression
rules.context: Multiple settings or components were changed simultaneously in one submission and a regression occurred, making it unclear which change is responsible.
rules.action: Revert all changed variables to the last-known-good configuration rather than attempting to isolate which individual change caused the regression. Then re-test only cheap binary toggles (e.g., post-processing on/off) one at a time to confirm the optimum.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: stop_and_diagnose_on_unexpected_deep_regression
rules.context: A revert or simplification intended to fix a regression instead produces a score much worse than both the regressed version and the original best, suggesting something beyond a hyperparameter issue.
rules.action: Do not make further tweaks on top of the broken state. Revert to the exact last-known-good version, submit to confirm it still works, and then make one isolated change at a time. A large unexpected regression after a revert likely indicates a bug (data misalignment, broken pipeline) rather than a modeling issue.
rules.exceptions: Both supporting items are from the same kernel (7670859); however the principle of diagnosing before further changes is echoed in the revert-first pattern across other kernels.

rules.name: two_consecutive_failures_trigger_full_revert
rules.context: A newly introduced feature or post-processing step caused a regression, and a follow-up fix attempt also failed to recover the previous best score (two consecutive failed submissions).
rules.action: Revert the feature entirely rather than continuing to debug it. Two consecutive failures provide strong evidence the approach is harmful. Optionally combine the revert with a separate, independent incremental improvement to maximize the next submission's value.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: abandon_lever_after_exhaustive_sweep_no_improvement
rules.context: When a hyperparameter sweep has tested values on both sides of the current best (or across multiple orders of magnitude) and no setting clearly dominates, or when 3+ variants of a new component all trail the baseline.
rules.action: Stop the sweep and move to a qualitatively different lever (e.g., feature engineering, model architecture, ensemble composition). Do not submit intermediate results from an inconclusive sweep. Do not continue fine-tuning a parameter with smaller step sizes when the optimum is already bracketed.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: isolate_one_variable_at_a_time
rules.context: When sweeping multiple interacting hyperparameters or configuration dimensions, and the expected effect size is small relative to leaderboard noise.
rules.action: Change only one variable per submission to isolate its effect. If you must change two variables simultaneously and the result regresses, revert both to the last known-good state before continuing. After bracketing an optimum on one parameter, fix it at the best value before sweeping the next parameter.
rules.exceptions: When the baseline is far from optimal, bundling multiple changes can sometimes work (50496431:e25#1 counter_evidence). Also see batching rule for when changes are believed independently beneficial.

rules.name: restore_removed_ensemble_members_on_regression
rules.context: When removing ensemble members causes a score regression larger than typical leaderboard noise.
rules.action: Restore the removed members immediately. Then try adding the new predictions as an additional group alongside the restored members rather than as a replacement. If the augmented ensemble still does not beat the prior best, abandon the new component or try a learned combiner instead of fixed weights.
rules.exceptions: Even after restoring all members, the score may not recover if the new component added noise to the blend (17616127:e17#2 counter_evidence).

rules.name: revert_immediately_on_clear_regression
rules.context: When a single-variable change (e.g., switching regularization type, removing a model, changing a component) produces a score drop clearly larger than typical noise.
rules.action: Immediately revert the change in the next iteration rather than trying to tune or rescue the new variant. Redirect effort to tuning the previously better variant's hyperparameters or to a different lever entirely. Do not spend multiple iterations trying to make a clearly inferior component work.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: ablate_joint_changes_to_isolate_contribution
rules.context: When two or more changes were made simultaneously and the combined result shows a large improvement, making it ambiguous which change helped.
rules.action: Revert one variable back to its previous value while keeping the other fixed, and submit. If the score stays the same or improves, the reverted variable's new value was unnecessary or harmful. Repeat for the other variable if needed. This isolates contributions with minimal submissions.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: never_bundle_cleanup_with_experimental_revert
rules.context: When reverting an unsuccessful experimental change and also wanting to clean up or refactor code that removes functional inference logic.
rules.action: Submit the experimental revert alone first to confirm the score recovers. Then clean up dead code or refactor in a separate submission. A regression after a combined change is unattributable and wastes a submission.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: use_cv_to_guide_sweep_save_submissions
rules.context: When sweeping hyperparameters or blend weights and each training run produces a reliable local CV metric, while leaderboard submissions are limited, expensive, or noisy.
rules.action: Run the full sweep locally using CV or OOF scores to identify the best value without submitting intermediate results. Submit only the single best candidate to the leaderboard to confirm. If you change a companion parameter, re-sweep locally before submitting again. Reserve LB submissions for confirming the best CV candidate rather than exploring.
rules.exceptions: 53747598:e8#1 warns that CV-guided blend weight selection may not transfer to LB, so submit the best CV candidate to verify rather than trusting CV alone.

rules.name: test_new_modality_standalone_before_blending
rules.context: When adding a new modality or model family to an existing strong ensemble, and the new component's standalone quality is unknown.
rules.action: First test the new modality/model in isolation to gauge its standalone quality before combining it with the existing ensemble. If standalone performance is much worse than the baseline, fix preprocessing or the model before blending. Once standalone quality is acceptable, add it alongside existing models rather than replacing them.
rules.exceptions: Testing in isolation on the leaderboard wastes submissions; prefer offline validation if possible (52551258:e11#1 counter_evidence).

rules.name: enumerate_then_ensemble_when_noisy
rules.context: When sweeping a small discrete set of options (e.g., checkpoints, model variants) and score differences between options are small relative to leaderboard noise.
rules.action: Enumerate all options once to get a rough ranking. If score differences are small relative to noise, stop trying to pick a single winner and instead ensemble the top candidates. Do not re-test options expecting different results unless you've changed something else in the pipeline.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: single_probe_before_deep_tuning
rules.context: When evaluating whether a new pipeline variant, training recipe, or model family is competitive against a strong baseline.
rules.action: Submit one representative configuration of the new variant quickly. If it scores substantially below your best (e.g., >0.5% regression), abandon that variant rather than tuning weights or hyperparameters within it. Reserve tuning effort for variants that are already close to your best.
rules.exceptions: Large score swings from weight tuning alone have been observed (55621328:e47#2 counter_evidence), so a single probe may underestimate potential for variants where post-processing has high leverage.

rules.name: sweep_checkpoints_individually_then_scale
rules.context: When you have many trained checkpoints from different experiments (varying backbone, training tricks, folds, seeds) and need to find the best combination for submission.
rules.action: First sweep single-checkpoint variants one at a time to identify the best training recipe on the leaderboard. Once the best recipe is found, scale up by adding all available folds from that recipe, then add multi-seed checkpoints. Do not mix recipes until you know which single recipe is strongest.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: stop_postprocessing_sweep_when_plateaued
rules.context: When tuning post-processing parameters (blend weights, additive corrections, thresholds) and 3-4 consecutive submissions return effectively the same score within noise.
rules.action: Stop sweeping that lever. The leaderboard resolution cannot distinguish the variants, so further submissions waste budget without information gain. Move to a structurally different lever (new model, new features, new loss) instead.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: ablate_ensemble_members_individually
rules.context: You have a multi-model ensemble achieving a good score and want to determine whether all members are contributing.
rules.action: Test each member in isolation by disabling all others, holding all other settings fixed. If every individual member scores worse than the full ensemble, keep all members and focus on adding/swapping rather than reducing. If one member alone matches or beats the ensemble, drop the weaker members. Do not change checkpoints or other settings simultaneously.
rules.exceptions: 50376011:e17#1 warns that confounding variables (e.g., config overrides like mt.init()) can invalidate the entire sweep; verify the test harness is clean before starting. 52551258:e3#1 shows checkpoint changes can confound ablation.

rules.name: stop_sweep_after_diminishing_returns
rules.context: You are sweeping a hyperparameter in one direction and consecutive improvements are shrinking (e.g., each gain is less than half the previous).
rules.action: Try at most one more step beyond the point where marginal gain halves twice or drops below a noise threshold (~0.0002). If that step shows no improvement, revert to the best-scoring value and switch to a different lever entirely. Do not keep pushing in the same direction.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: stop_after_consecutive_regressions_on_same_lever
rules.context: Three or more consecutive attempts on the same type of lever (e.g., preprocessing tuning, weight sweeping) all regress from the best known score.
rules.action: Stop that line of exploration, revert to the best-scoring configuration, and switch to a qualitatively different lever (e.g., from preprocessing to ensemble composition or architecture). Do not continue hoping the next tweak will work.
rules.exceptions: 50496431:e9#1 notes that if the parameter must match training-time settings, the sweep is fundamentally misguided and should stop after 2 attempts, not 3.

rules.name: ensemble_new_best_member_with_previous_best
rules.context: A newly tested single model outperforms the previous best single model, and ensembling has historically helped in this pipeline.
rules.action: Immediately test combining the new best member with the previous best member. If the pair beats both individuals, keep the pair. If not, keep the better individual. This one-step greedy addition is cheap and almost always worth trying before exploring further combinations.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: toggle_binary_option_after_each_change
rules.context: You have a binary postprocessing toggle (e.g., rank averaging vs raw averaging) whose optimal setting may interact with other pipeline changes.
rules.action: After every substantive change (model, resolution, weights), test both toggle states before moving on. Use the better state as the baseline for the next experiment. Do not assume the toggle's direction is stable across model changes.
rules.exceptions: 13848868:e8#2 counter-evidence suggests the toggle direction may be more stable than expected within a session, making re-checks occasionally unnecessary.

rules.name: ensemble_blend_weight_sweep_strategy
rules.context: You have 2-4 models producing predictions and want to find optimal blend weights, with limited submission budget.
rules.action: Start with simple weights (equal or near-equal). Toggle members in/out one at a time. When adding a new component to an already-good blend, give it small weight (≤20%). Increase the weight of the best-contributing model in steps of ~0.05-0.10. When a change causes a drop, reverse direction. Stop after 2 consecutive marginal improvements (<0.001). Do not restructure the entire blend after a single regression.
rules.exceptions: 17616127:e22#1 shows that even small-weight additions can hurt if the new component is weaker than existing ones.

rules.name: do_not_persist_with_larger_model_after_repeated_underperformance
rules.context: A larger model variant (e.g., large vs base) underperforms the smaller variant on the leaderboard across 2-3 attempts.
rules.action: Stop trying larger models and return to the smaller variant. Invest effort in ensembling the smaller model (more folds, more seeds) rather than scaling up model size. The ensemble of a well-trained smaller model often beats a single larger model.
rules.exceptions: 55621328:e16#3 notes that large+ITPT came close, suggesting large models might work with significantly more tuning, but the smaller model path is more reliable.

rules.name: fold_ensemble_when_checkpoint_swaps_plateau
rules.context: Swapping to alternative single-fold checkpoints yields diminishing or negative returns, but multiple fold checkpoints are available for the best model.
rules.action: Pivot to ensembling multiple folds of the best-performing checkpoint rather than continuing to swap single checkpoints. This reduces prediction variance without requiring new model training or architecture changes.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: noisy_lb_continue_sweep_before_reverting
rules.context: The public leaderboard has very few evaluation rows (e.g., <10), making individual submission scores very noisy, and a small regression occurs after toggling an ensemble member.
rules.action: Do not immediately revert a small regression. Continue the sweep to cover all candidate members. After the sweep, select the best-scoring configuration rather than greedily reverting each regression. This avoids being misled by noise on individual submissions.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: ensemble_ablation_one_at_a_time
rules.context: When you have a multi-member ensemble at a known score and want to understand which members are contributing.
rules.action: Ablate one ensemble member at a time by removing it and submitting. If the score drops, keep the member; if it holds or improves, remove it permanently. For a quick diagnostic, submit a drastically pruned version (1-2 strongest members) first—if it matches the full ensemble, many members are redundant. Do not ablate multiple members simultaneously.
rules.exceptions: On small/noisy public LBs, even a large delta from ablation could be noise (18350823:e7#2 notes 7-row LB).

rules.name: reprobe_rejected_option_after_major_upstream_change
rules.context: When a discrete configuration option (feature set, architecture variant, hyperparameter value) was previously rejected, but the model or data pipeline has changed substantially since the last test.
rules.action: Re-test the previously rejected option exactly once on the new baseline. If it still regresses, stop probing that option permanently—do not re-test a third or fourth time without a very large upstream change. The cost is one submission, which is justified by the possibility that the upstream change altered the interaction.
rules.exceptions: In 49576186:e28#1, the option never paid off across three attempts, suggesting the author could have skipped it after the second failure.

rules.name: test_changes_on_best_baseline_not_regressed
rules.context: When a recent change caused a regression and you want to test an orthogonal new idea (e.g., a post-processing transformation).
rules.action: Test the new idea on top of the last-known-best configuration, not on top of the regressed version. Stacking an unproven change on an already-regressed baseline makes it impossible to attribute gains or losses. Revert to the best baseline before adding the new transformation.
rules.exceptions: If the regression is tiny and within noise, testing on the current version may be acceptable to save time.

rules.name: avoid_bundling_features_with_infrastructure
rules.context: When adding a new feature source (e.g., embeddings, new columns) and simultaneously changing infrastructure (GPU mode, n_estimators, code restructuring).
rules.action: Do not bundle new features with infrastructure changes in the same submission. Submit the feature addition alone first to isolate its effect. If it regresses, you know the features are the cause. If you must change infrastructure, do it in a separate prior submission to establish a clean baseline.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: checkpoint_selection_via_val_loss_then_lb_verify
