rules.context: When multiple trained checkpoints (different epochs, training runs, or configurations) are available and can be swapped at inference time with zero cost.
rules.action: Compare validation losses across available checkpoints and select the set with better per-fold val losses. Submit once to verify on the leaderboard. Do not sweep many checkpoint combinations—use val loss as a proxy to pick one candidate, then verify. If per-fold val losses are mixed (some folds better, some worse), still submit for LB verification since ensemble-level performance may differ from per-fold signals.
rules.exceptions: Per-fold val loss is not a perfect proxy for ensemble LB score (50496431:e2#2 showed mixed fold losses but overall LB improvement).

rules.name: do_not_add_many_pruned_components_back_at_once
rules.context: When multiple components were previously removed for efficiency/stability and you want to re-add them to recover lost accuracy.
rules.action: Re-add pruned components one at a time or in small groups, submitting after each, so you can isolate which help and which hurt. A single large re-addition makes it impossible to diagnose regressions and may introduce bugs.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: change_one_variable_at_a_time
rules.context: When probing whether a new configuration (model variant, architecture, hyperparameter) improves over a strong baseline, and multiple changes are tempting to bundle together.
rules.action: Change only one variable at a time against the baseline. If you must bundle tightly coupled changes, accept that a regression won't tell you which change caused it. After a clear regression from bundled changes, revert all changes entirely rather than trying to compensate with minor tweaks. Re-test components individually only if the idea still seems promising.
rules.exceptions: When changes are logically inseparable (e.g., new checkpoint requires matching preprocessing), bundling is acceptable per 55621328:e48#1, but revert the entire bundle on regression.

rules.name: revert_and_switch_lever_on_regression
rules.context: When a single-step probe of a new idea (model variant, feature, configuration toggle) causes a clear leaderboard regression and there is no obvious fix or the previously productive lever still has headroom.
rules.action: Revert the change immediately and move to a qualitatively different lever rather than tuning around the failed change. For discrete choices (loss function, boosting type, toggle) where there is no gradient to follow, a single negative result is sufficient to deprioritize. Do not spend more than one or two recovery attempts before reverting.
rules.exceptions: If the regression is tiny and could be noise (e.g., 27389424:e13#2 dropped only 0.00037), re-tuning other hyperparameters under the new setting might recover the loss. Also, 73671444:e2#1 notes a tiny regression might warrant further exploration.

rules.name: switch_lever_on_diminishing_returns
rules.context: When repeated micro-adjustments to the same lever (e.g., ensemble weights, hyperparameter values, small parameter tweaks) show diminishing, oscillating, or null returns over multiple iterations.
rules.action: Pause the current lever and look for an orthogonal improvement (e.g., TTA, new model family, different feature engineering, structural architecture change). Apply it as a single probe. If it yields a new best, lock it in and optionally resume fine-tuning on the improved baseline. Reserve fine-tuning for after structural decisions are settled.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: revert_backbone_swap_on_regression
rules.context: When switching to a different model backbone/architecture causes a leaderboard regression, and the original backbone family still has unexplored variants or preprocessing improvements.
rules.action: Revert to the proven architecture but combine the revert with a queued improvement (e.g., better preprocessing, newer checkpoint, additional training) so the revert step also advances the score. Do not continue tuning inference around a weak backbone. If the regression is catastrophically large, suspect a weight-loading mismatch before blaming model capacity.
rules.exceptions: 18426209:e2#1 notes that catastrophic regressions (e.g., 0.46→0.74) likely indicate checkpoint/architecture mismatch rather than genuine model inferiority.

rules.name: single_probe_then_decide_for_new_components
rules.context: When adding a new component to a pipeline (stacking feature, ensemble member, architectural idea) and the baseline is already well-tuned.
rules.action: Treat the addition as a single probe: integrate it in one submission while keeping the rest of the pipeline stable. If the score improves, continue expanding in that direction. If it regresses or fails to improve, abandon the idea quickly rather than tuning integration details—a regression suggests the new component adds noise or redundancy rather than complementary signal.
rules.exceptions: 18550705:e1#2 notes the author also changed ensemble composition simultaneously, so the probe wasn't perfectly isolated. Cleaner probes give more actionable signal.

rules.name: gate_submissions_on_local_cv
rules.context: When making a structural change (new model family, new architecture, speculative feature) whose impact is uncertain and leaderboard submissions are limited.
rules.action: Do not submit until local CV confirms the change is at least competitive with the current best. Fix runtime issues first, reduce fold count to iterate faster, then evaluate. Only submit after CV scores match or exceed the current LB baseline. If CV is disappointing, abandon the probe without burning a submission.
rules.exceptions: When the leaderboard distribution differs substantially from CV (e.g., very small public test set), CV gating may be unreliable.

rules.name: rerun_to_verify_new_best
rules.context: When achieving a new best score that could be within run-to-run noise, especially with stochastic components (GPU non-determinism, neural network inference, AutoML ensembling).
rules.action: Re-submit the identical code 1-2 times without changes. If re-runs show similar or better scores, accept the change as beneficial. If they regress, treat the original gain as noise and consider reverting. For ensemble comparisons, run at least two submissions per configuration before concluding.
rules.exceptions: 50496431:e21#2 found a 0.016 swing with no code change, and 75924487:e1#2 saw a 0.00054 jump on re-run, suggesting substantial non-determinism that makes even re-run verification unreliable. 50376011:e24#1 applied the two-submissions-per-config rule loosely.

rules.name: stop_ablating_after_consecutive_regressions
rules.context: When ablation experiments (removing ensemble members, simplifying pipeline) show two or more consecutive regressions.
rules.action: Stop ablating after at most two consecutive regressions. Revert to the best-known configuration and pivot to the opposite direction (adding components or complexity). Do not spend more submissions confirming what two data points already show.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: revert_large_feature_batch_on_regression
rules.context: When adding a large batch of new features causes a leaderboard regression and one or two compensating tweaks fail to recover the prior best score.
rules.action: Revert the feature addition entirely rather than continuing to tune around it. Do not spend more than two recovery attempts. If the features are believed to contain some useful signals, consider adding them in smaller subsets in future probes rather than all at once.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: isolate_revert_from_other_changes
rules.context: When reverting a failed probe and you also want to make other code changes (cleanup, new features, fold logic changes).
rules.action: Make only the revert and submit to confirm the baseline is restored. Bundle unrelated changes into a separate commit afterward. Mixing revert with other changes makes it impossible to diagnose whether the revert worked or the other changes caused a new problem.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: test_weighted_blend_before_dropping_weak_model
rules.context: When adding a weaker model to an ensemble at equal weights hurts the score compared to the stronger model alone.
rules.action: Try a heavily skewed weight (e.g., 80/20) favoring the stronger model. If the weighted blend still underperforms the strong model alone, drop the weak model entirely rather than continuing to tune weights. The diversity benefit is insufficient to overcome the quality gap.
rules.exceptions: 60197293:e5#1 found the single model was only marginally worse than the ensemble (0.81788 vs 0.81799), suggesting the weaker member contributed minimally but didn't clearly hurt with proper weighting.

rules.name: debug_before_submitting_speculative_changes
rules.context: When a speculative change involves code that may fail at runtime (custom metrics, new preprocessing, device changes) or affects all predictions (TTA, inference-time augmentation).
rules.action: Run locally or add debug prints first without submitting. Fix any runtime errors (shape mismatches, type errors, degenerate outputs) in a separate step. Only submit once the pipeline runs cleanly and outputs look reasonable. This avoids wasting submissions on broken inference.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: permanently_mark_repeatedly_failed_toggle
rules.context: When a binary or small-set configuration option has been tested three or more times across different model states and always regresses.
rules.action: Permanently mark it as inferior and do not revisit it. Immediately move to a different, orthogonal lever. Continuing to re-test a consistently failing toggle wastes submissions.
rules.exceptions: If the model pipeline changes fundamentally (e.g., entirely new architecture), the toggle may warrant one more test.

rules.name: isolate_new_component_before_ensemble_integration
rules.context: A new model checkpoint or artifact is available and you want to know if it improves an existing multi-model ensemble, but the ensemble is complex enough that adding the component would make attribution difficult.
rules.action: First test the new component in isolation (standalone or with minimal partners) to establish its quality. If standalone score is far worse than existing components, try blending it with the single strongest existing component at a conservative weight (30-40%). Only integrate into the full ensemble if the partial blend shows promise. Do not add multiple new components simultaneously.
rules.exceptions: A weak standalone model can still help an ensemble through diversity (17616127:e12#1 counter_evidence). When LB noise is high (e.g., 0.00002 difference in 53424936:e8#1), trust offline validation over LB for inclusion decisions.

rules.name: single_variable_per_submission
rules.context: You want to measure the impact of a change on leaderboard score, especially after prior multi-factor changes produced ambiguous or negative results.
rules.action: Change exactly one factor per submission (e.g., only checkpoint path, only TTA strategy, only ensemble membership). If a multi-factor change regresses, decompose it into single-factor probes rather than reverting everything. Prioritize the highest-value change for the first isolated test.
rules.exceptions: The author in 53424936:e6#3 did not fully isolate but prioritized the backbone swap, suggesting perfect isolation is aspirational—prioritization of the key change is the practical minimum.

rules.name: checkpoint_swap_with_matched_settings_to_compare_models
rules.context: Model checkpoints or artifacts are trained offline or stored externally and a new version or alternative candidate becomes available. The inference pipeline is stable and functional.
rules.action: Change only the model-load path to point to the new artifact, matching inference settings (image size, preprocessing) to the checkpoint's training configuration, and re-run the inference notebook without any other modifications. Submit once with default post-processing, then optionally toggle post-processing (e.g., rank conversion) and submit again to isolate the checkpoint's contribution. Compare LB scores across candidates to identify the best variant before investing in ensembling or further tuning. If the score improves, keep the new artifact and iterate; if not, revert the path. Periodically re-run even unchanged code to detect upstream artifact updates.
rules.exceptions: If the gain is negligible (<~0.001 on LB), do not iterate further on this lever (73937748:e25#1). Inefficient if many checkpoints exist; pre-filter using offline CV first.

rules.name: stop_lever_after_exhaustion_or_consecutive_failures
rules.context: When 2-3 consecutive small variations on the same lever (e.g., blend weights, seed count, dropout, meta-learner hyperparameters) produce no improvement or regressions, or when you have probed the full natural range of a lever and all variants produce score differences smaller than the estimated leaderboard noise.
rules.action: Lock in the best value found and stop tuning that lever. Pivot to a qualitatively different lever with higher potential variance (e.g., adding a new model family, changing architecture, altering the feature set, using a stronger backbone). Continuing to micro-tune the same knob yields diminishing returns. If adding more seeds of the same architecture doesn't help, pivot to a different architecture rather than more seeds. Return to fine-tune the abandoned lever only after exhausting higher-impact options.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: rerun_failed_submission_before_concluding_change_is_bad
rules.context: A notebook version with a meaningful change was not submitted (possibly due to runtime error, timeout, or platform issue) and the code appears correct.
rules.action: Re-run the identical notebook without code changes to confirm the pipeline completes successfully, then submit. Do not assume a failed or unsubmitted run means the change was bad—verify by re-execution before drawing conclusions. Two consecutive failed runs from hasty edits waste submission budget.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: add_new_member_to_uniform_ensemble_then_tune_weights
rules.context: An ensemble uses uniform averaging and a new prediction source is available. Prior additions of diverse sources have yielded small LB improvements.
rules.action: Add the new prediction source to the uniform average (adjusting the denominator), submit once. If the score improves, keep the member and then move to weight tuning as a separate step. Do not tune weights and membership simultaneously. If weight tuning regresses, revert to uniform weights.
rules.exceptions: Weight tuning after membership change is not guaranteed to help (18837555:e4#1: v14 weight tuning regressed to 0.45784).

rules.name: selective_rollback_on_regression_from_bundled_changes
rules.context: Score regressed after multiple simultaneous changes (new features, new targets, new ensemble member, code refactor, infrastructure changes) and you need to identify the cause.
rules.action: Identify the single most likely harmful change—typically the most recently added or most easily toggled component (e.g., a new ensemble member, a new artifact, a suspicious preprocessing step like fillna, or an infrastructure artifact like batch size). Disable only that change and resubmit. If the score recovers, the other bundled changes were beneficial; if it only partially recovers, suspect other concurrent changes and investigate them next by further ablation. If the score does not recover, revert all and re-add incrementally.
rules.exceptions: Score may only partially recover (77276039:e4#2: 0.69142→0.69244, not back to 0.69330), indicating multiple changes contributed. When you cannot form a strong prior about which change is harmful, full revert may be safer (28093671 counter_evidence notes uncertainty about the true culprit).

rules.name: restore_diversity_after_simplified_ensemble_regresses
rules.context: A simplified ensemble (fewer models or variants of one architecture) scores much worse than the full diverse ensemble, and partial blending only partially recovers the score.
rules.action: Stop exploring the reduced architecture pair in isolation. Return to the full diverse ensemble and incorporate the new model as an additional member rather than a replacement. Diversity across architectures matters more than tuning weights between variants of one architecture.
rules.exceptions: Both items are from the same kernel but represent distinct episodes (e12 vs e32) with the same conclusion.

rules.name: repeated_submission_to_measure_noise_floor
rules.context: When the model training is stochastic (e.g., DART dropout, GPU non-determinism) or the public leaderboard uses very few rows, and you need to know how much of a score change is signal vs. noise before tuning.
rules.action: Submit the identical unchanged pipeline 2–5+ times and record the LB spread. Use the observed range as the minimum detectable effect size. Only treat subsequent changes as improvements if they exceed this noise band. Stop re-submitting once 3+ consecutive scores are identical.
rules.exceptions: If the public LB sample is extremely small (~7 rows), even repeated submissions may not converge to a stable noise estimate (18426209:e4#1 saw +0.002 on re-run).

rules.name: cheap_blend_weight_probe_before_investment
rules.context: When you have a multi-model ensemble and want to decide whether a secondary component deserves more development effort, and changing the blend weight requires no retraining.
rules.action: Submit one version with a meaningfully larger weight for the candidate model (e.g., double it). If the LB score improves, the component carries useful complementary information—invest in improving it. If it degrades, deprioritize. Limit to 1–2 probe submissions. For post-hoc additive adjustments, try halving the scalar; if it regresses, revert and keep the original.
rules.exceptions: When the gain is within noise (e.g., +0.00004), the conclusion may be unreliable; a CV-based weight search would be more robust (77450317:e1#1 counter_evidence).

rules.name: replace_pipeline_or_apply_known_fix_when_far_below_target
rules.context: Your score is far below competitive levels or a known reference score (e.g., >5 points AUC gap), and the cause is well-understood from reference solutions or domain knowledge, or the current pipeline uses a fundamentally limited architecture or data pipeline.
rules.action: Skip incremental tuning and apply most of the known improvement or replace the core pipeline (model architecture, data loading, accelerator strategy, feature engineering) in one large step. Reserve incremental A/B testing for when the baseline is already within a few points of the target and you are in diminishing-returns territory.
rules.exceptions: 28984551:e1#2 counter_evidence: switching too quickly (to dart) caused regression to 0.786, suggesting some single-model tuning may be needed before switching. When the gap is small or the cause is uncertain, incremental changes are safer.

rules.name: revert_after_single_negative_probe_move_on
rules.context: A single probe of an alternative setting or component produces a regression on the leaderboard—whether marginal or much larger than recent incremental gains (e.g., 3-4x the size of recent improvements)—and higher-impact levers are available.
rules.action: Treat the single negative probe as sufficient evidence to abandon that direction. Do not continue fine-grained search around the losing value. Revert to the best known setting and switch to a different lever entirely. Return to fine-tune only after exhausting higher-impact options.
rules.exceptions: If the regression is well within noise, the conclusion may be wrong; consider a second probe if the lever is theoretically promising. If the regression could be caused by a confounded infrastructure issue (batch size, non-determinism), verify before abandoning (see selective_rollback rule).

rules.name: ablation_test_complex_ensemble_components
rules.context: When an ensemble pipeline has multiple stacked components (e.g., meta-learner, postprocessing, multi-fold averaging) and it is unclear how much each component contributes to the final score.
rules.action: Disable all but one component (e.g., remove meta-learner or postprocessing) and submit the ablated version. Compare the degraded score to the full pipeline score. If the gap is large (e.g., ~0.025 RMSE), keep the component and invest effort in improving it rather than simplifying. This costs only 1–2 extra submissions to validate contributions.
rules.exceptions: 6803050 conflated two components (ensemble + quantile mapping) in re-enablement, so individual isolation was incomplete. Ideally isolate one component at a time.

rules.name: submit_baseline_before_further_tuning
rules.context: When you have been iterating on a pipeline for many versions without any leaderboard submission, and the pipeline is functionally complete or at least runnable end-to-end.
rules.action: Submit the current version as-is to establish a leaderboard baseline before making further tuning changes. This anchors subsequent modifications to a known public score and confirms the pipeline runs correctly in the competition environment. Do not continue offline-only iteration beyond the point where basic inference works.
rules.exceptions: 7240226 bundled an infrastructure fix with the first submission; if blocking bugs exist, fix them first but still submit immediately after.

rules.name: stop_tuning_weak_component_after_many_iterations
rules.context: A secondary model or architectural component has been tuned across ~5-10 hyperparameter or design variations without ever surpassing the best score achieved without it (or with a prior component).
rules.action: Stop tuning that component. Either replace it with a fundamentally different approach, revert to the previously successful component as a quick A/B probe, or try scaling up the component's capacity rather than continuing hyperparameter search. Limit the probe to 1-2 submissions before deciding.
rules.exceptions: The author in 13848868 found the probe's value was confirming the newer component needed more capacity rather than replacement, so a revert probe can inform scaling decisions rather than always leading to permanent revert.

rules.name: stop_single_fold_sweep_against_multi_fold_baseline
rules.context: Your current best uses a multi-fold ensemble and you are testing single-fold checkpoint variants from newer training runs against it.
rules.action: Try at most 2-3 single-fold variants. If none beats the multi-fold ensemble, stop and either train more folds of the promising variant or return to the multi-fold approach. Do not keep sweeping single-fold variants against a multi-fold baseline.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: do_not_perturb_training_normalization_at_inference
rules.context: You are at a score plateau with a fixed pretrained model checkpoint and are considering sweeping inference-time normalization statistics (mean/std) away from training-time values.
rules.action: Do NOT sweep normalization mean/std away from the values used during training. If you don't know the training config, keep ImageNet defaults. Deviating from training-time normalization almost always hurts. If the first perturbation degrades the score, revert immediately rather than continuing the sweep.
rules.exceptions: 15173072:e4#1: a very small perturbation showed +0.00048 gain, but this was within noise and subsequent steps lost it.

rules.name: try_one_alternative_before_reverting_on_noisy_lb
rules.context: A leaderboard regression occurred after a small hyperparameter change, but the public LB is very noisy (few evaluation samples or high run-to-run variance).
rules.action: Try one alternative configuration before concluding the direction is unproductive. If the alternative also fails or looks unpromising locally, revert to the known best and move on to a different lever entirely. Do not submit configurations that look worse on local CV.
rules.exceptions: This is riskier when submission budget is very limited; reverting immediately is safer in that case.

rules.name: one_variable_at_a_time_to_isolate_effects
rules.context: When testing hyperparameter, preprocessing, or configuration changes and using leaderboard scores as the primary feedback signal, especially when submissions are limited or noisy.
rules.action: Change only one variable per submission. Hold random seeds fixed while varying hyperparameters. If a multi-variable change regresses, revert all changes and re-introduce them individually against the known-good baseline rather than making further compound changes. Do not change seeds simultaneously with other parameters.
rules.exceptions: 60197293:e16#2 shows an alternative: when submissions are very limited, accumulate changes using local CV as filter and submit only the final bundle. This works when local CV is reliable.

rules.name: revert_fully_before_next_experiment_on_regression
rules.context: When a configuration change (single or compound) causes a clear score regression compared to a known-good baseline.
rules.action: Fully revert to the last known-good configuration before trying the next change. Never stack untested changes on top of a regression. If a partial revert doesn't recover the baseline score, inspect which components are actually running (e.g., missing ensemble members). Only after recovering the baseline, introduce the next candidate change.
rules.exceptions: 60759531:e3#1 notes the author never fully isolated single parameters and used partial rollbacks heuristically, which still sometimes worked but was less efficient.

rules.name: stop_diminishing_lever_and_pivot
rules.context: When 2-3 consecutive attempts on the same lever (e.g., blend weight tuning, single-model checkpoint selection, preprocessing variant) fail to beat the current best or produce changes smaller than the noise floor.
rules.action: Stop tuning the current lever and pivot to a qualitatively different lever: e.g., from blend weight tuning to adding a new diverse model; from single-model refinement to multi-model ensembling; from preprocessing changes to loss function or augmentation changes. Reserve remaining submission budget for higher-impact experiments.
rules.exceptions: 75145694:e14#1 notes the author continued for 3 declining submissions past the peak rather than stopping at 2, suggesting the stopping threshold is flexible depending on submission budget.

rules.name: upgrade_components_when_blend_tuning_regresses
rules.context: When ensemble blend weight tuning alone causes regression or plateaus, and the component model predictions themselves may be suboptimal or stale.
rules.action: Stop tuning blend weights on stale predictions. Upgrade the underlying component model predictions (retrained or improved versions), then retune blend weights jointly with the new components. Verify with a submission before iterating further.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: single_model_plateau_triggers_ensemble_diversity
rules.context: When fine-tuning a single model family (checkpoints, TTA, preprocessing) yields <1% relative improvement over 3+ iterations, indicating the marginal return of that lever is exhausted.
rules.action: Stop tuning the single model and invest effort in adding a complementary architecture (e.g., spectrogram CNN alongside 1D EEG CNN, or a different backbone) to the ensemble. The diversity gain from a second model family typically far exceeds further single-model tuning.
rules.exceptions: 17616127:e25#1 notes that simply adding more backbones with hand-tuned weights has diminishing returns compared to learned meta-ensembling (e.g., ridge regression).

rules.name: use_proxy_to_filter_before_submitting
rules.context: When you have many candidate configurations (checkpoints, weight sets, hyperparameter combos) but limited leaderboard submissions.
rules.action: Pre-filter candidates using an offline proxy signal (CV score, local validation). Only submit candidates whose proxy metric exceeds the current best or represents a meaningfully different configuration. Skip submission for candidates clearly inferior by proxy. When using local CV to accumulate changes, submit only the final best combination.
rules.exceptions: 15082684:e7#1 notes CV-LB correlation is not always monotonic, so proxy filtering should be used to prioritize, not to eliminate candidates entirely.

rules.name: rerun_to_confirm_before_iterating
rules.context: When a multi-factor change was made (new model versions + new blend weights, or code refactor + checkpoint swap) and the pipeline has stochastic elements, or when a revert doesn't recover the expected baseline score.
rules.action: Re-run the notebook unchanged and submit to confirm the score before making further modifications. This separates the signal of the change from run-to-run variance. If scores vary by more than ~0.01 across identical runs, treat the leaderboard signal as noisy. Only proceed to the next iteration after confirming improvement or diagnosing the discrepancy.
rules.exceptions: 50496431:e14#2 showed that two no-op runs gave ~0.014 spread, indicating moderate variance; both were still far from baseline, confirming a real regression rather than noise.

rules.name: diagnose_bug_before_abandoning_direction
rules.context: When a structural code change (architecture refactor, new branch, not just a hyperparameter) causes a regression.
rules.action: Inspect the changed forward pass or pipeline for correctness bugs (e.g., operations applied to wrong tensor, missing ensemble member, disabled component) before reverting the entire change. Fix the bug and re-evaluate. Only abandon the direction if the corrected version still regresses.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: checkpoint_sweep_with_early_stopping
rules.context: When you have a small number of discrete checkpoint versions (under ~10) and submissions are cheap (just swapping a path).
rules.action: Sort checkpoints by offline CV score and try the highest-CV candidates first. Submit sequentially. When two consecutive submissions yield nearly identical LB scores, or 2-3 consecutive checkpoints fail to beat the current best, stop the sweep—you have bracketed the optimum for that architecture.
rules.exceptions: 49524919:e3#1 notes the author continued sweeping after 3-4 consecutive regressions past the best, wasting submissions. An early-stopping rule after 2-3 regressions would have saved budget.

rules.name: reduce_cv_folds_for_expensive_variants
rules.context: You want to test an expensive training variant (e.g., DART booster, large model) and the existing CV/ensemble configuration with many folds and seeds would be prohibitively slow.
rules.action: Before testing the expensive variant, reduce the number of CV folds and ensemble seeds to the minimum needed for a reliable validation signal. Restore full folds/seeds only after confirming the variant is promising. This keeps iteration speed high during exploration.
rules.exceptions: 7670859:e5#1 emphasizes that before final submission, you must retrain on all data with full CV to avoid regression from data loss.

rules.name: match_inference_preprocessing_to_training
rules.context: You are sweeping a preprocessing parameter at inference time (e.g., crop offset, spectrogram settings) while using fixed pretrained weights.
rules.action: Before sweeping, verify that the model's weights were trained with the same preprocessing settings. If weights are fixed, the parameter must match training-time settings exactly—sweeping it will almost always regress. Abandon the sweep after 2-3 submissions that all regress from baseline.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: verify_pipeline_replacement_before_disabling_original
rules.context: You are replacing live inference with cached/precomputed predictions to save compute in a submission notebook.
rules.action: First verify the replacement produces identical or near-identical outputs before disabling the original code. Do not disable all original predictions simultaneously—keep a subset active as a sanity check. Only submit after confirming outputs match. If the score regresses, restore the original pipeline immediately.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: revert_after_consecutive_regressions
rules.context: Two or more consecutive experimental changes (e.g., blend adjustments, hyperparameter tweaks) all regress relative to the pre-episode best score.
rules.action: Stop the current line of experimentation and revert to the exact configuration that produced the best score. Do not escalate complexity after a regression—simplify or revert first. Use the pre-episode best as the anchor. If the reverted version recovers the score, move to a qualitatively different lever entirely.
rules.exceptions: If the regression is within the noise floor of the leaderboard, the direction may still be correct (see persist_through_noise_if_direction_justified rule).

rules.name: single_variable_per_submission
rules.context: You are submitting to the leaderboard to evaluate the effect of a change, and you have modified more than one factor (e.g., checkpoint + dropout, model index + initialization, data filter + architecture).
rules.action: Change only one variable per submission. If you accidentally varied two factors and got ambiguous results, isolate and fix the confound first, then restart from the known-good baseline. Do not draw conclusions from runs where multiple factors changed simultaneously.
rules.exceptions: After a negative A/B result, it may be acceptable to bundle the revert with other queued improvements to save submission budget (49576186:e26#2), but re-test the rejected option once more against the improved baseline.

rules.name: estimate_noise_floor_before_trusting_improvements
rules.context: Leaderboard scores show variance across identical or near-identical re-runs (e.g., ~0.002-0.03 variation with no code change), and the improvement from a candidate change is similar in magnitude to the observed noise.
rules.action: Re-run the same configuration at least 2-3 times to estimate the noise floor. Only count an improvement as real if it exceeds 2× the observed run-to-run variance. Compare distributions of scores rather than single-point estimates. Do not chase small regressions from cosmetic or no-op changes.
rules.exceptions: When submission budget is very limited, repeated identical submissions may not be affordable.

rules.name: stop_sweep_after_budget_exhausted
rules.context: You have tried 3-5+ meaningfully different configurations of a single lever (blend weights, feature variants, hyperparameter values) without any variant matching or exceeding the baseline on the leaderboard, or consecutive attempts produce score changes smaller than ~0.1-0.2% of the metric with no monotonic improvement trend.
rules.action: Abandon the current lever and move to a structurally different approach (new features, new model architecture, different ensemble strategy). Do not keep micro-tuning within the same narrow parameter range. Limit fine-grained sweeps of secondary parameters to 3-5 submissions before pivoting. Lock the parameter at the best-known value.
rules.exceptions: If the lever was only partially applied or a bug was present, complete the intended modification before abandoning (55591012:e14#2).

rules.name: ensemble_member_ablation_and_toggling
rules.context: You have a multi-component ensemble (3-5 members) and want to determine which members contribute positively to the score.
rules.action: Toggle one ensemble member at a time (add or remove), submit, and compare to baseline. If removing a member causes a clear regression, immediately re-enable it before testing other changes. Lock in members that consistently improve score when included. Test each candidate group independently before combining groups. Start with the strongest 2-3 members and only add weaker ones if verified by submission.
rules.exceptions: Weak members may still help if they provide diversity (50496431:e51#1 counter_evidence: v200 best score included all 5 members including weak ones at low weight).

rules.name: checkpoint_swap_sequential_testing
rules.context: Multiple pre-trained checkpoints are available from different training runs, epochs, or hyperparameter settings, and inference is cheap relative to training.
rules.action: Swap checkpoints one at a time in the inference pipeline, submit each, and track LB scores. If a checkpoint scores worse, move on immediately. Keep the best-scoring checkpoint. If after 5-6 tries none beats the current best and CV-to-LB correlation appears weak, stop the sweep and change approach rather than exhaustively testing all checkpoints.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: blend_weight_narrow_perturbation
rules.context: You have just achieved a new best score with a particular blend weight configuration and want to explore nearby values. The blend weight is a single continuous parameter.
rules.action: Test 2-4 perturbations around the current best weights in steps of 0.05-0.15. If the first perturbation worsens, try the opposite direction. If no improvement is found within 3-4 trials, stop and accept the current weight as near-optimal. Do not continue fine-grained sweeps beyond this budget.
rules.exceptions: When the upstream model or features have changed, the optimal blend weight may shift significantly, warranting a wider sweep.

rules.name: catastrophic_regression_check_for_bug
rules.context: A small, identifiable change causes a disproportionately large score regression (e.g., score jumps by >10% relative).
rules.action: Before abandoning the idea, check whether the change has a sign/logic error (e.g., == vs !=, include vs exclude, wrong path). Fix the suspected bug and resubmit. If the corrected version still underperforms, then remove the change entirely and revert to baseline.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: isolate_regression_cause_by_sequential_revert
rules.context: A bundle of changes (e.g., data change + architecture change, or window size + ensemble composition + blending method) caused a score regression, and you need to identify which factor hurt.
rules.action: Revert all changes back to the last-known-good configuration. Then re-apply changes one at a time, starting with the most likely beneficial change or reverting factors one at a time starting with the most suspicious. If reverting one factor recovers most of the loss, keep that reversion and test remaining factors individually. Do not re-bundle changes. Do not keep any part of the failed combination unless tested in isolation.
rules.exceptions: 73671444:e5#2 shows a forward-exploration alternative: rather than reverting, add the next planned component and test it solo, which is faster when many untested variants are queued but risks missing that a removed component was valuable.

rules.name: persist_through_noise_if_direction_justified
rules.context: A hyperparameter change causes a small regression that is within the leaderboard noise margin, and you have theoretical or empirical reason to believe the direction is correct (e.g., underfitting evidence).
rules.action: Check whether the change was fully and consistently applied before reverting. Complete the intended modification and submit again rather than immediately abandoning the direction. Only abandon after a clean, complete application still shows regression.
rules.exceptions: If the regression is large (clearly exceeding noise), revert immediately rather than persisting.

rules.name: save_submissions_with_unsubmitted_exploration
rules.context: You are exploring a continuous parameter space and have limited submission budget, with leaderboard feedback as the only reliable evaluation.
rules.action: Use unsubmitted runs (saved versions, local CV, or fast proxy modes) to narrow the search space cheaply. Only submit when you have converged on a promising region or want to verify a candidate. Make a small number of structurally distinct attempts (2-3) rather than fine-grained sweeps on the leaderboard.
rules.exceptions: When no local validation proxy exists and the leaderboard is the only signal, you may need to submit more frequently (27389424:e17#1 counter_evidence: 1-fold proxy was misleading).

rules.name: inline_score_annotation_for_rapid_iteration
rules.context: You are iterating rapidly on ensemble composition or configuration, toggling members frequently across many versions.
rules.action: Add comments next to each ensemble member's code line recording its associated LB score and version number. This creates a local log that survives across versions and helps decide which members to keep or drop without consulting external records.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: isolate_factors_after_combined_improvement
rules.context: When a combined change (multiple factors modified simultaneously) produced an improvement and you want to optimize further.
rules.action: Do not modify multiple factors again in the next iteration. Isolate each factor: test removing/changing one factor at a time while holding others constant. This prevents uninterpretable regressions. Accept some confounding only when submission budget is very tight, and if the combined result improves, lock it in and move on.
rules.exceptions: 49576186:e15#3 notes that when budget is limited, accepting confounding to maintain iteration speed is pragmatic—lock in combined improvements and only isolate on regression.

rules.name: switch_from_weight_tuning_to_diversity
rules.context: When reweighting a fixed set of ensemble components yields no improvement, or when several consecutive attempts to tune preprocessing/weights fail to beat the current best.
rules.action: Stop tuning weights and introduce a new diverse component (different model family, architecture, or checkpoint) to increase ensemble diversity. Only resume weight tuning after the new component is validated. Diminishing returns on weight sweeps signal that the current model set's capacity is saturated.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: revert_large_regression_immediately
rules.context: When a single change causes a leaderboard regression more than 5x the magnitude of recent incremental gains, or a regression much larger than typical noise.
rules.action: Treat it as a real signal and immediately revert. Do not submit intermediate recovery attempts until the full pipeline is restored to the last-known-good state. If there is a sibling parameter (e.g., L1 vs L2), try it once after reverting. If that also fails, abandon the entire lever.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: ensemble_member_ablation_search
rules.context: When you have a small pool of candidate ensemble components (3-7 members) and want to find the best subset composition.
rules.action: Establish a strong core pair from prior experiments. Then systematically add/remove one member at a time around that core. For each candidate, test its standalone quality first, then test the full set, then prune by dropping one member at a time. Compare each result to the previous best. Stop when removing or swapping any single member no longer improves the score.
rules.exceptions: 77347591:e7#1 found that no combination beat equal weights after ~5 trials, suggesting equal-weight baselines can be near-optimal for small ensembles.

rules.name: fix_config_before_blaming_variable
rules.context: When a configuration change (e.g., model checkpoint swap, model size change) causes a run failure, unexpected output, or no submission.
rules.action: Check whether the failure is due to infrastructure issues (mismatched paths, partial config updates, argument errors) rather than the experimental variable itself. Audit all related config fields for consistency (pretrained path, checkpoint path, tokenizer path). Fix infrastructure, then submit. Do not count the failed run as evidence against the variable.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: hp_tuning_before_feature_engineering_budget
rules.context: When HP tuning yields small incremental gains on a simple feature set and the gap to top scores is large, suggesting feature engineering has more headroom.
rules.action: Spend at most 2-3 submissions on hyperparameter tuning to capture easy gains, then switch to feature engineering. Resume HP tuning only after the feature set is enriched. If each HP step yields diminishing improvements relative to the gap to top scores, that confirms the feature set is the bottleneck.
rules.exceptions: 28093671:e8#2 shows that when each bundled change yields clear improvement, escalating magnitude (e.g., use all features) is preferable to many small increments.

rules.name: measure_noise_floor_before_tuning
rules.context: When leaderboard scores fluctuate significantly across identical or near-identical re-runs, or when the public test set is very small.
rules.action: Submit the same unchanged code multiple times (5-10) to measure run-to-run variance. Only treat score differences larger than the observed variance as signal. When variance is high, prefer ensembles or averaged submissions over single-model runs, and do not chase improvements smaller than the noise floor.
rules.exceptions: 50376011:e21#1 notes that high variance can occasionally be exploited by cherry-picking favorable runs, though this is unreliable.

rules.name: blend_weight_sweep_stopping
rules.context: When tuning ensemble blend weights and the ensemble has many components with the score near a plateau (improvements < 0.001).
rules.action: Try at most 3-5 weight perturbations after a new best. If two consecutive perturbations in the same direction both regress, stop—the optimum is bracketed. If no combination beats equal weights after ~5 trials, stop and try a different blending approach (e.g., stacking, rank averaging). Do not keep pushing weights in a losing direction.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: avoid_inference_time_feature_mismatch
rules.context: When pretrained model weights are frozen and you are considering changing feature extraction parameters (e.g., spectrogram settings, preprocessing) at inference time that differ from training.
rules.action: Avoid changing feature-extraction parameters at inference if the model was trained with different settings—the distribution shift almost always hurts. If you must explore this, make one small change at a time and revert immediately if the score regresses. Do not chain multiple preprocessing changes without reverting between them.
rules.exceptions: 50496431:e51#2 notes some changes may be net-neutral when combined with ensemble reweighting.

rules.name: isolate_one_change_per_submission
rules.context: When you have multiple candidate changes (e.g., blend weight + model version, preprocessing + checkpoint, discrete configuration options) and limited submission budget.
rules.action: Change only one lever per submission to enable attribution. If a change regresses, revert it before trying the next option. If a combined change regresses, you cannot tell which component caused it and must spend additional submissions to disentangle. If all options score below baseline after a full sweep, abandon the lever entirely. If you must bundle changes, first test each independently offline/locally. When a regression is so clear that one factor is obviously the culprit, it is acceptable to revert it while simultaneously testing the next option.
rules.exceptions: 7018718:e4#1 notes the author violated one-at-a-time when the model subset regression was so clear, combining revert with a new test. Acceptable to bundle changes when you have strong offline CV evidence for one component and are using the submission to validate the combination.

rules.name: bracket_then_stop_parameter_tuning
rules.context: When a 3-point bracket (current value, one step higher, one step lower) confirms the current parameter value is a local optimum — both directions regress or fail to improve. Also applies when verifying an ensemble size (repeat count or member count) is still optimal after a major pipeline change.
rules.action: Test one step above and one step below the current value. If both are worse on LB or validation, accept the current value and pivot to a qualitatively different lever (e.g., new features, different model, architecture change). Do not submit runs that validation already shows are inferior. Do not continue refining the same parameter with smaller steps unless score differences are very small relative to leaderboard noise. This brackets the optimum in 2-3 runs.
rules.exceptions: If the search was very narrow (only one direction tried), a broader sweep might still find improvements.

rules.name: revert_then_smaller_step
rules.context: When a single-variable parameter change in one direction caused a significant score regression.
rules.action: Revert to the previous best value first, then try a smaller step in the same direction. If the smaller step also fails to improve, abandon that direction and accept the original value. Do not try a larger step in the same direction after a regression.
rules.exceptions: 27799930:e9#1 shows that for feature selection, revising the drop list (not just reducing it) can help—the issue may be which items are changed, not just the step size.

rules.name: stop_sweep_after_three_failures
rules.context: When 3+ submitted attempts exploring the same lever (e.g., checkpoint variants, hyperparameter direction, backbone swaps) all fail to beat the current best score.
rules.action: Stop the sweep on that lever and pivot to a qualitatively different approach (e.g., new model family, different feature set, ensemble blending strategy). Preserve the best-scoring configuration as a component for future ensembles rather than discarding it.
rules.exceptions: If the leaderboard is extremely noisy (e.g., ~7 evaluation rows as in CommonLit), regressions may be noise rather than true signal, so consider local CV before abandoning.

rules.name: revert_multi_change_regression_by_restoring_ensemble
rules.context: When multiple changes were bundled in one submission (e.g., ensemble member removal + preprocessing change) and the score regressed significantly.
rules.action: First restore the ensemble members that were removed (highest-impact, most reversible change) to recover baseline performance. Then try smaller modifications one at a time. Revert one change at a time to diagnose which caused the harm.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: reoptimize_blend_weights_after_component_change
rules.context: When a component's predictions change (e.g., TTA added, new checkpoint, calibration applied) in a multi-component blended ensemble.
rules.action: Re-sweep blend weights after any change to a component's predictions. Change 1-2 weights per submission in small steps. If score drops, reverse direction. Stop when consecutive changes yield less than ~0.001 improvement or when 5-7 submissions show convergence.
rules.exceptions: When the public LB has very few evaluation rows, weight-only adjustments may be unreliable signals (18523075:e3#1).

rules.name: sweep_checkpoints_exhaustively_before_ensembling
rules.context: When you have multiple trained checkpoints (from different stages, epochs, or folds) and inference is cheap relative to training.
rules.action: Sweep all candidate checkpoints individually to rank their standalone quality before optimizing ensemble composition. Do not stop early based on one bad result — complete the full sweep when the candidate count is small (≤6). Use the ranking to inform which members to include in the final ensemble.
rules.exceptions: Individual rankings may not perfectly predict ensemble contribution due to diversity effects (50376011:e34#1). Best single model may be worse than best ensemble.

rules.name: test_new_model_solo_before_blending
rules.context: When a new model group or variant is available and you want to assess whether it should join an existing ensemble.
rules.action: First test the new model alone (or as a simple mean of its folds) to gauge standalone quality. If it underperforms the existing ensemble, add it alongside existing members rather than replacing them. If a blend with the new model regresses, isolate the new model solo to determine if it has any value before discarding it.
rules.exceptions: A model weak alone can still improve a blend through diversity; solo testing may underestimate ensemble contribution (73671444:e8#1).

rules.name: single_param_perturbation_after_multi_param_jump
rules.context: When a multi-parameter change yields a new best score and you want to verify which parameters contributed.
rules.action: Test individual parameter reversions one at a time. If reverting a single parameter hurts, keep the original value. If two consecutive single-param changes both regress, the multi-param configuration is likely near a local optimum — stop the sweep and lock in the configuration.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: toggle_component_to_verify_contribution
rules.context: When you have recently achieved a new best score with multiple changes and want to verify whether a specific component (e.g., TTA, postprocessing) contributes positively.
rules.action: Remove the component and submit, then re-add it and submit. If re-adding improves over removal, keep it. Accept that leaderboard noise exists and only trust differences larger than the observed noise floor. If the round-trip (A→B→A) does not reproduce the original score, flag the pipeline as non-deterministic.
rules.exceptions: Non-deterministic pipelines (GPU ops, data loading order) can produce different scores for identical code, undermining single-submission A/B tests (50496431:e23#2).

rules.name: paired_submission_for_binary_postprocessing
rules.context: When a binary postprocessing toggle (e.g., rank conversion, TTA) has inconsistent effects across model variants.
rules.action: For every architectural or model change, submit twice: once with postprocessing on, once off. Compare both to the previous pair. This brackets the true effect of the architecture change independent of postprocessing. If neither variant beats the prior best pair, abandon the architectural direction.
rules.exceptions: Doubles submission cost; only worthwhile when the interaction between model and postprocessing is empirically unpredictable.

rules.name: include_both_variants_when_swap_regresses
rules.context: When replacing component A with component B in an ensemble causes a regression, suggesting A had unique value.
rules.action: Include both A and B in the ensemble instead of choosing one. A regression from swapping suggests the removed component contributed diversity. If the combined ensemble beats both individual variants, keep it; otherwise revert to the better single variant.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: retune_thresholds_after_model_swap
rules.context: When swapping to a different model size or variant causes a score regression, and the pipeline includes post-processing thresholds (rounding, binning) tuned for the old model.
rules.action: Re-tune rounding/binning thresholds on validation data before concluding the new model is worse. If still below baseline after threshold re-tuning, try alternative checkpoints of the same model. If after 2-3 attempts the new model still underperforms, abandon the swap.
rules.exceptions: The regression may be fundamental rather than a threshold mismatch; threshold re-tuning alone may not recover performance (55621328:e12#1).

rules.name: probe_opposite_direction_after_regression
rules.context: When a directional hyperparameter change (e.g., lowering learning rate) causes a leaderboard regression, and the optimal direction is unknown.
rules.action: Explore the opposite direction with a large step to establish bounds (overshoot deliberately). Use fast local validation for exploratory runs. Once both directions have been probed, narrow in on the best region and submit only the refined candidate. This brackets the optimum with minimal LB submissions.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: sweep_full_range_under_noisy_lb
rules.context: When leaderboard scores are noisy (high variance between submissions) and you need to find the best value of a single scalar hyperparameter.
rules.action: Sweep the full plausible range at a fixed step size rather than greedily hill-climbing, because noisy feedback can mislead greedy search. After the sweep, return to the best-performing value and re-confirm it with a fresh submission. Hold all other parameters fixed during the sweep to avoid confounding.
rules.exceptions: The author in 55987255 confounded the signal by changing n_estimators simultaneously with blend weight.

rules.name: stop_weight_tuning_switch_to_new_lever
rules.context: When successive single-variable changes to blend weights yield improvements smaller than the noise floor or competition metric granularity (e.g., <0.001 or <0.0001 on AUC), start oscillating around the current best, or plateau after the first one or two adjustments.
rules.action: After a large improvement from adding a new component, make at most 2-3 single-variable tweaks. If improvements are sub-threshold and a regression appears, stop tuning weights and switch to a qualitatively different lever (e.g., new model, stacking method, post-processing, improving individual model quality). Do not invest more than ~8 trials on micro-weight tuning if gains plateau. Pruning weak members is less valuable than adding strong new ones when the ensemble is small.
rules.exceptions: 50376011:e43#2 notes the author continued iterating through very small gains (0.00019), suggesting practitioners sometimes violate this rule in practice.

rules.name: ablate_before_full_revert
rules.context: When adding a new component to an ensemble causes a small regression, and you suspect an existing component (not the new one) is the problem.
rules.action: Before reverting entirely, try removing the suspected weak component while keeping the new addition. If this second variant also regresses, accept that the original configuration was better and stop. Do not spend more than one additional submission on the ablation.
rules.exceptions: A faster strategy may be to revert immediately if the regression is large; ablation is only worthwhile for small regressions where the new component might still help.

rules.name: isolate_changes_after_regression
rules.context: A submission that bundled multiple changes (e.g., new checkpoints + weight changes, scaler + solver, model swap + post-processing) produced a score regression, making it unclear which change caused the drop.
rules.action: Revert to the previous best, then re-apply changes one at a time with a separate submission for each. Identify which single change caused the regression before combining changes again. Do not persist with bundled changes when the cause of regression is ambiguous.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: resubmit_identical_to_estimate_noise
rules.context: The difference between two configurations is small (e.g., <0.01) relative to observed run-to-run variance on the leaderboard, or you need to confirm a large score jump is real and not a fluke.
rules.action: Submit the same unchanged notebook 2+ times to estimate leaderboard noise. Compare configurations using median or best-of-N scores rather than single submissions. Only declare a winner when the gap exceeds the observed noise range. If scores diverge by more than ~0.005 across identical runs, treat small differences as unreliable.
rules.exceptions: Consumes submission slots; impractical when daily submission limits are tight.

rules.name: test_new_checkpoints_individually_before_blending
rules.context: New model checkpoints or checkpoint sets are available and you want to incorporate them into an existing ensemble.
rules.action: Test each new checkpoint set individually first (standalone or as a direct swap) to gauge its quality. Discard sets that cause large regressions. Only then combine top-performing sets into the ensemble. If the combined result doesn't beat the individual best or the prior baseline, revert.
rules.exceptions: 50376011:e39#2 — single-model scores were much worse than the ensemble, yet the author still included them, suggesting the diagnostic is about detecting degenerate checkpoints rather than strict gatekeeping.

rules.name: stop_weight_sweep_when_uninformative
rules.context: Multiple blend-weight configurations produce identical or near-identical leaderboard scores (e.g., due to a very small public test set), or the first blend attempt regresses and no local CV is available to guide further tuning.
rules.action: Stop tuning blend weights after 2-3 uninformative submissions. Instead, add a genuinely different model family to the ensemble or change the underlying models/checkpoints. Weight tuning on an uninformative leaderboard or without local CV is unlikely to yield measurable gains.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: verify_pipeline_before_tuning_after_refactor
rules.context: After a major code refactor, cleanup, or addition of a new model to the pipeline, you need to confirm the prediction logic is correct before exploring further changes.
rules.action: Submit with the exact same weights and model set as your previous best to verify the refactored pipeline reproduces the prior score (within noise). If it doesn't match, debug the pipeline before exploring. Also verify all model predictions are actually being aggregated in the final output — a dramatic regression after adding a model usually means only the new (weaker) model's predictions are being submitted.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: stop_adding_ensemble_members_after_repeated_degradation
rules.context: You have a working ensemble and are testing whether adding more members improves it, but 2-3 consecutive additions each degrade the score.
rules.action: Stop adding members and keep the original ensemble set. If the new members might be strong on their own, test them as a standalone ensemble. Consider down-weighting the new group before removing entirely. Do not persist with equal-weight blending when additions consistently regress.
rules.exceptions: 50376011:e7#1 — models 5-8 alone scored better than models 0-3, so the issue was blending incompatibility rather than weak models.

rules.name: reverse_direction_on_regression_with_halved_step
rules.context: A single-parameter sweep on the leaderboard shows a clear score drop after changing a hyperparameter or blend weight in one direction, and the drop is larger than typical noise.
rules.action: Immediately reverse direction and try a value between the current best and the failed attempt, halving the step size. Do not explore further in the regressing direction unless you have strong theoretical justification (e.g., reducing overfitting). If a theoretically motivated small regression occurs, consider one more step in the same direction before reverting—if that also regresses, revert both changes. If two consecutive reversals fail to beat the best, stop the sweep and keep the best value found. When removing a beneficial transform causes regression, restore it immediately and treat it as fixed for subsequent tuning.
rules.exceptions: 55591012:e5#2 — the author continued probing intermediate values beyond two reversals, spending extra submissions on marginal exploration. 27825577:e1#2 suggests continuing past small regressions when theoretically motivated, so the immediate-reversal rule applies mainly when the drop is clearly above noise or lacks theoretical backing.

rules.name: weight_models_by_individual_performance
rules.context: You have 3+ models with known individual scores (CV or LB) and need a starting point for blend weights.
rules.action: Allocate more weight to models with higher individual CV or LB scores as a starting point. One approach: compute weights as (1 - individual_score) for lower-is-better metrics, then normalize. Start with equal averaging as a baseline, then try performance-weighted averaging. Adjust from there by changing one or two weights per submission.
rules.exceptions: 15164527:e4#1 — fold-averaged multi-head predictions got high weight despite unknown CV, suggesting CV alone doesn't determine optimal weights.

rules.name: continue_search_after_large_gain
rules.context: A structural change (e.g., adding/removing ensemble members, swapping checkpoints) produced a large improvement relative to recent gains, suggesting the current lever is highly productive.
rules.action: Make one or two small perturbations in the same direction (e.g., swapping a single member, slight weight adjustment) to check for further improvement. If the marginal gain drops to near-zero after 1-2 attempts, stop and move on to a different lever rather than exhaustively searching all combinations.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: use_local_cv_before_submitting_ablations
rules.context: You want to test whether a sub-component of your ensemble or a parameter sweep direction is viable, but leaderboard submissions are limited.
rules.action: Check local validation or notebook output before spending a leaderboard submission. Make multiple monotonic changes guided by local CV without submitting, and submit only after the sweep stabilizes. If the submitted LB score contradicts the CV trend, suspect CV-LB distribution mismatch rather than continuing the sweep.
rules.exceptions: 55987255:e27#2 — the batched local-CV-guided sweep led to a suboptimal submission because the CV signal was misleading.

rules.name: retrain_meta_learner_when_changing_base_models
rules.context: You have a stacked ensemble where a meta-learner (e.g., ridge regression) was trained on a specific set of base model outputs, and you want to add or remove base models at inference time.
rules.action: Retrain the meta-learner on the expanded or reduced feature set before submitting. If you must use a pre-trained meta-learner, feed it exactly the features it was trained on. Submitting with mismatched inputs will regress even if the new base models are individually strong. If some folds/members hurt, build a separate meta-learner for them rather than toggling them on and off.
rules.exceptions: Both items are from the same kernel (17616127) but from different episodes with different configurations; the principle is consistent across both.

rules.name: prefer_ensemble_over_single_model_under_noisy_lb
rules.context: The public leaderboard has very few test samples or high evaluation variance (e.g., from test-time augmentation or random preprocessing), making individual submission scores unreliable.
rules.action: Prefer ensembling your best checkpoints/models over selecting a single one based on LB scores. A weighted average of diverse models is more robust to LB noise. When gains between versions are smaller than observed run-to-run variance, make structural changes (e.g., switching to optimized weights, adding diverse members) rather than fine-tuning individual model inclusion.
rules.exceptions: 17616127:e1#1 notes the author abandoned their best ensemble to search single checkpoints, possibly to understand individual model quality before re-ensembling.

rules.name: retest_toggle_across_configurations
rules.context: A binary postprocessing toggle or cheap configuration option may interact with other hyperparameters (model architecture, resolution, fold count), and you have changed the base configuration since last testing it.
rules.action: Re-test the toggle each time you change the base configuration. Toggle it on and off in consecutive submissions to isolate its marginal effect under the current setup. Do not assume a result from one configuration transfers. If consistently neutral or negative across multiple configurations, deprioritize it.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: remove_correlated_ensemble_member_over_downweighting
rules.context: Adding a new ensemble member from the same model family (same architecture, different training stage or checkpoint) worsens the ensemble score.
rules.action: Remove the weaker member entirely rather than trying to down-weight it. Correlated members from the same architecture rarely help even at low weight. After removing, re-optimize the remaining blend weights since optimal ratios shift when membership changes.
rules.exceptions: 53762022:e1#2 notes the improvement from removal conflated member removal and weight shift, so individual contributions are uncertain.

rules.name: stop_weight_tuning_switch_to_diversity
rules.context: Blend-weight tuning across existing ensemble members has plateaued (diminishing returns, regressions, or 3-4 failed attempts) and the current set of component models has been fixed for several iterations, with component predictions likely correlated.
rules.action: Stop tuning blend weights. Instead, invest effort in adding a new, architecturally diverse model component (new architectures, retrieval-based features, more folds) to expand ensemble diversity. If a weak but diverse component is available, blend it at moderate weight (30-40%) first to confirm improvement. Resume weight optimization only after the new component is integrated and restart weight tuning with the expanded set.
rules.exceptions: 18423958:e4#2 notes that subsequent new-model experiments performed worse, suggesting sometimes continued weight tuning may be more productive than exploring weak new models. If the new model is weaker than existing members, it may hurt the ensemble (50496431:e56#1: stripped ensemble sometimes beat the full one).

rules.name: isolate_changes_on_regression
rules.context: A submission that bundled multiple changes simultaneously (e.g., new checkpoint + new transforms, hyperparameters, features, post-processing, model swap + preprocessing change) caused a score regression, making it impossible to attribute the cause.
rules.action: Revert the most speculative/auxiliary changes first (e.g., novel post-processing, hyperparameter tweaks) while keeping the primary structural change being tested. Submit the simpler variant to isolate the primary change's effect. If the score still doesn't improve, the primary change itself is the problem; if it does improve, the reverted auxiliary change was harmful. Only after confirming the feature's value, layer on hyperparameter tuning one change at a time. Do not try entirely new combinations on top of the failed bundle.
rules.exceptions: 60197293:e18#3 notes the final best score itself combined multiple changes, so strict one-at-a-time is not always necessary once individual components have shown positive signal. 52551258:e4#2 argues against immediate full revert: if you suspect a preprocessing mismatch, try fixing the mismatch first rather than discarding the whole direction. This is risky when submission budget is limited.

rules.name: batch_changes_submit_selectively
rules.context: When each leaderboard submission is costly (limited daily quota or noisy public LB) and you are iterating on hyperparameters or ensemble configurations.
rules.action: Make multiple incremental code changes without submitting, reserving submissions for configurations that represent qualitatively different hypotheses or show CV improvement. Use non-submitted versions for code setup, debugging, and infrastructure. Submit at most every other configuration, and only after the pipeline is stable and the sweep is complete.
rules.exceptions: 55987255:e22#2 notes that withholding submissions for many versions may indicate being blocked by bugs rather than deliberate strategy.

rules.name: sweep_then_stop_on_flat_response
rules.context: When sweeping a one-dimensional preprocessing parameter (e.g., fraction of features kept) and the response surface is flat or noisy across a wide range of values.
rules.action: Sweep upward in roughly doubling steps (e.g., 10%→20%→25%→33%→50%→75%), submitting every 1-2 steps. When the score drops after an increase, the optimum is bracketed. If the gain across the range is small, remove the preprocessing step entirely and rely on the model's native regularization (e.g., feature_fraction, bagging_fraction) instead of bisecting further.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: submit_partial_configs_after_long_dev
rules.context: After a long development/debugging phase (10+ versions) building a complex new feature pipeline without beating the previous best score.
rules.action: Submit partial configurations with systematic toggling (feature on/off, selection on/off) across 3-5 submissions to identify which components contribute before combining everything. The final combination should include only components that showed positive signal individually or in small groups.
rules.exceptions: 55987255:e22#2 had no submissions at all during the phase, suggesting this rule is aspirational; in practice bug-fixing may dominate.

rules.name: resweep_after_metric_change
rules.context: When the training loss function, evaluation metric, or training API has been changed mid-experiment, and previously tuned hyperparameters were optimized under the old setup.
rules.action: Restart sweeps of key hyperparameters (especially those interacting with the metric, like feature selection thresholds or class weights) from the beginning of the search range rather than continuing from the last value. Use the same step schedule as the original sweep.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: stop_sweep_after_consecutive_regressions
rules.context: 3-4 consecutive submissions tuning the same lever (e.g., augmentation, hyperparameters, preprocessing, checkpoint variants) all score below the established best, with no improving trend.
rules.action: Stop the sweep on that lever. Revert to the last-known-best configuration and switch to a qualitatively different lever (e.g., architecture, loss function, ensembling, new model family). Do not continue making small perturbations to the same set of parameters.
rules.exceptions: If scores are trending upward within the sweep (58130512:e37#3: 0.81999→0.82240), one more attempt may be warranted. Some authors use a threshold of 4-5 rather than 3 (13542132:e3#1: continued one extra step).

rules.name: one_variable_at_a_time
rules.context: You are tuning hyperparameters or configuration knobs near a plateau and need to attribute gains or losses to specific changes.
rules.action: Change only one knob per submission so you can attribute the result. If you changed multiple knobs simultaneously and regressed, revert to the last-known-good configuration, then vary only one parameter per subsequent submission. Avoid confounded results that waste submissions.
rules.exceptions: When two settings are inherently coupled (e.g., feature-selection file must match the model ensemble), they must be changed together (58130512:e37#1). Authors frequently violate this rule in practice (58130512:e30#1, 55621328:e17#2).

rules.name: revert_before_exploring_after_regression
rules.context: A configuration change caused a score regression and you want to continue experimenting.
rules.action: Revert to the last-known-best configuration before trying the next experiment. Do not layer new changes on top of a regressed configuration. This ensures each new experiment is compared against a clean baseline rather than compounding unknown degradations.
rules.exceptions: When you suspect the regression is from a preprocessing/pipeline mismatch rather than the core change, try fixing the suspected mismatch before reverting entirely (52551258:e4#2).

rules.name: prefer_fixed_weights_on_noisy_lb
rules.context: The public leaderboard is very small (e.g., ~7 rows) or very noisy, and you are choosing between fixed blend weights and data-adaptive conditional blending logic.
rules.action: Use fixed blend weights rather than data-adaptive conditional logic. If a conditional strategy does not clearly beat the simple fixed-weight version, revert to fixed weights immediately. On tiny leaderboards, trust local CV over LB for ranking individual models and limit LB-only probes to 2-3 before pivoting.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: isolate_component_before_tuning_in_ensemble
rules.context: You are sweeping checkpoints or variants of one model component within a multi-model blend, and the blend weights are not yet finalized.
rules.action: Temporarily remove blending and submit only the component being optimized to get a cleaner signal for checkpoint/variant selection. Re-introduce blending after identifying the best component version. This avoids noise from blend interactions masking the component's true quality.
rules.exceptions: If the component is too weak to score well alone, this approach may not give useful signal. The full cycle (isolate → select → re-blend) was not always completed in practice.

rules.name: bracket_continuous_hp_with_bisection
rules.context: You are sweeping a continuous hyperparameter (e.g., regularization, blend weight) near a plateau, and large steps cause regressions while moderate steps yield small gains.
rules.action: Start with coarse steps to identify the direction of improvement. When a step causes regression, reverse direction and halve the step size. When two consecutive submissions differ by less than noise, declare the optimum bracketed and stop sweeping that parameter. Move to a qualitatively different lever.
rules.exceptions: 18426209:e7#1 counter-evidence: the author did not revert to the known-best after regression, instead trying a different blend, which deviates from strict bisection.

rules.name: treat_lever_as_exhausted_in_noise_band
rules.context: 4-5 consecutive submissions tuning the same lever all land within a narrow band (~0.002 or less) around the previous best score, with no clear trend.
rules.action: Treat the lever as exhausted. Revert to the best-scoring configuration within the band and switch to a qualitatively different lever (e.g., adding new models, changing features, blending external predictions). Do not continue fine-grained sweeps within the noise band.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: repeated_submissions_for_variance_estimation
rules.context: Leaderboard scores fluctuate significantly across identical or near-identical submissions (run-to-run variance comparable to or larger than expected improvement from configuration changes).
rules.action: Submit the same code 3-5+ times to estimate the variance of the public LB score. Use the distribution (median, range) rather than any single score to judge configurations. Only accept a configuration change as beneficial if its improvement exceeds the observed variance band.
rules.exceptions: This strategy is expensive in submission budget and only worthwhile when variance is high relative to signal. It would be wasteful if scores are deterministic.

rules.name: validate_new_component_locally_before_submitting
rules.context: You are integrating a new model, feature source, or pipeline component that requires code changes and may introduce bugs.
rules.action: First run locally (or in a non-submitted notebook run) to verify the component loads correctly, doesn't break the pipeline, and produces reasonable CV scores. Only submit after confirming CV is reasonable. If the new component doesn't help on CV, revert it before spending a submission.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: fix_data_pipeline_bugs_before_weight_tuning
rules.context: A model that should be strong based on standalone performance is performing poorly within an ensemble, and you suspect a data/preprocessing mismatch (e.g., shape mismatch, wrong normalization).
rules.action: Inspect the data pipeline for shape mismatches, preprocessing inconsistencies, or dead code before continuing the weight search. Fix the bug, then re-run the best-known ensemble configuration to get a clean baseline before further tuning.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: ensemble_weight_tuning_start_equal_then_shift
rules.context: You have a small number of ensemble members (≤5) and want to find good blend weights, with each submission being cheap (inference-only).
rules.action: Start with equal weights, then submit one or two unequal-weight variants that favor the model you believe is strongest. Use each LB result to decide which model deserves more weight. Change only the weights per step. Stop after 2-3 submissions once improvements shrink below ~0.001. If shifting weight toward one model worsens the score, do not continue in that direction.
rules.exceptions: 77347591:e5#3 notes that scaling all weights by a constant has no effect on normalized weighted average—only ratios matter.
